**Summary.** This paper rigorously analyzes the relaxation time of the triangular plaquette model using advanced mathematical tools from combinatorics and Markov process theory. It derives super-Arrhenius scaling laws for this relaxation time, demonstrating how kinetic constraints lead to complex, non-trivial dynamical behavior even in the absence of explicit quantum interactions.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the study of slow relaxation times (glassy behavior) in lattice models is highly relevant to understanding quantum dynamics in disordered or frustrated quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper analyzes the super-Arrhenius relaxation time of a specific statistical physics model, the triangular plaquette model, in arbitrary dimensions.

**Main result.** It establishes precise scaling laws for the relaxation time ($T_{	ext{rel}}$) at high inverse temperatures ($eta$), showing both exponential and much larger polynomial/exponential divergences depending on boundary conditions.

**Method.** The proofs combine advanced techniques from extremal combinatorics, renormalization group ideas applied to dynamics (Ledrappier subshift), and path coupling methods for Markov processes.

**Model / system.** The system is the triangular plaquette model defined on a lattice ($\mathbb{Z}^d$), whose energy Hamiltonian relates to local excitations (plaquettes). The dynamics are governed by Glauber dynamics associated with the Gibbs measure $\mu_	au^\Lambda(\sigma) \propto e^{-eta H}$.

**Key observables.** Relaxation time ($T_{	ext{rel}}$), uniqueness of the infinite volume Gibbs measure ($\mu$), and the scaling behavior of these quantities.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Inverse temperature ($eta > 0$), lattice dimension ($d \ge 2$), and finite domain size ($n$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on establishing structural properties of 'good chains' and admissible sets via combinatorial lemmas, and uses path coupling arguments for upper bounds.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the configuration on the triangular lattice (plaquette model) and show canonical paths used in bounding the relaxation time through coupling constructions.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by defining the dynamics and relaxation time using Dirichlet forms, deriving combinatorial tools related to plaquettes and chains, establishing lower bounds via these combinatorial bottlenecks, and finally proving upper bounds using path coupling techniques on tori.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Consider the following plaquette model from statistical physics: a lamp lies at every vertex of the triangular lattice and a switch lies at every even vertex of the (bipartite) dual hexagonal lattice. Each switch toggles the three lamps on its face. The energy of a configuration is the number of ON lamps.   For the Glauber dynamics associated with the Gibbs measure defined by this Hamiltonian at any inverse temperature $β>0$, we show that, in any dimension $d\ge 2$, the infinite volume relaxation time satisfies \[e^{β^2/C}/C \le T_{\mathrm{rel}}\le Ce^{e^{Cβ}}\] for some $C>0$. Our result entails that the Gibbs measure is unique. The $e^{β^2}$ scaling was conjectured by Newman and Moore in 1999 and matches the behaviour of supercritical rooted kinetically constrained models such as the East model, thus recovering fragile glass phenomenology in the absence of kinetic constraints. More precisely, we show that, on a torus of side length $2^k$, when $β\to\infty$ and $k/β\to0$, we have $T_{\mathrm{rel}}=e^{2βk(1+o(1))}$. Quite surprisingly, however, we also prove that, on non-periodic finite domains of size $n\le e^{β/C}$ for large $C>0$, we have the much larger asymptotics $\ln T_{\mathrm{rel}}=βn^{Θ(1)}$.   The main ingredients of the proofs are new results in extremal and enumerative combinatorics and rely on renormalisation ideas for the dynamics and its groundstates also known as the Ledrappier subshift. We note consequences of our results to geometric group theory (more precisely to the complexity of the word problem for the Baumslag finitely presented group) and to ergodic theory.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a theoretical framework to adapt model selection techniques for complex statistical models operating under finite resources. It replaces equilibrium free energy calculations with a finite-time analogue by incorporating the dynamics of learning processes into singularity theory. This provides a new, resource-aware measure of model complexity relevant for time-bounded inference.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on ML inference, the methodology of deriving complexity measures from dynamical processes and resource limitations has parallels in non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics, particularly when analyzing relaxation or measurement protocols that are inherently time-limited.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper extends model selection criteria, traditionally derived from equilibrium statistical mechanics (like WAIC/WBIC), to the regime of finite-time, resource-constrained learning dynamics.

**Main result.** It formulates a finite-time analogue of Watanabe's BIC ($WBIC_R$), which replaces equilibrium complexity measures with a resource-dependent real log canonical threshold ($\lambda_R$).

**Method.** The authors adapt singular learning theory by modeling the learning process as a stochastic path governed by a transition kernel, allowing for the calculation of an effective free energy based on this finite-time ensemble.

**Model / system.** The model is statistical inference applied to machine learning, specifically addressing parameter estimation in singular models (like deep neural networks). The dynamics are approximated using processes like Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) under a resource constraint $R$.

**Key observables.** Finite-time free energy ($WBIC_R$), Resource-dependent Real Log Canonical Threshold ($\lambda_R$), and the structural information measure called epiplexity.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Resource constraint ($R$), Time horizon ($T$), Inverse temperature $eta^* = 1/\ln N$, and the effective loss function $L_R(	heta)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation assumes that the endpoint density of the learning process can be locally represented by an analytic effective potential, which is crucial for applying singular theory.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the failure of classical criteria in singular models. It then develops the non-equilibrium extension by replacing equilibrium posteriors with ensembles generated by learning dynamics under resource constraints. The core mathematical machinery involves adapting singularity theory to this finite-time, path-dependent setting.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Information criteria such as WAIC and WBIC extend model selection to singular learning machines, but they are usually derived for equilibrium posteriors. We formulate a finite-time analogue of WBIC by replacing the equilibrium posterior with an effective ensemble generated by learning dynamics under a resource constraint. When this ensemble admits an analytic effective potential, singular learning theory yields a resource-dependent real log canonical threshold. The resulting estimator gives a computable thermodynamic contribution to time-bounded MDL and identifies the finite-time singular complexity relevant to the structural information measured by epiplexity.

</details>

**Summary.** This work optimizes the measurement resources required for Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) in quantum systems. It shows that assuming structural knowledge about noise channels allows for significantly tighter, and thus more efficient, resource bounds than worst-case analyses suggest. The methodology involves advanced constrained optimization over error and confidence budgets.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on quantum estimation theory rather than direct AMO Hamiltonian simulation, the rigorous resource bounding techniques and the explicit handling of structured noise are highly relevant for designing practical quantum measurements in experimental platforms like trapped ions or cavity QED systems where noise characterization is key.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses optimizing resource bounds for Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE), a technique used to estimate quantum state fidelity without full tomography.

**Main result.** By incorporating structural information about noise channels, the required number of measurements can be significantly reduced compared to worst-case theoretical bounds. Furthermore, optimal allocation of error and confidence budgets between sampling and estimation steps improves resource efficiency.

**Method.** The authors reformulate the analysis into a constrained optimization problem involving separate error ($\epsilon$) and confidence ($\delta$) parameters for the two probabilistic stages of DFE. They compare symmetric vs. optimized budget splitting.

**Model / system.** The system involves estimating the fidelity $F(ho, \sigma)$ between an experimentally prepared state $\sigma$ and a target pure state $ho$ in an N-qubit quantum system. The analysis considers general states and specialized stabilizer states under structured noise assumptions.

**Key observables.** Fidelity ($F$), total estimation error ($E$), confidence level ($\Delta$), and the required number of measurements ($m$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Noise parameter $p$ (for structured noise), qubit number $N$, accuracy $\epsilon$, and confidence $\delta$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a two-stage probabilistic estimation process. A key limitation noted is that the derived theoretical bounds might be overly conservative compared to actual experimental fluctuations.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare upper bounds on measurements ($E(m)$) for general vs. stabilizer states under structured noise assumptions, and show histograms comparing different protocols' performance.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces DFE, details the two-step probabilistic error control, develops the constrained optimization framework to optimally allocate accuracy/confidence budgets, and demonstrates savings using structured noise models.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Direct fidelity estimation provides a way to estimate the fidelity between an experimentally prepared state and a desired pure target state without performing full tomography. Two influential formulations were introduced in 2011 by Flammia and Liu and by da Silva, Landon-Cardinal, and Poulin. In these protocols, the total estimation error is controlled through two distinct probabilistic steps: first, the fidelity is approximated using randomly sampled Pauli observables; second, each sampled expectation value is estimated from finitely many measurement outcomes. In this work we show that additional structural information about the noise can substantially sharpen the corresponding resource bounds. In particular, for some canonical channels the effective number of sampled Pauli settings can be reduced, leading to lower measurement cost both in the general pure-state setting and in the case of a stabilizer state. These results illustrate a broader point: worst-case confidence bounds in direct fidelity estimation can be significantly conservative when experimentally relevant structure is ignored. As a technical ingredient, we also revisit the allocation of the total accuracy and confidence budgets between the two probabilistic steps. Reformulating the analysis in terms of separate error parameters yields a constrained optimization problem whose solution lowers the average number of measurements in the general pure-state setting. Numerical simulations based on quantum circuits implemented in Qiskit illustrate both the improvement obtained under structured-noise assumptions and the conservativeness of the original worst-case bounds.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes the persistence properties during phase ordering in an Ising model subjected to competing spin-flip and spin-exchange dynamics at zero temperature. While standard measures of persistence retain universal scaling behavior consistent with nonconserved dynamics, the composite measure reveals a strong, non-universal dependence on the competition parameter $p_r$, highlighting distinct physical consequences for different types of memory.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study provides a detailed quantitative comparison of how different microscopic dynamics (conserved vs. nonconserved) affect macroscopic memory effects (persistence), which is crucial for understanding relaxation in complex many-body systems relevant to AMO physics or condensed matter modeling.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how persistence properties change during phase ordering when a system evolves under competing dynamics involving both nonconserved (spin-flip) and conserved (spin-exchange) interactions.

**Main result.** For total and spin-flip persistence, the exponents remain universal and consistent with purely nonconserved dynamics; however, the composite persistence measure shows strong dependence on the relative probability of the competing moves, breaking expected scaling relations.

**Method.** The analysis relies heavily on Monte Carlo simulations at zero temperature to track time evolution and calculate various persistence probabilities and their associated spatial correlation functions.

**Model / system.** The system is a two-dimensional Ising model undergoing phase ordering. The dynamics are mixed, controlled by the probability $p_r$ of executing a nonconserved spin-flip move versus a conserved spin-exchange move.

**Key observables.** Total persistence probability ($P_t(t)$), spin-flip persistence probability ($P_f(t)$), and composite persistence probability ($P_c(t)$); decay exponents ($	heta_i$); fractal dimensions ($d_i^f$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The relative probability $p_r$ controlling the competition between dynamics; zero temperature ($T=0$); spatial dimension $d=2$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that asymptotic power-law decay and dynamic scaling forms can be successfully applied to characterize long-time behavior.

**Figures summary.** Figures show snapshots of domain growth, confirmation of scaling behavior using correlation functions, and double-logarithmic plots demonstrating the collapse of scaled persistence probabilities for different dynamics.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the model and defines three distinct persistence measures. It then analyzes the asymptotic decay and scaling relations for the total and spin-flip measures, finding consistency with known results. Finally, it contrasts this by analyzing the composite measure, demonstrating its unique dependence on $p_r$ and failure to satisfy the established scaling laws.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the persistence properties during phase ordering in the two-dimensional ($d=2$) Ising model evolving under competing nonconserved spin-flip and conserved spin-exchange dynamics by means of Monte Carlo simulations at zero temperature. We examine three distinct persistence probabilities: (i) the total persistence probability, defined as the probability that a lattice site has never experienced a change in the sign of the spin residing there; (ii) the spin-flip persistence probability, which exclusively measures the fraction of sites that have never undergone a spin-flip event; and (iii) the composite persistence probability, defined as the fraction of sites that have experienced neither a spin-flip nor a spin-exchange event. In the asymptotic regime, both the total and spin-flip persistence probabilities exhibit identical power-law decay, irrespective of the relative occurrence probability of the spin-flip move $p_r$. The corresponding persistence exponent $θ_i \approx 0.225$, is found to be consistent with the value reported for systems evolving purely under nonconserved dynamics. We further demonstrate that both persistence measures satisfy the scaling relation $d-d_f^i=θ_i/α_i$, where $d_f^i$ is the fractal dimension of the corresponding persistence lattice and $α_i\approx 1/2$ characterizes the asymptotic power-law growth of spatially correlated regions of non-persistent spins. In contrast, although the composite persistence probability also exhibits asymptotic power-law decay, both the corresponding persistence exponent $θ_{\rm c}$ and the fractal dimension $d_f^{\rm c}$ of the persistence lattice show strong dependence on $p_r$. Combined with the presence of a universal growth exponent $α_{\rm c}\approx 1/2$, this leads to the breakdown of the scaling relation among the characteristic exponents for the composite persistence.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically explores high-temperature superconductivity arising from the coupling between electrons and hyperbolic photon modes found in polar insulators like hBN. By treating the HM interaction within a generalized pairing framework, the authors show that even repulsive interactions can induce unconventional pairing via an energy-space mechanism. The results suggest that $T_c$ can be significantly enhanced, potentially reaching hundreds of Kelvin under favorable material configurations.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete theoretical framework for unconventional superconductivity in hybrid quantum materials, linking topological photonics (HM modes) directly to high-$T_c$ mechanisms typically associated with strong electronic correlations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the possibility of achieving high-temperature superconductivity mediated by coupling between conduction electrons in a metal film and hyperbolic photon modes (HM) present in insulating substrates like hBN.

**Main result.** The HM interaction, despite being repulsive, facilitates unconventional pairing via an energy-space mechanism analogous to Anderson-Morel theory, leading to estimates of very high critical temperatures ($T_c$).

**Method.** The analysis employs Green's function formalism and diagrammatic techniques to calculate the electron self-energy ($\Sigma$) and project the resulting interaction onto the Cooper pairing channel.

**Model / system.** The model considers a 2D Fermi sea (metal) placed on top of hBN, where the coupling is mediated by longitudinal hyperbolic photon modes. The physics differs significantly from standard electron-phonon coupling due to the HM's energy dependence.

**Key observables.** Superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$), quasiparticle renormalization factors ($Z$, $v_1/v_F$), and the effective pairing interaction strength ($\lambda_{	ext{eff}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Dimensionless coupling constant ($\lambda_0$), characteristic HM frequency ($ar{\omega}$), energy cutoff scale ($\Lambda$), and physical separation distance ($z$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on weak coupling approximations, the Anderson-Morel step approximation in frequency space, and various continuum/small parameter limits for mathematical tractability.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate diagrammatic contributions to the effective low-energy pair interaction (e.g., Kohn-Luttinger diagrams) and show how the superconducting gap modifies the density of states over a wide energy window.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from calculating the self-energy correction ($\Sigma'$) due to HM exchange, determining quasiparticle renormalization effects, deriving the effective pairing interaction ($V_{	ext{pair}}$), and finally solving the linearized gap equation to estimate $T_c$.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The hyperbolic mode (HM) refers to a polariton mode in a polar insulator where the dielectric function is negative in some direction of propagation. Within a frequency window the light occupies a greatly expanded region in momentum space. The HM in hexagonal Boron Nitride (hBN) has been under intense study and we consider placing a metal directly on top hBN and ask whether its physical properties can be strongly affected. While the problem resembles superficially the electron phonon coupling problem, there are important differences. Due to the longitudinal nature of the HM mode the coupling is driven by time dependent charge fluctuations which results in a coupling that strongly increases with the energy difference of the initial and final states. We find a significant modification of the wavefunction and velocity renormalization and we identify the dimensionless coupling constant $λ_0$ that controls this effect. The virtual exchange of HM leads to a repulsive interaction. However, due to its strong energy dependence, pairing is possible by a process analogous to the Anderson-Morel mechanism, but in energy space instead of frequency space. We estimate the effective pairing interaction and find that very high $T_c$ is possible, even for small $λ_0$ where the theory is controlled. We provide estimates using realistic parameters.

</details>

**Summary.** This work tackles the mathematically challenging Dirac inverted oscillator, a relativistic system exhibiting non-Hermitian behavior. By proving its pseudo-$\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry and employing a specific transformation, the authors successfully map it onto the well-understood standard Dirac oscillator. This allows for the calculation of its energy spectrum in the non-relativistic limit.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study of pseudo-$\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric Hamiltonians and their connection to solvable models is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems where exact analytical solutions are sought despite non-Hermiticity.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper analyzes the relativistic quantum system known as the Dirac inverted oscillator, which is non-Hermitian but admits an exact analytical solution.

**Main result.** A connection between the non-Hermitian inverted system and the standard Dirac oscillator is established via a non-unitary transformation, allowing for the derivation of its energy spectrum in the non-relativistic limit.

**Method.** The analysis involves deriving coupled differential equations from the modified Dirac equation and solving them using approximations (non-relativistic limit) and mathematical transformations ($ho$ operator).

**Model / system.** The system is governed by a Hamiltonian $H_{rD}$ derived from modifying the standard Dirac Hamiltonian. This leads to an inverted oscillator potential, resulting in pseudo-$\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry.

**Key observables.** Energy eigenvalue $\epsilon_{nlj}$, which depends on quantum numbers $n, l, j$, and is related to harmonic oscillator and spin-orbit coupling terms.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The non-relativistic limit parameter $\epsilon \ll 1$ is crucial for simplifying the governing equation. The characteristic frequency $\omega$ sets the energy scale.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is the validity of the pseudo-$\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry and the use of a non-unitary transformation to map the problem onto a known solvable form.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the inverted Dirac oscillator Hamiltonian, establishes its pseudo-$\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry, derives the governing differential equation, and then proceeds by applying a non-unitary transformation to map it to the standard Dirac oscillator. Finally, it analyzes the non-relativistic limit to obtain the energy spectrum.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Dirac oscillator is obtained from the Dirac Hamiltonian $H^{\mathrm{D}} = \left( c\vecα\cdot \vec{p} + mc^{2}β\right)$ by modifying the momentum through a non-Hermitian substitution $\overrightarrow{p} \rightarrow \overrightarrow{p} \pm iωβ\overrightarrow{q}$. Despite the non-Hermitian nature of this momentum operator, the full Hamiltonian remains Hermitian due to the presence of the Dirac matrix $\vecα$. However, if one instead introduces a Hermitian modification of the form $\vec{p} \rightarrow \vec{p} \pm ωβ\overrightarrow{q}$, the resulting Hamiltonian is no longer Hermitian. In this case, the system corresponds to an inverted Dirac oscillator $H^{\mathrm{r}}$, where the potential becomes unbounded from below, the energy spectrum becomes continuous, and the eigenfunctions fail to be square-integrable, leading to normalization difficulties. We show that the Hamiltonian $H^{\mathrm{r}}$ is a pseudo-$\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric operator, and we introduce an unbounded, non-unitary transformation that establishes a connection between $H^{\mathrm{r}}$ and $H^{\mathrm{D}}$. The purpose of this work is to analyze this relativistic quantum system -- known as the Dirac inverted oscillator -- which, despite its various applications, admits an exact analytical solution

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes linker-mediated colloidal aggregation, showing that its kinetics are not classical but instead exhibit a sharp kinetic critical point. By controlling the linker concentration relative to this critical value, researchers can tune the system between an arrested state and one undergoing self-accelerating coarsening. This work provides a detailed model connecting chemical resource limitations to macroscopic changes in aggregation dynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on colloids, the concept of a kinetic phase transition or bifurcation in reaction rates due to resource depletion (linkers) shares conceptual parallels with non-equilibrium dynamics studied in open quantum systems or complex chemical reactions.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how linker-mediated colloidal aggregation deviates from classical Smoluchowski kinetics due to the dynamic evolution of cluster reactivity during growth.

**Main result.** The system exhibits a kinetic critical point controlled by linker abundance, leading to two distinct regimes: arrested growth below a critical linker concentration and self-accelerating coarsening above it.

**Method.** The research combines theoretical modeling using rate equations with experimental validation employing DNA-linked gold nanoparticles measured via DLS.

**Model / system.** The system involves colloidal particles linked by molecules, modeled by considering the interplay between diffusion and surface reactivity. The kinetics are governed by linker conservation laws leading to a critical point separating different aggregation fates.

**Key observables.** Hydrodynamic radii ($R_h$), cluster mass ($M$), and the existence/location of the kinetic critical point ($C^*_l$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Linker concentration ($C_l$), critical linker concentration ($C^*_l$), and dimensionless time ($	au$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Initial linker adsorption is assumed to be nearly irreversible, and the system is analyzed using mean-field rate equations.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically illustrate the kinetic critical point separating arrested growth (low $C_l$) from unlimited coarsening (high $C_l$), with DLS measurements confirming this separation in $R_h$ distributions over time.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the departure from classical kinetics, derives rate equations incorporating linker depletion, identifies the critical point mathematically, and validates these theoretical predictions using colloidal experiments.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Linker-mediated aggregation plays an important role in modern nanoscience. We demonstrate that it departs sharply from classical Smoluchowski kinetics because cluster reactivity evolves during growth. Combining theory with DNA-linked gold-nanoparticle experiments, we establish kinetic critical point controlled by linker abundance. Below threshold, active linkers are depleted and growth arrests; above threshold, clusters accumulate reactive sites, self-accelerate, and cross over to diffusion-limited coarsening. Experiments verify the predicted arrest, accelerated growth, and scaling collapse.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates the transport of quantum magic—a specific nonstabilizer resource—through spin chains using the XX Hamiltonian. By analyzing three different state-transfer protocols, the authors demonstrate that the initial state geometry dictates transfer efficiency and reveal a mechanism where the spin chain can actively amplify the injected quantum magic. This establishes a new diagnostic tool for assessing quantum channel capabilities beyond standard fidelity measures.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses non-local quantum resource transfer in physical systems like trapped ions or superconducting circuits, providing quantitative metrics (SN) beyond simple fidelity to characterize channel quality. The concept of 'magic amplification' suggests novel ways to process quantum information.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the transport of quantum magic, a nonstabilizer resource, through quantum spin chains, treating it as a distinct problem from standard Perfect State Transfer (PST). It aims to characterize how this resource is preserved and amplified during state transfer.

**Main result.** The geometry of the initial state significantly influences transport quality, showing an asymmetry where lower-hemisphere states transfer better than upper-hemisphere states. Furthermore, the system can act as a magic-amplification channel when the transported magic exceeds the initial encoding.

**Method.** The analysis uses theoretical modeling based on the XX Hamiltonian and quantifies resource transfer using the stabilizer norm (SN) of the reduced density matrix at various sites and times.

**Model / system.** The system is a one-dimensional quantum spin chain governed by an XX Hamiltonian. Three state-transfer protocols are analyzed, interpolating between homogeneous, ballistic, and power-law decaying couplings. The analysis focuses on T-states initialized in the upper or lower Bloch hemisphere.

**Key observables.** Stabilizer Norm (SN) of the reduced density matrix ($	ext{D}(ho)$), Maximum Transferable SN ($D_{	ext{max}}$), and Average Fidelity ($\langle F_j(t) angle$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Interpolation parameter $\alpha$ controlling coupling regimes, initial state geometry (upper vs. lower Bloch hemisphere), and system size $L$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the validity of using the stabilizer norm to quantify nonstabilizerness and assumes specific forms for Hamiltonian interpolation between different transfer limits.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate how magic transfer depends on the initial state's Bloch hemisphere, show site-dependent SN dynamics across protocols, and plot $D_{	ext{max}}$ versus Hamiltonian parameters ($\alpha$, $\gamma$).

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes quantum magic transport as a resource problem, analyzes three specific spin chain protocols (A, B, C) using the XX Hamiltonian, derives the evolution of local Bloch vectors, and presents results showing state-geometry dependence and potential for magic amplification.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum communication protocols based on spin chains have been extensively studied, yet their ability to transmit nonstabilizer resources has not been systematically addressed. We investigate the transport of quantum magic in spin chains through the natural dynamics of systems initialized in nonstabilizer states, and quantify the transported resource via the stabilizer norm. We analyze three experimentally feasible state-transfer protocols, ranging from noisy to (quasi-)perfect transfer, including one realizable in trapped-ion platforms. We find that the geometry of the injected state strongly influences transport: states in the lower Bloch hemisphere achieve higher transfer quality, whereas states in the upper hemisphere give rise to an efficient magic transport only beyond a threshold value of the parameter controlling the tendency towards perfect transfer. These features are robust across all protocols and identify the Hamiltonian and state properties that favor high-quality transfer. Moreover, we identify a parameter region, relevant to the initial state preparation, in which the transported magic exceeds the initial encoding, indicating that such spin systems can act as magic-amplification channels. Our results establish the conditions for efficient transport of nonstabilizer resources and demonstrate quantum magic as a sensitive probe of quantum transport beyond population dynamics.

**Summary.** This work establishes fundamental quantum limits for learning processes where information is gathered by a single-atom sensor. It reveals a critical tradeoff: optimal performance requires either pre-existing entanglement between the sensor and memory, or an efficient coherent transfer of quantum information during operation. The findings link quantum sensing directly to the capabilities of quantum agents.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides rigorous theoretical benchmarks for quantum sensing protocols, quantifying exactly how initial entanglement resources can enhance computational tasks beyond classical or simple estimation limits.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the ultimate quantum limits for a learning agent's ability to sense external inputs (via a single-atom sensor) and translate that information into actions (rotating a target spin). It specifically determines the fundamental tradeoff between entanglement at sensing and coherence at action.

**Main result.** The optimal quantum strategy surpasses both estimation-based methods and measurement-and-operate strategies, demonstrating that initial entanglement between the sensor and memory is crucial for achieving the best performance bound.

**Method.** The analysis uses fully quantum models of learning machines, deriving upper bounds on fidelity using techniques involving Choi operators, spectral theory of tridiagonal matrices, and asymptotic analysis (e.g., solving differential equations).

**Model / system.** The model involves a single-atom sensor interacting with an environment parameterizing the input ($x$), which then transfers information to an internal quantum memory controlling an actuator acting on a target spin qubit.

**Key observables.** Fidelity ($F$ or $F^{(e)}$), entanglement fidelity, and the largest eigenvalue ($\mu$) of associated tridiagonal matrices.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The size parameter $L$ (related to sensor basis size) and the initial entanglement structure between the sensor and memory.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis compares optimal quantum strategies against measure-and-operate protocols, assuming that the optimal channels can be taken as unitary in certain limits.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the ultimate quantum limit fidelity versus estimation-based machine fidelity; one figure illustrates the overall process flow from Sensor $	o$ Environment $	o$ Memory $	o$ Actuator to the Target System.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds by first establishing the general framework, then deriving bounds for specific strategies (optimal vs. measure-and-operate), and finally using advanced mathematical techniques like solving differential equations and asymptotic expansions to determine the ultimate scaling laws for fidelity.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The ability to gather information and to act upon it is at the core of every learning agent. But what is the impact of quantum mechanics on an agent's ability to sense external inputs and to translate them into actions? Here we address the question for a prototype task of learning agency at the quantum scale: rotating a single spin based on information gathered by a single atom. We determine the ultimate performance limit for this task, revealing a fundamental tradeoff between entanglement at the sensing stage and coherence at the action stage: if the single-atom sensor is not entangled with the quantum system serving as the agent's internal memory, then the best learning strategy requires a coherent transfer of quantum information from the sensor to the system that controls the agent's actions. In contrast, if the sensor is initially entangled with the agent's memory, then the transfer of quantum information is no longer necessary. Our results indicate that the quantum properties of the sensor radically affect the optimal way to convert external stimuli into actions, revealing a link between quantum sensing and the behavior of quantum agents.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper refines the Unified Colored-Noise Approximation (UCNA) by developing a rigorous time-scale separation procedure. It derives next-to-leading order corrections to the dynamics for systems driven by colored noise. This improves theoretical accuracy over standard methods, providing better predictions for physical observables like stationary distributions.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a systematic, higher-order theoretical tool for analyzing open quantum systems or classical stochastic processes where noise correlations are non-Markovian, which is crucial when simple approximations fail.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of accurately modeling stochastic dynamics driven by colored noise, which possesses non-trivial temporal correlations.

**Main result.** By refining the Unified Colored-Noise Approximation (UCNA) using a time-scale separation procedure, the authors derive next-to-leading order corrections to the system's evolution equations and stationary distributions.

**Method.** The core method involves applying a systematic time-scale separation technique to an equivalent two-variable system, allowing for a perturbative expansion in a small parameter $\epsilon$.

**Model / system.** The analysis is applied to general stochastic differential equations (Langevin equations) driven by colored noise, exemplified by a particle in a quartic potential and stochastic logistic growth.

**Key observables.** Stationary probability distributions ($\hat{p}_{st}$), the Kullback-Leibler divergence ($	ext{DKL}$) used to quantify approximation accuracy.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The correlation time ($	au$), diffusion coefficient ($D$), and the small expansion parameter $\epsilon$ are crucial parameters governing the approximations' validity.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumptions are the applicability of a time-scale separation procedure and performing an expansion in the small parameter $\epsilon$.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the performance (via DKL) of the standard UCNA versus the newly derived corrected approximation for both transient and stationary regimes across two physical examples.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the mathematical shortcomings of the original UCNA. It then rigorously derives the next-to-leading order correction using time-scale separation, presenting the corrected evolution equation. Finally, it applies this framework to specific models (quartic potential and logistic growth) to derive and compare the improved stationary solutions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Countless biological and physical systems experience fluctuations that exhibit non-trivial temporal correlations. The Unified Colored-Noise Approximation (UCNA) is a framework providing an approximate description of such stochastic dynamics with colored noise, valid in the limits of vanishing and infinite correlation time of the noise. We first pinpoint and address some criticalities in its original derivation, recasting the result through a time-scale separation procedure. By using our approach, we derive the next-to-leading order correction to the dynamics in both limiting regimes, and highlight the relevant physical scalings of these approximations. Our result helps frame the limits of validity of both the original and the refined formulas, especially in comparison with those derived through different approximation procedures. We show our findings in two paradigmatic examples, a quartic potential and a stochastic logistic growth with multiplicative noise.

</details>

**Summary.** The research characterizes the magnetism of a bond-disordered pyrochlore antiferromagnet using multiple advanced probes. It establishes that strong spin-orbit coupling dictates the formation of $J_{	ext{eff}}=1/2$ moments, leading to an unconventional, partially frozen glassy state upon cooling. This finding highlights SOC as the crucial ingredient differentiating its magnetic fate from related, simpler systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is interesting because it uses advanced spectroscopic techniques ($\mu$SR, XMCD) to map out complex many-body quantum states in disordered magnetic insulators, providing insights into how crystal field effects (SOC) stabilize exotic glassy phases over simpler theoretical models.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how bond disorder influences the magnetic ground state of frustrated pyrochlore antiferromagnets, specifically comparing spin-orbit-entangled Co$^{2+}$ moments to simpler $S=1/2$ counterparts.

**Main result.** The system realizes an unconventional, partially frozen spin-glass-like state with persistent low-temperature dynamics, fundamentally different from a canonical spin glass or random-singlet state.

**Method.** A combination of experimental techniques including high-field magnetization, XAS/XMCD (to probe orbital moments), $\mu$SR (for local field dynamics), and $^{23}$Na NMR (for spin relaxation) was employed.

**Model / system.** The physical system is the bond-disordered pyrochlore antiferromagnet NaCdCo$_2$F$_7$, which hosts localized $J_{	ext{eff}}=1/2$ Kramers doublets due to strong spin-orbit coupling. The analysis compares its behavior against isostructural compounds like NaCdCu$_2$F$_7$.

**Key observables.** Magnetization curves $M(H, T)$, $\mu$SR relaxation rates ($\lambda_{	ext{ZF}}$), $^{23}$Na NMR spin-lattice relaxation rate ($1/T_1$), and orbital moment ratios ($\langle L_z angle / \langle S_{	ext{eff}} angle$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The key physical parameters are the strength of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and the degree of bond disorder, which dictate whether the system enters a glassy or random-singlet state.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that SOC is the dominant mechanism governing the magnetic response in these frustrated lattices, leading to $J_{	ext{eff}}=1/2$ moments.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate temperature dependence of magnetization under high fields and directional dependence at low temperatures. $\mu$SR and NMR data show characteristic signatures of progressive spin fluctuation slowing down below $\sim 10 	ext{ K}$.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds by first characterizing the magnetic moments using XAS/XMCD, then probing the bulk dynamics via magnetization measurements, and finally detailing the low-temperature freezing behavior using highly sensitive local probes like $\mu$SR and NMR.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Bond disorder in frustrated pyrochlore antiferromagnets can give rise to fundamentally different quantum ground states depending on the nature of the local magnetic moments. Here, we show that the bond-disordered pyrochlore NaCdCo$_2$F$_7$ realizes an unconventional spin-glass-like state with continued dynamics, in stark contrast to its isostructural $S=\frac{1}{2}$ NaCdCu$_2$F$_7$ counterpart. High-field magnetization and Co $L_{2,3}$-edge XAS/XMCD establish spin-orbit-entangled $J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2}$ Co$^{2+}$ moments with a substantial unquenched orbital contribution, consistent with local $XY$ anisotropy seen in the isostructural Na$A''$Co$_2$F$_7$ ($A''$ = Ca, Sr) analogues. $μ$SR and $^{23}$Na NMR measurements reveal progressive slowing of spin fluctuations below $\sim10$ K, culminating in a partially frozen state with persistent low-temperature dynamics that deviates from a canonical spin glass. Comparison with the isostructural bond-disordered pyrochlore NaCdCu$_2$F$_7$, which realizes a random-singlet state, reveals a fundamentally different response of spin-orbit-entangled Co$^{2+}$ moments to bond disorder. These results identify spin-orbit coupling as a key ingredient governing the fate of bond-disordered frustrated pyrochlore magnets.

</details>

**Summary.** This work explores novel quantum critical points by studying the cluster O’Brien–Fendley model. The authors establish a distinct $	ext{TCI}^*$ universality class characterized by unique boundary physics and an exponential energy splitting of its topological edge modes. This research advances the understanding of how topology enriches criticality in low-dimensional quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a rigorous theoretical framework for identifying symmetry-enriched topological phases beyond standard critical theories, which is highly relevant to modern condensed matter theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To investigate whether a topologically distinct Tricritical Ising (TCI) universality class ($	ext{TCI}^*$) exists beyond the ordinary TCI criticality, particularly concerning topological aspects at quantum critical points.

**Main result.** The $	ext{TCI}^*$ QCP exhibits a twofold topological degeneracy with an exponential energy splitting, distinguishing it from the ordinary TCI point and revealing distinct boundary structures.

**Method.** The study employs field-theoretic analysis, large-scale numerical simulations (DMRG), and Conformal Boundary Field Theory (BCFT) techniques to analyze critical exponents and low-energy spectra.

**Model / system.** The system is based on the cluster O’Brien–Fendley (OF) model, a spin-1/2 chain with multiple three-body interactions, analyzed near its tricritical point ($g_c \approx 0.428$).

**Key observables.** Central charge ($c$), boundary magnetization ($m_{bdy}$), boundary correlation exponent ($\Delta_{s\sigma}$), and the energy splitting ($\Delta E$) of edge modes.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Tuning parameter $g$, critical coupling constants, and system size $L$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on mapping the low-energy physics to established CFT/BCFT frameworks for comparison.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate finite-size scaling of correlation functions ($\Delta_{s\sigma}$), comparisons of low-energy spectra under different boundary conditions, and plots showing exponential decay of energy splitting at $	ext{TCI}^*$.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares the critical behavior of the cluster OF model to ordinary TCI theory by analyzing boundary correlation functions, confirming distinct scaling dimensions ($\Delta_{s\sigma}$), and demonstrating the unique exponential energy splitting characteristic of the $	ext{TCI}^*$ point.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Recent advances have revealed that quantum critical universality can be enriched by nontrivial topology. Here we study the tricritical point of the one-dimensional cluster O Brien-Fendley model and show that it realizes a topologically nontrivial tricritical Ising ($\text{TCI}^*$) universality class. The transition shares the local bulk conformal data of ordinary TCI criticality, while realizing a distinct symmetry-enriched topological sector, manifested through a protected twofold degeneracy under open boundary conditions. We further show that TCI criticality admits two spontaneously fixed boundary conditions, realized respectively through symmetry enrichment and boundary renormalization-group flow, which are distinguished by the $\mathbb{Z}_2^T$ charge of the disorder field. Remarkably, we find that the topological twofold degeneracy at the $\text{TCI}^*$ critical point exhibits an exponential energy splitting, in stark contrast to the algebraic splitting at the $\text{Ising}^*$ critical point. These results reveal a symmetry-enriched form of TCI criticality and uncover topologically distinct boundary structures beyond those of the ordinary TCI theory.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper demonstrates how incorporating finite memory into the environment (bath) of a mesoscopic conductor can act as a resource to enhance transport precision. By deriving a dual impedance-matching condition, authors predict optimal bath bandwidths that suppress current noise below Markovian limits. This offers a practical strategy for designing next-generation quantum electronic devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides concrete, tunable engineering principles—a 'design blueprint'—for enhancing quantum coherence and reducing noise in solid-state devices by controlling environmental coupling memory effects.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is developing a predictive criterion for when utilizing 'bath memory' enhances quantum transport precision, addressing the lack of such a transferable connection between bath timescale and noise reduction in mesoscopic devices.

**Main result.** Optimal transport precision (minimum Fano factor) can be achieved by implementing a 'dual impedance-matching condition' that synchronizes internal mode splitting, boundary dissipation, and finite bath bandwidth.

**Method.** The analysis employs the Landauer–Büttiker formalism combined with Non-Equilibrium Green's Function (NEGF) techniques to calculate current noise statistics in the presence of structured baths.

**Model / system.** The model is fermionic transport through a noninteracting quantum-dot chain coupled to two external fermionic baths. The bath structure is varied from Markovian wide-band limits to finite memory models using Lorentzian, Gaussian, or Newns spectral densities.

**Key observables.** Current Fano factor (F), thermodynamic and kinetic precision coefficients ($Q_T, Q_K$), and the transmission function $T(\omega)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Bath bandwidth ($\eta$), coupling strength ($g$), bias voltage ($eV$), and system size ($N$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often relies on the high-bias regime ($eV \gg T$) for analytical tractability, though generalizations are made.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate Fano factor minima (a1) and optimal parameter pairs $(g, \eta)$ compared to theory; Figure 4 shows how the predicted minimum tracks across different bath spectral densities (Lorentzian, Gaussian, Newns).

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically derives a dual impedance-matching condition by analyzing how finite memory ($\eta$) allows for constructive interference between transport modes. This leads to an analytical scaling law that predicts optimal bandwidths matching the internal system parameters.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Structured baths can reshape transport fluctuations in mesoscopic quantum devices, yet a predictive criterion for when this enhances precision has been lacking. We propose a route towards such precision advantages by utilizing bath memory in coherent fermionic transport through a noninteracting quantum-dot chain. Using the Landauer-Büttiker formalism, we derive a dual impedance-matching condition that synchronizes the conductor mode splitting, boundary dissipation, and bath bandwidth, and sustains constructive multimode interference across the transmission window. The analytical predictions for the optimal bath bandwidths show excellent agreement with exact nonequilibrium Green's function calculations of the transport for Lorentzian, Gaussian, and Newns spectral densities. The prescription yields an optimal bath bandwidth at which the current Fano factor is minimized and the thermodynamic and kinetic precision coefficients are simultaneously enhanced beyond their Markovian limits. The alignment of the optimal precision regime with the experimentally accessible current Fano factor minimum thus provides a practical strategy for designing precision-enhanced transport in mesoscopic platforms such as semiconductor quantum-dot arrays and ultracold fermionic channels.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces fuzzy processing as a novel paradigm for enhancing quantum computation robustness against decoherence and control errors. By encoding states into probability distributions and using fuzzy logic for state recognition and feedback, it significantly improves performance over traditional methods. This makes the framework highly promising for fault-tolerant quantum computing applications.

**Why it may be interesting.** For AMO physicists studying open quantum systems, this work provides a mathematical toolset (fuzzy logic) to model and mitigate the effects of unavoidable measurement uncertainty and environmental noise in complex quantum hardware implementations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses decoherence and control errors in quantum computation by proposing a novel framework that integrates fuzzy processing into existing protocols.

**Main result.** Integrating fuzzy recognition, encoding, and feedback significantly improves the robustness of quantum circuits, allowing for high fidelity even when gate fidelities are imperfect or precise state information is unavailable.

**Method.** The core method involves replacing exact quantum state representations with fuzzy probability distributions (fuzzy encoding) and using fuzzy logic rules to interpret noisy measurement outcomes (fuzzy recognition/feedback).

**Model / system.** The model utilizes standard qubit systems undergoing unitary operations, specifically applied within the context of Quantum Error Correction (QEC) circuits involving multiple qubits.

**Key observables.** Average fidelity ($ar{F}$), target qubit population ($P_L$), and output state distribution spread.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Noise intensity ($\lambda$ or $eta$), number of gates ($N_g$), and the degree of gate infidelity ($1-ar{F}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that fuzzy set theory provides a mathematically sound framework to handle uncertainty, though it notes limitations regarding the inclusion of full decoherence effects.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare performance metrics (like $P_3(0)$ or $P_L$) for single-state versus fuzzy-encoded inputs under increasing noise/infidelity, consistently showing superior robustness for the fuzzy approach.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds conceptually by first introducing fuzzy recognition to reduce fidelity requirements, then detailing fuzzy encoding to stabilize output distributions, and finally integrating both into a full QEC framework using fuzzy feedback for robust control.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum computation has attracted numerous attentions and develops rapidly in the recent decades. To against the decoherence and the control errors upon the qubits, quantum error corrections are adopted. Such approaches require lots of redundant qubits, accurate measurement and timely feedback. Here we investigate a new framework of quantum computation that is associated with fuzzy processing. It will benefit significantly from three aspects: the fuzzy recognition of qubit states reduce the required gate fidelity; the fuzzy encoding encodes the information of the qubits into a distribution of probability, suppressing the fluctuations in the output of long quantum circuits; the fuzzy feedback offers a more efficient way to control the qubits when precision information of quantum states are absent. Furthermore, the fuzzy processing can be integrated into quantum error correction, eliminating the need for immediate correction operations. The proposed scheme will be fairly suitable for the solution of decision problems, which has significant applications in the optimization problems and control problems.

</details>

**Summary.** This review surveys the theoretical landscape of unconventional superconductivity in bilayer nickelates. It focuses on two competing mechanisms—hybridization and Hund's coupling—to explain interlayer pairing mediated by strongly correlated $d_{z^2}$ spins coupled to itinerant $d_{x^2-y^2}$ electrons. The work highlights that structural tuning, doping, and defect chemistry critically control the superconducting dome and pairing symmetry.

**Why it may be interesting.** The detailed modeling of orbital physics and strong correlation effects in a layered structure provides rich ground for understanding how quantum fluctuations mediate high-temperature superconductivity, which is relevant to many open problems in AMO physics regarding interacting quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central goal is understanding the microscopic mechanism responsible for superconductivity in bilayer nickelate superconductors.

**Main result.** Strong correlation theories suggest that interlayer pairing arises from $d_{z^2}$ local singlet pairs, whose coherence is promoted by hybridization with itinerant $d_{x^2-y^2}$ electrons. The superconducting state exhibits complex symmetry and strong dependence on doping and structural parameters.

**Method.** The work employs theoretical modeling using the bilayer two-orbital Hubbard model and its minimal t-J variants, analyzed through mean-field theory and advanced quantum simulation techniques.

**Model / system.** The system is bilayer nickelates ($	ext{La}_3	ext{Ni}_2	ext{O}_{7-\delta}$), characterized by two active orbitals ($d_{z^2}$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$) exhibiting strong electronic correlations, Hund's coupling, and significant interlayer magnetic coupling.

**Key observables.** Superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$), pairing symmetry ($	ext{s}\pm$-wave), orbital-selective mass renormalization, and normal state behaviors (FL, NFL, pseudogap).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Interlayer superexchange coupling ($J_{\perp}$), Hund's coupling ($J_H$), doping level ($\delta_d$), and the hybridization strength ($V$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often separates the physics into strong correlation limits (localized $d_{z^2}$) coupled to itinerant electrons ($d_{x^2-y^2}$), or treats both orbitals within a two-orbital Hubbard framework.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the Interlayer Valence Bond State (VBS) and its emergent excitations, as well as simulated superconducting $T_c$ dependence on hybridization strength ($V$) and doping ($\delta_d$).

**Paper structure.** The review progresses from identifying key physical ingredients (orbital structure, correlations) to introducing theoretical models (Hubbard/t-J), detailing competing pairing mechanisms (hybridization vs. Hund's coupling), analyzing the resulting superconducting symmetries, and finally discussing external tuning effects like pressure and oxygen vacancies.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The discovery of superconductivity in Ruddlesden-Popper bilayer nickelates under both high pressure and ambient conditions has opened a new paradigm for exploring unconventional superconductivity. This review provides a brief survey of theoretical progress on bilayer nickelate superconductors. Drawing from the key experimental observations, we summarize essential physical ingredients including the hybridized Ni-3$d_{x^2-y^2}$ and 3$d_{z^2}$ electronic structure, orbital-dependent electronic correlation, Hund's coupling, and strong interlayer magnetic coupling. The fundamental theoretical models including the bilayer two-orbital Hubbard model and its minimal $t$-$J$ variants are introduced. Starting from the atomic-limit interlayer valence bond picture of the half-filled $d_{z^2}$ orbital, we elaborate on strong correlation interlayer pairing mechanisms based on different limiting considerations. Specific emphasis is placed on the hybridization mechanism, where the $d_{z^2}$ local singlet pairs provide the pairing energy and their hybridization with itinerant $d_{x^2-y^2}$ promotes superconducting phase coherence. We further analyze the pairing symmetry, the dependence of $T_c$ on various internal and external parameters, the nontrivial normal state properties including the Fermi liquid, non-Fermi liquid, weakly insulating and pseudogap behaviors. Effects of pressure tuning, oxygen content, and Kondo scattering induced by oxygen vacancies are also discussed. Finally, weak correlation theories based on spin fluctuations associated with Fermi surface nesting are briefly covered.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper presents an end-to-end methodology for extracting physical knowledge from experimental quantum computation results. By applying SKQD and variational optimization to generate ground state data for the 2D XXZ model, they train advanced neural networks to predict complex observables. This demonstrates a powerful paradigm shift: using near-term quantum hardware not just for simulation, but as a scalable source of training data for predictive physics models.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work bridges theoretical condensed matter physics with practical quantum machine learning, showing a concrete path to using noisy, limited quantum hardware outputs as high-fidelity training data for complex many-body simulations that are otherwise computationally intractable or too resource-intensive classically.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is developing a workflow to learn ground-state observables of interacting quantum many-body systems directly from data generated by near-term quantum computing experiments.

**Main result.** The authors successfully trained machine learning models on quantum data for the 2D Heisenberg XXZ model, demonstrating accurate prediction of local observables even in out-of-distribution regimes approaching a phase boundary.

**Method.** A combined approach uses Sample-based Krylov Quantum Diagonalization (SKQD) to generate approximate ground states, followed by training sophisticated neural networks (comparing global vs. geometry-aware architectures) on the resulting expectation values.

**Model / system.** The system studied is the spin-1/2 XXZ model on a heavy-hexagonal lattice, parameterized by the anisotropy $J_z$. The study focuses on the antiferromagnetic phase and its approach to quantum critical points.

**Key observables.** Single-site expectation values ($\langle Z angle$), two-point correlations ($C_{zz}$), 12-body loop correlations ($\langle Z_{	ext{loop}} angle$), and the staggered magnetization ($m_s$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** System sizes up to $n=115$ qubits; anisotropy parameter $J_z$; training regimes span from $1.6 \le J_z \le 6.0$, with testing near $J_z = 1.0$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumptions involve the feasibility of SKQD generating sufficiently accurate data, and that ML architectures (especially geometry-aware ones) can capture complex spatial correlations beyond simple parameter dependence.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the workflow overview, energy error convergence relative to DMRG across $J_z$, and comparative plots showing the mean relative error ($\Delta O_{ML}$) of observables predicted by different ML architectures when extrapolating towards phase boundaries.

**Paper structure.** The paper details a multi-step process: first, generating data using SKQD combined with variational basis optimization to improve ground state estimates; second, designing and training two distinct neural network architectures (global vs. local/geometry-aware) on this quantum data; and finally, rigorously testing the models' generalization capability both within and outside the trained parameter regime.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Recent theoretical progress has established conditions under which machine learning models can efficiently predict ground-state properties of gapped local Hamiltonians when trained on quantum-generated data. Previous experimental demonstrations in this paradigm, however, have largely been limited to small systems or highly structured states, due to the difficulty of preparing many-body ground states on quantum processors. In this work, we demonstrate learning from experimental quantum data generated from approximate ground states of the two-dimensional Heisenberg XXZ model with system sizes up to 115 qubits. We construct a dataset of single-site expectation values, two-point correlations, and 12-body loop correlations across the antiferromagnetic phase. We then train neural networks on this data and show that they can accurately predict spatially resolved observables for previously unseen Hamiltonian parameters, both within the training distribution and in an out-of-distribution regime approaching the phase boundary. Our results demonstrate the practical realization of learning from quantum data for an interacting two-dimensional many-body system at scale, motivating a path toward regimes where quantum processors could provide training data beyond the reach of classical approximation methods.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a comprehensive theory for exactly mapping underlying Markov-jump dynamics onto observable semi-Markov processes via 'milestoning.' It rigorously characterizes the resulting kinetics by decomposing waiting times into dwell and transition components. The key findings establish thermodynamic consistency, quantify kinetic hysteresis, and provide methods to infer hidden physical affinities from observed time statistics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides powerful, general theoretical tools for analyzing non-equilibrium steady states in complex biological or chemical systems where direct observation is impossible. The rigorous connection between coarse-graining, memory effects, and fundamental thermodynamic quantities like entropy production is highly relevant to open quantum system modeling.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is deriving an exact, thermodynamically consistent coarse-graining of underlying Markov-jump processes into observable semi-Markov dynamics (milestoning). This addresses how memory effects arise when observing a system only at discrete points in time.

**Main result.** The theory successfully decomposes the waiting time distribution into conditionally independent dwell and transition times, proves its thermodynamic consistency, and demonstrates that kinetic hysteresis persists even when the observed process approaches Markovian behavior.

**Method.** The authors use rigorous mathematical derivations involving generator matrices, Laplace transforms, and renewal theory to analyze the joint probability densities of state transitions across hidden intermediate states.

**Model / system.** The model is a generic ergodic Markov-jump process on a full state space $\Omega$, which is partitioned into observable states ($\Omega_{	ext{obs}}$) and unobserved hidden states ($\Omega_{	ext{hidden}}$). The dynamics are analyzed by constructing an effective semi-Markov generator matrix.

**Key observables.** Waiting-time distributions, dwell times, transition-path times, steady-state entropy production rate ($\dot{\sigma}$), and the affinity ($A_{ij}$) between states.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Time-scale separation limits ($\lambda/\kappa 	o \infty$), barrier heights ($B$), driving intensities ($M$), and the number of parallel hidden mechanisms ($V$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The underlying microscopic dynamics satisfy detailed balance (or are analyzed under conditions that allow for thermodynamic consistency checks). The analysis relies on specific structural assumptions about how hidden states connect observed nodes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate model structures, the manifestation of kinetic hysteresis via non-zero KL divergence in waiting time densities, and numerical validation showing the recovery of entropy production rates using milestoning estimators.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the mathematical framework for coarse-graining (Chunk 1), deriving the decomposition of waiting times into dwell/transition components (Chunk 2), proving thermodynamic consistency and reflection symmetry properties (Chunk 3), generalizing to multiple parallel hidden mechanisms (Chunk 4), and finally applying these results to continuous systems like diffusion on a ring potential (Chunk 5).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We derive an exact coarse graining of generic Markov-jump processes into observable semi-Markov dynamics. Exact results for waiting-time distributions for jumps between observable states are derived and proved that these decompose into conditionally independent dwell and transition times. Dwell times are proved to be a local property of mesostates - they depend on the initial but not final state. Conversely, transition-path times depend on both states, trigger kinetic hysteresis, and, under suitable conditions on the hidden sub-network, are shown to obey a reflection symmetry. We characterize the stationary properties of the milestoned dynamics, prove its thermodynamic consistency, and demonstrate robustness to milestone positioning. Surprisingly, even in the limit of a time-scale separation rendering the observed dynamics approximately Markovian, the effect of kinetic hysteresis on the dissipation persists. A minimal example shows how the results lay the foundation for inferring affinities of hidden dissipative cycles from observations of transition-path times.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates multiband transport in EuAuBi, a material with vastly different electron and hole carrier densities. By analyzing the Nernst effect across various magnetic fields and temperatures, the authors establish that the large signal originates from conventional semiclassical physics involving two distinct pockets. They derive a new scaling law for $
u/T$ specific to asymmetric multiband systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter transport, the rigorous derivation of scaling laws in multi-component systems (like those involving multiple electronic bands) provides generalizable principles applicable to open quantum systems where different coupling channels might dominate response functions.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study addresses how transport coefficients, particularly the Nernst effect, behave in materials with coexisting carrier pockets of vastly different densities.

**Main result.** The large Nernst effect is shown to be a semiclassical multiband phenomenon governed by a specific scaling relation ($
u/T \propto \mu_e/E_{F,tot}$), rather than being purely topological.

**Method.** The authors combine experimental measurements (resistivity, Hall effect, Seebeck, Nernst) with theoretical modeling using semi-classical two-band transport equations.

**Model / system.** The research focuses on the polar semimetal EuAuBi, which exhibits an extreme carrier density mismatch between a dense hole pocket and a dilute, high-mobility electron pocket. The analysis employs a two-band model to describe total transport properties.

**Key observables.** Longitudinal resistivity ($ho_{xx}$), Hall effect ($ho_{yx}$), Seebeck coefficient ($S_{xx}$), and Nernst signal ($S_{xy}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Carrier densities ($n_e \sim 10^{16} 	ext{ cm}^{-3}, n_h \sim 10^{21} 	ext{ cm}^{-3}$), electron mobility ($\mu_e$), and the total Fermi energy scale ($E_{F,tot}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on semi-classical two-band expressions for transport coefficients and assumes an asymmetric limit where specific cancellations occur in the Nernst coefficient derivation.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the crossover of $ho_{xx}$ to hole dominance, the temperature dependence of $S_{xx}$, and the low-field step-like feature in $ho_{yx}(B)$ attributed to the electron pocket. The scaling analysis plots $
u/T$ against different energy scales.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes a transport hierarchy using measurements on EuAuBi, showing which pocket dominates which coefficient. It then derives the theoretical low-field Nernst response for an asymmetric two-band system, leading to a revised scaling law that is confirmed by fitting experimental data.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In correlated materials, coexisting pockets of vastly different carrier densities raise two fundamental questions: which pocket governs the various transport coefficients, and does the conventional Nernst scaling $ν/T \propto μ/E_F$, originally derived for single-band systems, still hold? We address both questions in the polar semimetal EuAuBi, where a dilute electron pocket ($n_e \sim 10^{16}~\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$) coexists with a dense hole pocket ($n_h \sim 10^{21}~\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$). We find a clear hierarchy: the hole pocket dominates the longitudinal resistivity; the Hall effect crosses from electron- to hole-dominance with increasing field; the Seebeck coefficient is dominated by the electron pocket at low temperature and by both pockets at high temperature. Remarkably, the Nernst effect is governed entirely by the ultrahigh-mobility electron pocket, yielding a large low-field signal of $\sim 5~μ\mathrm{V/K}$ near 1~T at 202~K, comparable to anomalous Nernst signals in magnetic Weyl semimetals. By analyzing the two-band thermoelectric conductivity, we show that the Nernst coefficient follows a scaling $ν/T \propto μ_e/{E_{F, tot}}$. This scaling originates from a compensation between the electron-to-hole conductivity ratio and the Fermi-energy ratio, establishing that the large Nernst effect is a semiclassical multiband phenomenon rather than a topological Berry-curvature contribution. This understanding advances the thermoelectric transport physics of multiband electronic systems and offers a guiding principle for low-field transverse thermoelectric design.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper shows how anisotropic hyperbolic media can enable visible/near-IR light-matter interactions even when the source itself has no conventional dipole moment. By exploiting the unique field confinement and directional properties of these materials, a 'dark' emitter becomes radiatively active. This establishes a new platform for controlling quantum optical processes in solid-state systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a novel mechanism for achieving strong light-matter coupling using solid-state platforms that overcome fundamental spectral limitations by engineering the vacuum structure via hyperbolic dispersion. It extends quantum optics into regimes previously thought inaccessible.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is reconciling the spectral mismatch between low-loss hyperbolic media (limited to mid-IR) and robust quantum emitters operating at visible/near-IR frequencies.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate that a source with zero dipole moment, which would be non-radiating in isotropic media, becomes radiatively active and exhibits strong directional coupling within an anisotropic hyperbolic environment.

**Method.** The analysis uses quasistatic approximations to calculate the electric field and emitter-emitter interaction energy ($U$), focusing on how anisotropy modifies radiative processes.

**Model / system.** The system involves using visible/near-IR emitters coupled into hyperbolic dielectric media, exemplified by hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The key mechanism relies on inducing mid-infrared population dynamics to generate radiation in the desired frequency band.

**Key observables.** Radiative activity of 'dark sources,' strong directional emission patterns following hyperbolic cones, and highly anisotropic interaction energy scaling as $1/r^3$ or enhanced at focal points ($\propto 1/\ell_f^3$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The effective permittivity $\epsilon_{	ext{eff}}(\hat{\mathbf{r}})$, the separation distance ($r$ or $\delta z$), and the characteristic length scales related to hyperbolic dispersion bands.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes low material losses in the hyperbolic medium and utilizes the quasistatic approximation for field calculations at short distances.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the frequency-dependent permittivity of hBN, momentum space contours showing high-momentum mode propagation along hyperbolic cones, and finally, the strong emission pattern and periodic refocusing/autofocusing of interaction energy within a cylindrical geometry.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the spectral mismatch problem. It then theoretically derives how anisotropic hyperbolic media allow non-dipolar sources to radiate. Finally, it applies this theory to model emitter-emitter interactions in confined geometries, showing strong enhancement at focal points.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Hyperbolic media enable ultra-strong light-matter interactions through their extreme field localization and small mode volumes, but low-loss realizations are fundamentally limited to the mid-infrared, owing to the long lifetimes of optical phonons in high-quality crystals. Here we show that bright emitters operating at visible or near-infrared frequencies can be used to generate radiation in this regime by inducing mid-infrared population dynamics, thereby creating a source in the hyperbolic frequency band without a corresponding dipole transition. We demonstrate that even a source with vanishing dipole and higher multipole moments - strictly non-radiating in any isotropic medium - becomes radiatively active in a hyperbolic environment. This enables visible and near-infrared control of light-matter interactions in polaritonic hyperbolic materials, establishing a new low-loss solid-state quantum optics platform.

</details>
