**Summary.** This paper theoretically analyzes Kasevich-Chu atom interferometers using motional squeezing states to boost measurement sensitivity. It rigorously compares performance under ideal conditions versus realistic Doppler broadening effects by calculating both Quantum and Classical Fisher Information for different measurement types. The key finding is that joint measurement of population and position provides a robust enhancement mechanism capable of overcoming significant Doppler suppression.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it pushes quantum metrology into regimes where real-world noise sources like Doppler shifts are present, providing concrete guidance on how entanglement resources (MSS) can maintain high precision measurements.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to enhance the sensitivity of Kasevich-Chu atom interferometers beyond the standard quantum limit while quantifying the detrimental effects of Doppler broadening.

**Main result.** Joint measurement of population and position shows superior robustness, allowing quantum enhancement to dominate even in the presence of strong Doppler broadening effects. For population measurement alone, enhancements up to four times the semi-classical limit were achieved.

**Method.** The authors systematically derived computational frameworks for both Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) and classical Fisher information (CFI) by analyzing two distinct measurement protocols: population measurement and joint population–position measurement.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a Kasevich-Chu atom gravimeter utilizing cold atomic ensembles. The theoretical model incorporates the hybridization of internal and external atomic degrees of freedom, allowing for the use of Motional Squeezing States (MSS) as input states.

**Key observables.** Quantum Fisher Information ($F_Q$) and Classical Fisher Information ($F_C$), sensitivity ($\delta g$), contrast ($C$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Squeezing strength ($eta$), squeezing angle ($	heta$), interrogation time ratio ($r=T_1/T$), Doppler effect magnitude.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis compares 'Ideal' scenarios (neglecting Doppler effects) with 'Doppler' scenarios that incorporate momentum broadening. In some calculations, optimal control parameters from the ideal case were adopted for the Doppler calculation due to numerical complexity.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare maximum CFIs/QFIs across different measurement protocols and squeezing parameters ($eta, 	heta$) in both Ideal and Doppler regimes, highlighting the superior performance of joint measurements.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds by first establishing the theoretical framework using QFI/CFI for ideal vs. Doppler scenarios (using MSS input). It then optimizes control parameters to maximize CFI for population vs. joint measurement protocols, concluding with a comparative analysis showing robustness in the joint measurement regime.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Hybridization of internal and external atomic degrees of freedom in a Kasevich-Chu interferometer enables the possibility to enhance the sensitivity significantly even under quantum-standard limit. By introducing motional squeezing state as an input, we systematically derive the computational framework of quantum and classical Fisher information of two measurement protocols for arbitrary strength of Doppler effects. Through maximizing the corresponding classical Fisher information, we obtain the optimal control parameters and the corresponding quantum Fisher information. For population measurement, the largest sensitivity can be as large as four times than the semi-classical limit through enlarging the atom coherence length. For joint measurement of population and position, the competition between quantum enhancement and Doppler suppression induces two three behaviors, in one regime, the quantum enhancement dominates even in presence of strong Doppler broadening effects where the sensitivity is significantly enhanced; while in another regime, an optimal squeezing parameter is observed where the classical Fisher information reaches the maximum. Our results clearly demonstrate the robustness of external quantum enhancement against Doppler suppression. Our proposal can be readily applied to gravimeter of mobile platform where decoherence from noise will damage the many-body entanglement of internal spin squeezing.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces 'symveig,' a novel package that computes mathematically rigorous enclosures for the eigenvalues of Hermitian quantum Hamiltonians. By exploiting symmetries to decompose large matrices into smaller, independent sectors, it achieves both significantly tighter bounds and massive speedups compared to full diagonalization methods. This provides computational physicists with unprecedented certainty regarding their calculated spectral properties.

**Why it may be interesting.** For theorists studying strongly correlated systems using numerical methods, this provides a crucial tool to move beyond approximate results. It allows for quantitative verification of spectral properties (like gaps or ground state energies) with mathematical certainty within standard computational environments.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is obtaining rigorous, machine-checkable enclosures for all eigenvalues of Hermitian matrices derived from quantum Hamiltonians, circumventing the uncertified nature of standard floating-point diagonalization results.

**Main result.** The package successfully computes guaranteed eigenvalue enclosures that are significantly tighter (3–9x) and dramatically faster (up to 130x speedup) than verifying the full matrix spectrum by exploiting symmetry conservation laws.

**Method.** It uses a specialized, rigorous bounding technique based on the Bauer–Fike theorem, enhanced by explicit floating-point error analysis (Higham's $\gamma_k$) and dramatically accelerated via symmetry-sector decomposition.

**Model / system.** The method is validated on quantum lattice Hamiltonians, including 1D Heisenberg chains (open/periodic), J1–J2 Heisenberg models, and 2D Heisenberg lattices. These systems are characterized by conserved quantities like total magnetization ($S_z$).

**Key observables.** Rigorous eigenvalue enclosures $[\mu_i - h_i, \mu_i + h_i]$, spectral gaps, and certified ground-state energies.

**Important parameters / regimes.** System size $L$ (tested up to 12), the matrix norm $\|A\|_F$, and the degree of symmetry conservation ($S$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method assumes the conserved quantity is exactly diagonal in the working basis; furthermore, the rigorous bound used is dominated by a worst-case error term ($\gamma_4 n \|A\|_{	ext{F}}$) when full rigor is applied.

**Figures summary.** Figures demonstrate data collapse confirming scaling laws for enclosure widths ($h \propto d_s \|A\|_F$), and show the substantial speedup achieved by using sector decomposition over global diagonalization.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem of uncertified eigenvalues, details the mathematical framework involving rigorous error bounding (Bauer-Fike), presents the efficiency gain via symmetry-sector path analysis, validates the method on multiple lattice models, and concludes with performance comparisons.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Exact diagonalization of quantum lattice Hamiltonians returns floating-point eigenvalues whose accuracy is not certified: rounding error, eigensolver behaviour, and ill-conditioning can corrupt a result without warning. We present \texttt{symveig}, a pure NumPy/SciPy package that computes rigorous, machine-checkable enclosures of all eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix, with an optional symmetry-sector decomposition. For a matrix that commutes with an abelian conserved quantity diagonal in the working basis (for example the total magnetization of a spin model), the package verifies each symmetry sector independently. Because each sector block is much smaller than the full matrix, this yields enclosures that are both tighter (by a factor of $3$-$9$ across system sizes $L = 4$-$12$) and dramatically faster (a wall-clock speedup of up to $130\times$ at $L = 12$) than verifying the full matrix, while never forming or diagonalizing it. Every enclosure half-width is a guaranteed upper bound on the distance from a computed eigenvalue to the nearest true eigenvalue under IEEE~754 round-to-nearest arithmetic, obtained by explicit floating-point error analysis with no heuristic slack. The implementation requires neither INTLAB nor MATLAB, bringing rigorously verified eigenvalue enclosure into the standard scientific-Python stack used in computational physics. We validate the package on $1$D Heisenberg (open and periodic), $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg, and $2$D Heisenberg lattices, confirming that every computed eigenvalue is contained in its enclosure across all tested configurations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to determine the limit free energy of multi-species spin glasses, specifically addressing cases where the underlying covariance function ($\xi$) is non-convex.

**Main result.** The authors establish a modified variational formula for the limit free energy and show that this limit function satisfies a specific Hamilton–Jacobi equation. They also derive a one-species reduction for balanced multi-species models.

**Method.** The analysis heavily employs advanced techniques from statistical mechanics, including viscosity solution theory for Hamilton–Jacobi equations, comparison principles, and rigorous limiting procedures over infinite dimensions (e.g., using Stegall's variational principle).

**Model / system.** The model is a multi-species spin glass defined by centered Ising spins ($\sigma \in \{-1, 1\}^N$). The Hamiltonian involves Gaussian fields whose covariance structure depends on the species overlaps and proportions.

**Key observables.** Limit free energy $f(t,q)$, overlap functions ($R_{N,s}$, $R_N$), and the function $\psi_{\circ}(q)$ related to the convexity properties of the system's effective potential.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Time parameter $t$, species proportions $\lambda_\infty$, and the covariance function $\xi$ (which can be non-convex).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The result is restricted to centered Ising spins. The proof requires advanced mathematical machinery, including assumptions about path spaces ($Q_S^\infty$) and handling limits across different species proportions.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds iteratively: first establishing the general variational formula (Theorem 1.1) for non-convex $\xi$; then proving convexity properties of related functions ($\psi_{\circ}$) using recursive relations and path analysis; finally, deriving the single-species reduction for 'balanced' models by comparing multi-species bounds to one-species solutions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We identify the limit free energy of all multi-species spin glasses with centered $\pm 1$ spins. The result was previously known only under a convexity assumption on the covariance function of the Hamiltonian. We also obtain a one-species reduction of the formula for balanced multi-species models.

**Summary.** This paper reformulates Bohmian mechanics by replacing the vague 'distribution postulate' with a precise condition: the initial particle configuration must be Martin-Löf random relative to the Born measure. This algorithmic constraint ensures that the deterministic evolution yields measurement statistics consistent with standard quantum mechanical predictions in the limit.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a mathematically rigorous, non-standard way to derive quantum probabilities from a deterministic theory by imposing an objective randomness constraint on the initial state.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses how to objectively formulate the 'distribution postulate' required for Bohmian mechanics to reproduce standard Born quantum statistics.

**Main result.** By adopting an algorithmic approach, the authors show that requiring the initial particle configuration to be Martin-Löf random relative to the Born measure guarantees that measurement outcomes follow standard quantum statistical predictions in the limit.

**Method.** The core method involves applying concepts from algorithmic information theory, specifically Martin-Löf randomness, to constrain the initial conditions of a deterministic Bohmian flow.

**Model / system.** The model is Algorithmic Bohmian Mechanics (aBM), which describes particle dynamics deterministically based on a wave function $\psi$. It analyzes measurements using spin-1/2 particles and sequential measurement outcomes.

**Key observables.** Measurement outcome sequences ($\omega$-sequences) and the empirical relative frequencies of these outcomes.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The limit $n 	o \infty$ for statistical convergence; the initial state's randomness relative to the Born measure $\mu_\psi$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** 1. The initial configuration must be Martin-Löf random relative to the quantum probability measure ($	ext{MLR}_{\mu_\psi}$). 2. Measurement interactions are assumed to be 'layerwise computable'. 3. For statistical equivalence, exchangeable credences are assumed.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates an x-spin measurement in Bohmian mechanics, showing the particle being carried by probability currents associated with different wave packets.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the need for a distribution postulate (Chunk 1) to proposing algorithmic randomness as the solution (Chunk 2). It then develops the rigorous mathematical machinery using layerwise computability to define this postulate (Chunk 3), culminating in proving that this assumption guarantees Born statistics for computable measurement sequences (Chunk 4 and Chunk 5).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In order to make the right empirical predictions Bohmian mechanics requires a special statistical boundary condition -- the distribution postulate -- but it is unclear how best to understand this condition. We show how one might use the theory of algorithmic randomness to formulate the distribution postulate as an objective constraining law. The framework requires us to say something about admissible quantum-mechanical states and measurements. In return, algorithmic Bohmian mechanics (aBM) guarantees the standard Born statistics for a collection of canonical quantum experiments in the limit, not just with high probability. The algorithmic distribution postulate provides a sharp typicality condition, clarifies the status of quantum probabilities in the deterministic theory, and provides a concrete example of how notions provided by the theory of algorithmic randomness can aid in specifying the content of a physical law.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper investigates vortex cores in flat-band superconductors using the attractive Hubbard model. It finds that the characteristic size of these cores is not determined by standard Fermi surface physics but instead emerges directly from the underlying geometric structure (quantum metric) of the electronic bands. This establishes a novel link between quantum geometry and superconducting properties.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete theoretical framework demonstrating how geometric properties (quantum metrics) can dictate macroscopic superconducting behavior (vortex structure) when conventional kinetic energy mechanisms fail, which is highly relevant for understanding exotic superconductivity in engineered quantum materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To determine the characteristic spatial scale (coherence length) of superconducting inhomogeneities, such as vortex cores, in flat-band superconductors where conventional BCS theory fails due to the lack of a well-defined Fermi surface.

**Main result.** The coherence length is governed by a 'geometric pair mass' arising from virtual interband processes encoded in the quantum metric, establishing the vortex core size as a direct real-space manifestation of flat-band quantum geometry.

**Method.** A combination of momentum-space mean-field analysis and self-consistent Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) calculations performed on a finite disk was used to compare theoretical predictions with real-space profiles.

**Model / system.** The system is a flat-band superconductor modeled by the attractive Hubbard model on the Mielke checkerboard lattice. The analysis uses mean-field approximations derived from the underlying Hamiltonian, leading to quasiparticle spectra dependent on band structure and pairing gap.

**Key observables.** Coherence length ($\xi$), superconducting order parameter profile $\Delta(r)$, local particle density $ho(r)$, and the quantum metric tensor $g_{k,ij}$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Filling ($F$), interaction strength ($U/t$), and the ratio of band energies to pairing gap.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes uniform pairing initially, and later relies on mapping continuum momentum-space results onto real-space BdG calculations using specific cutoffs for consistency.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the flat band structure, self-consistent solutions for $\Delta_0$ and $\mu$, radial profiles of $\Delta(r)$ and $ho(r)$ showing vortex core formation, and comparisons between momentum-space estimates ($\xi_B$) and real-space BdG results ($\xi_v$).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the model (Hubbard/Mielke lattice) to deriving mean-field equations in momentum space. It then calculates self-consistent solutions for the gap and chemical potential, culminating in solving the full real-space BdG equations on a disk to extract the vortex core size.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the real-space vortex structure of a flat-band superconductor described by the attractive Hubbard model on the Mielke checkerboard lattice. Using a momentum-space mean-field analysis, we derive a closed-form expression for the coherence length in terms of the quantum metric of the Bloch states and a particle-hole-symmetric pair density. Self-consistent Bogoliubov-de Gennes calculations on a finite disk confirm this prediction across a wide range of fillings and interaction strengths. The coherence length is minimized at half filling, diverges toward both band edges as the pair density vanishes, and depends only logarithmically on the interaction strength. These features differ qualitatively from the conventional BCS picture, which relies on a well-defined Fermi surface and a kinetic mechanism for pair transport. Instead, the vortex-core size is governed by a geometric pair mass arising from virtual interband processes encoded in the quantum metric. Our results establish the vortex core as a direct real-space manifestation of flat-band quantum geometry.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically models the quantum behavior of vortex filaments in flowing fluids, revealing that the system's energy spectrum can exhibit states with negative effective mass. By analyzing how external flow momentum ($p_0$) influences this spectrum, the authors propose a framework for determining the critical quantum Reynolds number associated with the onset of turbulence.

**Why it may be interesting.** The investigation into negative effective mass in a macroscopic fluid dynamics context, derived from quantum principles, provides novel theoretical insights into non-linear wave phenomena and energy dissipation mechanisms relevant to complex physical systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the quantum dynamics of a vortex filament moving within a flowing fluid, specifically focusing on how external flow influences the energy spectrum to reveal negative effective mass states and mechanisms for turbulence.

**Main result.** The energy spectrum $E(p)$ exhibits states with both positive and negative effective masses, and increasing the external momentum ($p_0$) can change the number of stationary points from one to three, signaling a transition towards turbulent regimes.

**Method.** The analysis employs a group-theoretical approach combined with quantization techniques applied to classical vortex filaments, deriving energy eigenvalues $E_{m,n}(p; p_0)$ that depend on external flow parameters.

**Model / system.** The system models a thin, circular quantum vortex filament in an infinite cylindrical pipe subjected to a non-zero background fluid velocity $v$. The dynamics are governed by an energy spectrum $E(p)$ derived from a Hamiltonian structure incorporating the additional momentum $p_0 = Mv$.

**Key observables.** Energy spectrum $E(p)$, effective mass ($M_{	ext{eff}}$), stationary points of $E$, and the critical quantum Reynolds number ($	ext{Re}_{c}^q$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Fluid velocity ($v$), additional momentum ($p_0$), quantized circulation values ($\Gamma_{m,n}$), and dimensionless parameters $\kappa$ and $\kappa_0$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the Local Induction Approximation (LIA) at times, treats vortex interactions in a weakly coupled manner, and uses specific quantization techniques for closed filaments.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the physical setup of the vortex in flowing fluid. Figure 2 demonstrates how changing $p_0$ alters the number of stationary points in the energy function $E$. Figure 3 shows the dependency of velocity on $p_0$ for different effective mass selections.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by defining the physical system and Hamiltonian, developing quantization methods to find the energy spectrum $E(p; p_0)$, analyzing how external momentum $p_0$ modifies this spectrum (leading to negative masses), and finally applying these findings to establish criteria for quantum turbulence onset.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We explore the movement of a thin, circular quantum vortex filament within an infinite cylindrical pipe.   The fluid surrounding the vortex ring moves through the pipe at a non-zero velocity denoted by $v$. Our study examines the energy spectrum $E = E(p)$, where $p$ represents the total momentum of a vortex ring.   We have demonstrated that the function $E(p)$ significantly depends on the velocity $v$. The discovered spectrum $E(p)$ reveals the existence of states with both negative and extremely large effective masses. We also explored the hypothesis regarding the existence of coupled vortex pairs possessing finite summary effective masses. Every pair consists of vortices that possess both positive and negative masses, with the magnitude of these masses being unrestricted.   In our model, the criterion for the appearance of these states is based on comparing two numbers. The first is seen as a quantum counterpart to the Reynolds number, while the second represents its critical value for a flow with a single vortex. We also explore how this studied effect might contribute to the emergence of quantum turbulence. This study discusses a method for determining the critical Reynolds number in quantum turbulence, using the proposed model as a framework. Here, we use a new quantization technique for classical closed vortex filaments developed by the author earlier.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper improves upon the Curzon-Ahlborn model for heat engines by incorporating a specific dependence of process duration on temperature differences. This modification allows the calculation of absolute energy and time scales, successfully recovering the reversible Carnot limit while optimizing the power output across different operational regimes.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical thermodynamics, the rigorous treatment of finite-time processes and approaching reversible limits shares conceptual links with non-equilibrium quantum dynamics where time scales are crucial.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To augment the Curzon-Ahlborn (CA) model for endoreversible Carnot machines to recover the standard Carnot cycle limit while determining absolute time and energy scales.

**Main result.** The modified model successfully determines absolute time and energy scales, showing that maximum power is achieved at an intermediate efficiency value corresponding to the CA model's optimal point.

**Method.** The analysis augments the CA model by specifying a relationship between isothermal process duration and temperature difference, utilizing the low-dissipation regime assumption for entropy production ($S_{ir} \propto 1/t$).

**Model / system.** The system is an endoreversible Carnot engine operating between hot and cold reservoirs. The model incorporates finite-time thermodynamics where irreversibility occurs during heat exchange with the environment.

**Key observables.** Efficiency ($\eta$), Work output per cycle ($W$), Maximum Power ($P_{max}$), Optimal temperature ratios ($	au^*$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature difference, process duration ($	au$), dissipation parameters ($\kappa, \sigma, 	heta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The core assumption is relating process duration ($t$) and temperature difference ($\delta T$) to ensure recovery of the reversible limit in the quasi-static limit; it also uses a low-dissipation approximation.

**Figures summary.** Not specified by notes, but the analysis involves deriving optimal parameters for power vs. efficiency trade-offs.

**Paper structure.** The paper first addresses the limitations of the CA model and then introduces an augmentation based on process duration dependence. It analyzes performance metrics (efficiency, work) under this modified framework, culminating in optimization procedures for maximum power output.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The well-known Curzon-Ahlborn (CA) engine [Am. J. Phys. {\bf 43}, 22 (1975)] runs in finite time and yields a finite power output. In order to recover the standard Carnot cycle from the CA model, the limit of quasi-static operation has to be concurrent with the reversible limit, a condition strangely missing from the CA model. We augment this model by specifying the duration of the isothermal process as a monotonic decreasing function of the temperature difference between the working substance and the reservoir. As an illustration, we analyze the machine's operation in the low-dissipation regime in which the entropy production in each isothermal branch is inversely proportional to the duration of the process. The modified model is able to determine the optimal durations of isothermal processes as well as heat and work per cycle, while retaining the optimal power conditions of the CA model.

</details>

**Summary.** This work unifies three seemingly independent descriptors—nonextensive entropy index ($q$), fractal dimension ($D$), and memory exponent ($\alpha$)—into a single, self-consistent algebraic closure applicable to critical systems. By deriving this 'Troika relation' from fundamental physical constraints, the authors demonstrate its remarkable universality by successfully predicting measurements across diverse fields like seismology and EEG.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical critical phenomena, the concept of non-Markovian dynamics ($\alpha$) and generalized statistics ($q$) are highly relevant to open quantum systems where memory effects and non-equilibrium dynamics dominate. The search for universal closures is a key theme in advanced statistical physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to establish a single, self-consistent algebraic relationship connecting three key macroscopic features observed in self-organized critical systems: nonextensive thermodynamics ($q$), structural fractality ($D$), and non-Markovian dynamics ($\alpha$).

**Main result.** A unique closure relation is derived, $\alpha = D/(2D - 1)$, which leads to the universal 'Troika closure' $\alpha = 1/(3-q)$. This relationship successfully predicts measured values across eight diverse experimental systems.

**Method.** The derivation relies on imposing phase-space self-consistency constraints and utilizing known physical boundary conditions (e.g., Euclidean limit, infinite dimension limit) to uniquely determine the functional form connecting the three parameters.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on general self-organized critical systems exhibiting long-range spatio-temporal correlations, analyzed using frameworks involving Tsallis entropy and anomalous diffusion characterized by a memory exponent $\alpha$.

**Key observables.** $q$ (Tsallis index), $D$ (Hausdorff dimension), and $\alpha$ (memory exponent).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The closure is validated for various regimes, including the Euclidean limit ($\alpha(1)=1$) and the maximally subdiffusive regime ($D	o\infty$, $\alpha 	o 1/2$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The core assumption is that phase-space self-consistency dictates a unique algebraic closure among $q$, $D$, and $\alpha$. It notes limitations regarding the $q<1$ regime.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the 'Troika critical curve' in $(q, D, \alpha)$ space, showing that experimental data points from various physical systems cluster closely around this theoretical parametric curve.

**Paper structure.** The paper first identifies the three independent parameters ($q, D, \alpha$) and then derives the necessary algebraic closure by enforcing self-consistency constraints. It subsequently validates this derived 'Troika relation' against a wide array of empirical data sets.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Self-organized critical systems often exhibit three macroscopic features simultaneously: nonextensive thermodynamics (quantified by the Tsallis index $q$), structural fractality (measured by the Hausdorff dimension $D$), and non-Markovian dynamics (characterized by the memory exponent $α$). Historically, these parameters have been treated as independent, to be empirically fitted case by case. Here we demonstrate that phase-space self-consistency imposes a unique algebraic closure: $α=D/(2D-1)$. This relation, together with $q=1+1/D$ derived from the extensivity of Tsallis entropy on fractal supports, yields the known result $α=1/(3-q)$ as a consequence, not as an independent assumption. The closure contains no free parameters and satisfies the physical boundary conditions $α(1)=1$ (ballistic transport in Euclidean spaces) and $α\to1/2$ as $D\to\infty$ (maximally subdiffusive regime). We validate the Troika relation across eight independent experimental systems, including seismicity, electromagnetic precursors, EEG, urban networks, botanical architectures, and space plasma. All measured values fall within error bars of the theoretical prediction, establishing the universality of the closure.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops the Principle of Biological Time Equivalence (PBTE), framing aging not by chronological time but by the consumption of a finite 'entropy budget' derived from physiological cycles. By applying open-system thermodynamics, it shows that the cardiac clock exhibits a robust, mass-independent entropy cost per beat across mammals, while the respiratory clock fails this test when measured empirically.

**Why it may be interesting.** The application of entropy balance principles to biological time provides a novel physical constraint on life history evolution. The successful prediction of mass-independent energy costs across vastly different body sizes is analogous to finding universal scaling laws in complex quantum or condensed matter systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a thermodynamic framework (PBTE) explaining persistent temporal invariants, such as fixed lifetime cycle counts in cardiac or respiratory systems, across vast variations in body size and metabolism.

**Main result.** The mass-specific entropy cost per physiological cycle ($ar{\sigma}_0$) is predicted to be invariant with body mass for the cardiac clock, providing a robust thermodynamic interpretation of allometric cancellation. However, this invariance fails when tested using measured metabolic rates for the respiratory clock.

**Method.** The framework uses open-system thermodynamics ($\dot{S} = \dot{e}_p - \dot{h}_d$) to define biological proper time based on accumulated entropy production relative to an average cycle cost. This leads to a cycle-count relation $N^\star = \Sigma / \langle\sigma_0angle$.

**Model / system.** The model treats living organisms as open, non-equilibrium dissipative systems. The core concept is the Principle of Biological Time Equivalence (PBTE), which reinterprets physiological cycles as accumulating a finite 'entropy budget' ($\Sigma$).

**Key observables.** Mass-specific entropy cost per cycle ($ar{\sigma}_0$), Lifetime Cycle Count ($N^\star$), and the derived biological proper time coordinate ($	ext{APBTE}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Metabolic Power ($P$), Body Temperature ($T$), Physiological Frequency ($f$), and Body Mass ($M$). The scaling laws $P \propto M^{3/4}$ and $f \propto M^{-1/4}$ are crucial.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the homeostatic approximation $\dot{e}_p \simeq P/T$ and assumes that life history variations (clade differences) can be systematically parameterized by multiplicative factors ($\Phi_C$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the near-perfect flatness of the mass-specific cardiac entropy cost ($ar{\sigma}_H(M)$) vs. body mass, confirming $M^0$ scaling, while also showing that respiratory cycle counts exhibit clade-dependent vertical offsets rather than continuous mass dependence.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from fundamental open-system thermodynamics to derive the PBTE relation ($N^\star = \Sigma / \langle\sigma_0angle$). It then tests this theory by comparing the scaling invariance of cardiac vs. respiratory clocks, concluding with an interpretation of clade differences as structured thermodynamic strategies.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Warm-blooded vertebrates accumulate approximately conserved numbers of physiological cycles over a natural lifetime: of order $10^9$ heartbeats and $10^8$--$3\times10^8$ breaths. These regularities are not exact constants, but their persistence across orders-of-magnitude variation in body mass, metabolic power, physiological frequency, and lifespan suggests that biological time is not measured by chronological duration alone. We develop the Principle of Biological Time Equivalence (PBTE), a thermodynamic framework in which lifetime cycle count is determined by the ratio between total lifetime entropy production and the entropy cost of one physiological cycle. Starting from the open-system entropy balance $\dot S=\dot e_p-\dot h_d$, we define the entropy cost per cycle as $σ_0=dΣ/dN$, where $dΣ$ is the entropy produced as the physiological clock advances by $dN$ cycles. For an adult homeostatic regime, this gives the cycle-count relation $N_\star=Σ/\langleσ_0\rangle$, with $Σ=\int_0^L \dot e_p(t)\,dt$, where $N_\star$ is the lifetime cycle count, $Σ$ is total lifetime entropy production, and $\langleσ_0\rangle$ is the lifetime-averaged entropy cost per cycle. In the homeostatic limit, $\dot e_p\simeq P/T$, so direct measurement of metabolic power $P$, body temperature $T$, and physiological frequency $f$ gives $σ_0\simeq P/(Tf)$. PBTE converts the empirical lifetime-cycle invariants into entropy-cost invariants. Under Kleiber metabolic scaling and quarter-power physiological-frequency scaling, the mass-specific entropy cost satisfies $\barσ_0=P/(TfM)\propto M^{3/4+1/4-1}=M^0$, providing a thermodynamic interpretation of allometric mass cancellation.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a unified theoretical framework by merging the entropic-neck picture with the Mori-Zwanzig formalism to explain glassy slowing down. It demonstrates that structural relaxation is governed by the entropy loss associated with passing through narrow configurational bottlenecks. This mechanism naturally explains the crossover from high-temperature local dynamics (Rosenfeld scaling) to low-temperature activated behavior (Adam-Gibbs relation).

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous application of projection operator techniques (Mori-Zwanzig) to derive non-Markovian memory kernels from geometric constraints (the bottleneck) provides a powerful template for understanding slow dynamics in complex many-body systems, applicable beyond simple liquids.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work addresses the origin of the dramatic dynamical slowdown observed in supercooled liquids, specifically explaining the crossover between high-temperature local dynamics and low-temperature activated structural relaxation.

**Main result.** A unified theoretical framework is developed showing that structural relaxation is controlled by the narrowing of configurational pathways (entropic bottlenecks), naturally unifying Rosenfeld excess-entropy scaling with the Adam-Gibbs relation.

**Method.** The authors combine Zwanzig's entropic-neck picture with the Mori-Zwanzig memory-function formalism to derive an effective generalized Langevin equation for slow variables.

**Model / system.** The system is supercooled liquids whose dynamics are mapped onto a configuration space featuring metastable basins separated by narrow, entropy-controlling 'necks.' The model uses coupled slow variables: progress (interbasin motion) and neck openness.

**Key observables.** Relaxation times ($	au(T)$), configurational entropy ($S_{conf}$), excess entropy ($S_{ex}$), and the effective memory kernel components.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature ($T$), Configurational Entropy ($s_c(T)$), Neck Deficit ($\Delta\Sigma_{	ext{neck}}$), and the crossover temperature $T_{cross}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The theory assumes that structural relaxation can be decomposed into dynamics governed by local structure (high T) and rare, cooperative passage through narrow entropic bottlenecks (low T). The derivation relies on linearizing the free-energy surface near these bottlenecks.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically illustrate the entropic bottleneck picture, showing progress ($X$) between basins connected by a variable cross-section neck ($Q$), which dictates the effective potential and memory kernel.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing the physical problem (slowdown) to introducing the theoretical tools (Mori-Zwanzig/Entropic Neck). It then derives the dynamics, showing how eliminating the fast neck coordinate generates a long-lived, entropy-controlled memory kernel that dictates the crossover between RS and AG regimes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The dramatic slowdown of dynamics in supercooled liquids is accompanied by a sequence of dynamical crossovers, most notably the transition from high-temperature collision-dominated transport to low-temperature activated structural relaxation. A particularly striking manifestation of this change is the crossover from Rosenfeld excess-entropy scaling to the Adam--Gibbs relation. In this work we develop a theoretical framework based on a configuration-space extension of Zwanzig's entropic-neck picture and combine it with a Mori--Zwanzig memory-function formalism to address anomalies of supercooled liquids. The central idea is that structural relaxation is controlled by the narrowing of configurational pathways connecting metastable basins of the inherent-structure landscape. Starting from coupled slow variables describing intrabasin motion and neck fluctuations, we derive a reduced generalized Langevin description in which elimination of the neck coordinate generates a long-lived memory kernel and naturally leads to entropy-controlled activated dynamics. At high temperatures the neck is broad and readily accessible, yielding Rosenfeld-type transport governed primarily by local structural entropy. Upon cooling, progressive neck constriction produces an increasing entropy deficit, leading to Adam--Gibbs behavior and activated relaxation. Within this picture, fragility acquires a simple geometric interpretation: fragile liquids are characterized by a rapid collapse of the effective configurational neck with decreasing temperature, whereas strong liquids exhibit a much slower evolution of accessible pathways. The framework does not by itself compute the configurational entropy, mismatch penalty, or cooperative length from microscopic interactions; its aim is to provide a dynamical and geometrical interpretation.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper presents a novel, fully quantum algorithm for simulating the 1D advection-diffusion equation using the Lattice Boltzmann Method. **Why it may be interesting.** This work directly applies advanced quantum computation techniques (quantum walks, unitary evolution) to solve a fundamental problem in fluid dynamics, bridging theoretical quantum algorithms with practical condensed matter/fluid physics modeling.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to develop a fully quantum algorithm capable of solving the one-dimensional linear advection-diffusion equation using the Lattice Boltzmann Method (LBM). This aims to surpass the limitations of existing hybrid quantum-classical approaches.

**Main result.** The proposed fully quantum algorithm was successfully simulated on a quantum simulator, matching classical results. While testing on physical hardware showed expected decoherence noise fluctuations, it demonstrated the potential for a measurement-free time evolution step.

**Method.** The work compares a hybrid quantum-classical scheme with an improved, fully quantum approach that minimizes measurements by encoding state information across time steps to calculate subsequent equilibrium distributions directly within the quantum circuit.

**Model / system.** The simulation targets the 1D linear advection-diffusion equation solved via the LBM. The computational platform involves quantum circuits implemented on simulators and tested on a 133-qubit quantum processor.

**Key observables.** Particle density (rho) and fluid velocity (u), extracted from the final state vector $|\psiangle$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The system size is defined by the number of lattice points ($N$), and time evolution involves discrete steps ($\Delta t$). The hardware test utilized a 133-qubit machine.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The key assumption for improvement is that information can be retained quantum mechanically across time steps, bypassing the classical measurement bottleneck inherent in hybrid methods. Decoherence noise limits current hardware performance.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

A fully quantum algorithm for solving the one-dimensional linear advection-diffusion equation using the Lattice Boltzmann method as a numerical procedure is presented in this work. We start by presenting a state of the art of the current usage of quantum algorithms for solving ordinary and partial differential equations. We then describe two algorithms for the one-dimensional Lattice Boltzmann method with two degrees of freedom. The first one is an existing hybrid quantum-classical algorithm with measurements at each time step, and the second one is our improved version, viz. a fully quantum algorithm where only one measurement is needed at the end of the algorithm. The fully quantum algorithm is first executed on a quantum simulator and then compared with a classical approach. Subsequently, the fully quantum algorithm is run on a quantum system with 133 qubits to investigate the effect of noise and the depth of the circuit on the output state. We find fluctuations in the final result due to the decoherence noise of the qubits.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study demonstrates that incorporating ions only at the termini of one block in diblock copolymers can stabilize highly frustrated network phases. The stabilization arises because the resulting ion clustering generates a favorable electrostatic correlation energy that compensates for the inherent geometric packing frustration. This establishes curvature-selective end-group association as a general design principle for accessing complex polymer topologies.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on polymer physics, the mechanism—where local electrostatic interactions (ion correlation energy) overcome entropic/packing penalties to stabilize a specific geometry—is analogous to understanding complex ordering driven by localized quantum or strong Coulombic forces in other many-body systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to identify physical mechanisms that can stabilize topologically complex, highly frustrated phases (like the primitive cubic $	ext{Im}ar{3}	ext{m}$ network) in diblock copolymers, which are otherwise unstable due to severe packing penalties.

**Main result.** End-functionalized ions introduce a stabilizing electrostatic energy gain by promoting local ion clustering into curved geometries, allowing these frustrated phases to become thermodynamically stable below the neutral system's order-disorder transition.

**Method.** The research employs an advanced 'ion-correlation augmented self-consistent field theory,' which allows for the explicit calculation of nonperturbative electrostatic correlation energy contributions.

**Model / system.** The model uses AB diblock copolymer melts where one block is end-functionalized with localized charges (ions). The system's phase behavior is mapped by comparing the free energies of various ordered morphologies.

**Key observables.** Free energy decomposition, particularly the electrostatic correlation energy ($\Delta f_{e,corr}$), and the relative stability of candidate phases (L, $	ext{Im}ar{3}	ext{m}$, etc.).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Strong ion-correlation regime ($\Gamma \approx 25$), ion size ($a$), and segregation strength ($\chi N$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The theory assumes a uniform dielectric constant, neglecting dielectric contrast between blocks, and initially neglects excluded volume interactions among ions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate schematics of ion clusters and spontaneous curvature in the copolymers, alongside free energy comparisons for various candidate morphologies (L, $	ext{Im}ar{3}	ext{m}$, etc.).

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem by noting the instability of frustrated phases; it then introduces end-functionalization as a solution. The core is the theoretical derivation showing how ion correlations stabilize these structures, culminating in the general principle that curvature-selective association dictates phase stability.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Block copolymers self-assemble into ordered nanostructures whose geometry is governed by a competition between interfacial energy and chain conformational entropy. While this competition produces a rich sequence of morphologies, topologically complex ``frustrated'' phases such as the primitive cubic ($Im\bar{3}m$) network incur severe packing penalties and are difficult to access in neutral systems. Here we show that ions functionalized at the termini of one block in an AB diblock copolymer melt introduce a qualitatively new stabilization mechanism. Strong ion correlations drive chain-end association and generate a curvature preference toward the charged domain; the resulting tendency of end-localized ion clusters to adopt compact, curved geometries selectively favors the highly frustrated $Im\bar{3}m$ single-network over the classical phases, in a region of parameter space lying below the order-disorder transition of the neutral system. Free energy decomposition reveals that the electrostatic energy, arising almost entirely from beyond-mean-field ion correlations, becomes increasingly negative with increasing interfacial curvature. In the primitive cubic network, pronounced local segregation of ions into the cylindrical struts generates compact curved clusters whose correlation energy gain more than offsets the enhanced packing frustration, so the very geometry that is the source of packing frustration in neutral systems becomes the source of its stability here. Increasing ion size weakens correlations and suppresses the $Im\bar{3}m$ phase, consistent with experimental observations. Our results establish curvature-selective end-group association as a general principle for accessing frustrated topologies in block copolymer systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates the complex interplay between magnetism, orbital physics, and lattice vibrations in kagome antiferromagnets like $	ext{ScFe}_6	ext{Ge}_6$. By comparing it to a CDW-hosting analogue ($	ext{FeGe}$), the researchers show that while charge order is absent in $	ext{ScFe}_6	ext{Ge}_6$, its magnetic transition ($T^*$) is marked by orbital-selective band shifts and magnetoelastic coupling. This highlights that out-of-plane correlations and orbital degrees of freedom are crucial drivers in these correlated materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** The detailed investigation into how subtle changes in spin order (magnetoelastic coupling) can manifest as measurable electronic band shifts or phonon anomalies provides a rich platform for studying coupled quantum orders, relevant to understanding emergent phenomena in strongly correlated systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research aims to understand the general conditions governing spin-correlated Charge Density Wave (CDW) order in kagome antiferromagnets, contrasting systems that exhibit CDW with those that do not.

**Main result.** In $	ext{ScFe}_6	ext{Ge}_6$, a magnetic transition at $T^*=195 	ext{ K}$ is linked to orbital-selective band shifts and magnetoelastic coupling involving out-of-plane phonon modes, suggesting orbital physics plays a key role where CDW order is absent.

**Method.** The study combines multiple experimental techniques including Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES), Raman spectroscopy, and magnetic/resistivity measurements, supplemented by theoretical calculations.

**Model / system.** The physical system is the FeGe-family of kagome antiferromagnets, specifically comparing $	ext{FeGe}$ (CDW exhibiting) with $	ext{ScFe}_6	ext{Ge}_6$ (lacking CDW). The focus is on the interplay between spin, orbital, lattice, and charge degrees of freedom.

**Key observables.** Orbital-selective band shifts ($	ext{ARPES}$), anomalous kinks in phonon frequencies ($	ext{Raman}$), magnetic susceptibility ($\chi(T)$), and resistivity ($ho(T)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** $T^* = 195 	ext{ K}$ (magnetic transition temperature); $\lambda \approx 0.3$ (electron-phonon coupling constant).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on assigning specific orbital characters ($	ext{dz}^2$) to the observed electronic bands based on polarization dependence and analogy with known materials.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate structural details, magnetic susceptibility curves, $	ext{ARPES}$ spectra showing Dirac cones and band shifts across $T^*$, and Raman spectra revealing an anomalous kink in the out-of-plane phonon mode near $T^*$.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares $	ext{ScFe}_6	ext{Ge}_6$ to $	ext{FeGe}$, using structural, magnetic, electronic ($	ext{ARPES}$), and vibrational ($	ext{Raman}$) measurements to pinpoint the mechanism driving anomalies at $T^*$, ultimately arguing for the enhanced role of orbital-selective physics.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In strongly correlated materials such as high-temperature superconductors, the relation between charge density wave (CDW) order and magnetism remains an important unresolved problem. FeGe is the first kagome metal known to exhibit CDW order deep within an antiferromagnetic state, accompanied by an unconventional evolution of lattice symmetry. To elucidate the general conditions governing such spin-correlated CDW order, we investigate ScFe$_6$Ge$_6$, which lacks CDW order and therefore exhibits reduced involvement of charge degrees of freedom while retaining other properties of FeGe. Instead of a CDW order, ScFe$_6$Ge$_6$ undergoes a magnetic transition at $T^*$ = 195 K. Across this transition, angle-resolved photoemission and Raman spectroscopy reveal orbital-selective behavior confined to a single kagome Dirac band, together with electron-phonon and magnetoelastic coupling to an out-of-plane phonon mode. These results suggest that orbital-selective physics and out-of-plane correlations play enhanced roles in realizing spin-correlated CDW order in magnetic kagome metals.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper proposes a novel, highly efficient method for distributing entanglement globally using satellites equipped with rare-earth ion qubits. It models the entire process—from atmospheric channel loss to multi-stage entanglement swapping—to demonstrate that this transportation-based repeater scheme is superior to existing proposals. This work advances the feasibility roadmap for global quantum internet infrastructure.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the engineering challenges of scaling quantum networks by providing a detailed theoretical framework for overcoming distance limitations inherent in photonic quantum communication.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to develop a viable scheme for distributing quantum entanglement over global distances using satellite links.

**Main result.** A transportation-based, quantum repeater approach utilizing rare-earth ion qubits in satellites is theoretically shown to outperform other methods by minimizing link losses and achieving high fidelity (e.g., 93.9% globally).

**Method.** The analysis combines theoretical modeling of free-space optical channel losses with quantum information protocols like heralded entanglement generation and deterministic entanglement swapping.

**Model / system.** The system involves ground stations connected via Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) satellites carrying nodes based on rare-earth-ion qubits. The process models the sequential steps of generating, storing, and swapping entangled pairs across multiple passes.

**Key observables.** EPR pair fidelity ($F$), entanglement generation probability ($p_{HEG}$), achievable rate ($	ext{N}_{	ext{tot}}$), and background light induced error ($\epsilon_B$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** VLEO altitude (250 km), coherence time ($T_2 > 13$ hours), sky brightness ($H_b$), and various loss coefficients ($\eta_{at}, \eta_{SMF}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The scheme assumes the feasibility of active error correction, sufficient qubit coherence times, and that background light noise can be quantified using Poisson statistics.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the entanglement distribution process (Satellite $	o$ Ground $	o$ Swapping), performance comparisons between different protocols (e.g., transport vs. memory-based), and the dependence of fidelity on network length or error sources.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the physical link efficiency ($\eta_c$) via atmospheric modeling, to developing the quantum protocol using Markov chains for pair generation, and finally comparing this repeater scheme against direct relaying or memory-limited approaches.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose a scheme for distributing entanglement over global distances in a heralded manner by using satellites to physically transport entangled processor nodes with rare-earth-ion qubits. A full analysis of channel losses, errors and background light is performed to determine the fidelity and number of entangled pairs that can be distributed between two ground stations. We show that the scheme works already with a single satellite and can distribute close to the theoretical maximum number of entangled pairs that can be generated in a satellite overpass. In addition, we argue that in theory transportation-based schemes outperform other satellite-based schemes and can be scaled up to a constellation without additional channel losses. Daytime operation seems feasible as long as the sky is clear, with an EPR pair fidelity ranging from 99.3% at shorter network lengths to 93.9% with global coverage and can be further improved by active error correction or entanglement purification.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces particle exchange statistics as a novel computational resource for Quantum Machine Learning. By constructing kernels that smoothly interpolate between bosonic and fermionic limits using photonic simulation, the authors show that intermediate 'anyon' statistics significantly enhance feature space geometry and classification accuracy over standard limits.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a concrete physical mechanism—particle statistics—to tune the representational power of quantum circuits for ML tasks, bridging fundamental condensed matter concepts (anyons) with applied quantum computation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To investigate whether particle exchange statistics can serve as an intrinsic, physical design principle for enhancing Quantum Machine Learning (QML).

**Main result.** Anyonic kernels consistently outperform their bosonic and fermionic counterparts on classification benchmarks, demonstrating that exchange statistics fundamentally reshape the quantum feature space structure.

**Method.** The authors constructed a quantum kernel family interpolating between bosonic, fermionic, and anyonic statistics using photonic encoding. They analyzed this framework by calculating effective dimension, kernel geometry diagnostics, and direct machine learning performance.

**Model / system.** The model uses an N-particle quantum feature state $|\Phi_\phi(\mathbf{x})angle$ derived from linear optical unitaries applied to entangled photons, where the exchange phase $\phi$ controls the statistics. This simulates fractional exchange behavior.

**Key observables.** Test accuracy on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST; Effective Dimension ($D_{	ext{eff}}(\phi)$); Geometric diagnostic ($gC_\phi$); Model complexity ratio ($R_\phi$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Exchange Phase ($\phi$), which controls the statistics (Bosonic $\phi=0$, Fermionic $\phi=\pi$, Anyonic $0 < \phi < \pi$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model simplifies physical anyons by reducing the braid structure to permutations, retaining only the exchange phase information.

**Figures summary.** Figures show that intermediate fractional phases maximize effective dimension and geometric separation. Test accuracy plots confirm peak performance at intermediate $\phi$, while KTA and inter-class distance diagnostics also favor these non-integer statistics.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the quantum kernel across different exchange phases ($\phi$). It first establishes the theoretical framework using particle state preparation, then quantifies the enhancement via feature space analysis (dimension/geometry), and finally validates the findings through supervised learning benchmarks.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The power of quantum computing and quantum machine learning relies on harnessing uniquely quantum phenomena as computational resources. While superposition, coherence and entanglement have been central to this effort, the role of particle exchange statistics remains largely unexplored. Here, we introduce a quantum kernel framework that unifies bosonic, fermionic, and anyonic (fractional) exchange statistics within a single learning paradigm. We study this family of kernels from three perspectives. At the representation level, Haar-averaged effective-dimension analysis shows that fractional exchange phases access feature-space directions inaccessible to the purely symmetric or antisymmetric limits. At the level of kernel geometry, the corresponding Gram matrices show greater separation from the distinguishable-particle baseline and reduced label-dependent model complexity. Finally, on learning benchmarks, anyonic kernels consistently outperform their bosonic and fermionic counterparts, with stronger target alignment and more favorable class geometry. Together, these findings show that exchange statistics reshape the structure and geometry of quantum feature space, leading to enhanced learning performance. Our work identifies particle exchange statistics as an overlooked computational ingredient for quantum machine learning and provides the first systematic comparison of quantum learning models across exchange phases.

</details>

**Summary.** This work applies theoretical models, including Stochastic Agglomeration Theory and constraint analysis, to understand the structural stability and glass transition temperature of borosilicate glasses. By linking local network connectivity (isostaticity) to overall composition, the authors successfully predict how varying the $	ext{B}_2	ext{O}_3$ content affects the material's physical properties.

**Why it may be interesting.** The application of topological concepts like isostaticity and network connectivity to predict macroscopic phase transitions ($T_g$) in amorphous materials bridges solid-state physics with graph theory, which has parallels in complex system modeling relevant to quantum networks.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To validate simple mathematical models for glass transition by applying them to borosilicate glasses, linking structural constraints (isostaticity) to macroscopic properties like the glass transition temperature ($T_g$).

**Main result.** The stochastic agglomeration model successfully predicts the $T_g(z)$ dependence on modifier concentration, and isostaticity theory provides necessary compositional constraints for optimal network structure.

**Method.** Theoretical modeling combining concepts from constraint theory (isostaticity) with statistical mechanics principles derived from an agglomeration model.

**Model / system.** The system studied is a mixture of $	ext{SiO}_2$ and $	ext{B}_2	ext{O}_3$ glass formers modified by $	ext{Na}_2	ext{O}$ and $	ext{CaO}$. The theory uses structural units ($	ext{Q}^4, 	ext{Q}^3$) and analyzes network connectivity via constraints to predict stability.

**Key observables.** Glass transition temperature ($T_g(z)$), average coordination number ($\langle m angle$), constraint ratio ($	ext{N}_c/	ext{N}_a$), and structural rigidity defect ($r$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Modifier concentrations (e.g., $z$ for $	ext{B}_2	ext{O}_3$), optimal coordination number ($m=2.4$), and temperature dependence parameters derived from energy barriers.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The system can be modeled by stochastic agglomeration, the network structure is governed by local constraints (isostaticity), and structural integrity requires maintaining a specific average ring count (near 6).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate Bethe lattices used to model connectivity and show the evolution of $T_g(z)$ across different compositions.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the physical system (borosilicate glasses) to applying theoretical tools: first, constraint theory determines optimal local structure ($\langle m angle = 2.4$); second, ring counting provides compositional constraints; finally, the stochastic agglomeration model predicts the temperature dependence of $T_g$.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present a structural analysis of glasses formed by mix of SiO2 and B2O3 glass formers with soda and lime modifiers (Na2O and CaO), which provide a good testing ground for Stochastic Agglomeration Theory. With local structural units properly identified, we can reproduce the one-parameter glass transition temperature T_g (z) curve for the family of (0.75-z) SiO_2 + 0.15 Na_2O + 0.10 CaO + z B_2O_3 glasses studied experimentally by Smedskjaer et al.

**Summary.** This theoretical work explores emergent electronic orders in three-valley moiré superlattices. By analyzing symmetries and using advanced mean-field techniques, the authors map out a phase diagram showing competition between valley-polarized and intervalley-coherent states. The findings highlight that complex correlated physics, distinct from simpler two-valley systems like graphene, dictates the ground state depending on stacking geometry and interaction strength.

**Why it may be interesting.** The detailed symmetry analysis and classification of correlated phases in a multi-valley system provide a template for understanding complex electronic ordering driven by geometry, relevant to topological materials and strongly interacting quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates interaction-induced symmetry breaking and determines the energetically favored ground state orders (IVC vs. flavor-polarized) in moiré superlattices possessing three electronic valleys.

**Main result.** The system exhibits a rich variety of intervalley-coherent (IVC) phases, which can be stabilized either by superexchange at moderate bandwidths or deep within the strong-coupling regime due to deviations from flat-metric conditions.

**Method.** The analysis combines symmetry arguments with advanced theoretical techniques, including unrestricted Hartree-Fock calculations and analytical strong-coupling frameworks applied to a continuum model.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled as moiré superlattices formed by twisting two identical materials whose low-energy physics resides near the M points, featuring three distinct valleys ($\eta=1, 2, 3$). The Hamiltonian incorporates both single-particle dispersion and repulsive density-density interactions.

**Key observables.** Valley Polarization (VP) order parameters, Intervalley Coherent Order parameters ($	ext{IVC}_{3\pm}$, NIVC), and the resulting band structure gaps/insulating nature.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Twist angle ($	heta$), interaction strength parameterized by relative permittivity ($\epsilon_r$), and electron filling fraction ($
u$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on mean-field decoupling (Hartree-Fock) and often assumes the strong-coupling limit or uses perturbation theory to treat deviations from ideal conditions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate moiré band structures, phase diagrams mapping ground state character ($	ext{VP}$, $	ext{IVC}$ phases) against parameters like $	heta$ and $\epsilon_r$, and order parameter dependencies on these tuning knobs.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the symmetry constraints of the three-valley system, then applying strong-coupling/Hartree-Fock methods to map out candidate ordered states ($	ext{IVC}$ vs. $	ext{VP}$), and finally using perturbation theory to determine which state minimizes the total energy under varying physical conditions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate interaction-induced symmetry breaking in moiré superlattices created by twisting two identical materials where the electronic low-energy degrees of freedom reside in the vicinity of the $M$ points. Based on general symmetry arguments, we identify and classify the possible candidate instabilities that, besides flavor polarized states, also involve a variety of intervalley-coherent (IVC) orders. This complexity is related primarily to the presence of three valleys, instead of the well-studied scenario of two, e.g., in graphene: IVC states can couple all three valleys identically, with a non-trivial sign structure, or even with different magnitudes. We study the energetics using an analytical strong-coupling framework and unrestricted Hartree-Fock applied to the full continuum model, with very good agreement between the two approaches. Interestingly, depending on stacking, IVC instabilities not only appear due to superexchange at moderate bandwidths, but also deep in the strong-coupling regime as a result of deviations from the flat-metric condition. Our work demonstrates that twisted $M$-point materials provide a rich playground for complex correlated physics and highlights differences and similarities to twisted multilayer graphene.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces the Multi-Axial Projective Sphere (MAPS) as a novel geometric framework designed to overcome the visualization limitations encountered when representing qudit quantum states ($d \ge 3$). It successfully maps these complex state spaces onto an intuitive $S^2$ structure using multiple intersecting axes. Furthermore, the authors propose phase-axial gates ($	ext{PASS}_d$) that allow for controlled manipulation and transformation of these high-dimensional quantum states.

**Why it may be interesting.** For AMO/open systems researchers, this work provides a powerful conceptual tool to visualize complex high-dimensional phase spaces that might otherwise require intractable mathematical formalism, potentially aiding the understanding of multi-level atomic or superconducting qubit interactions.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is developing a generalized visualization framework for the high-dimensional quantum state-space of qudits ($d \ge 3$), as standard methods like the Bloch sphere fail beyond qubits.

**Main result.** The authors introduce the Multi-Axial Projective Sphere (MAPS), a novel $S^2$ framework that successfully visualizes global and relative phases for higher-$d$ qudit states. They also propose associated phase-axial gates ($	ext{PASS}_d$) to manipulate these states geometrically.

**Method.** The method involves constructing the MAPS using $n$ intersecting spatial axes, which provides a structural generalization of the Bloch sphere by mapping complex state spaces onto an easily visualized 3D manifold. Novel unitary gates are defined based on phase rotations along these axes.

**Model / system.** The system under study is the qudit, characterized by $d$-valued quantum states $|\psiangle$ and density operators $ho$. The mathematical framework relies on generalizing concepts from $	ext{SU}(2)$ to $	ext{SU}(d)$.

**Key observables.** Global and relative phases of the quantum state; visualization of pure states (circles) and mixed states (polygons/polyhedra).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimension $d$ of the qudit ($d \ge 3$), the number of axes $n$, and pseudo-orthogonal angles $\Delta_d = 2\pi/d$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that a generalized, simplified geometric representation (MAPS) can capture the essential topological features of high-$d$ quantum state spaces for visualization purposes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the Bloch sphere ($d=2$), and then show specific MAPS constructions for $d=3, 4, 5$. Subsequent figures demonstrate how mixed states are visualized as polygons and how $	ext{PASS}_d$ gates perform controlled swiveling and shifting of these phases.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the limitations of existing visualizations (Bloch sphere failure for $d \ge 3$), introduces MAPS as the solution, details its geometric construction using multiple axes, proposes the $	ext{PASS}_d$ gate operation, and concludes with examples showing state transformations and potential applications in quantum machine learning.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Visualizing the d-valued quantum state-space of quantum systems serves as a foundational pillar for the scientific research and practical applications in quantum computing and information science, where d >= 2. The 2-valued quantum states of a qubit are elegantly visualized on the three-dimensional Bloch sphere. In contrast, expanding this geometrical paradigm to visualize higher d-valued quantum states of a qudit (d >= 3), e.g., a qutrit (d=3), ququadit (d=4), and quintit (d=5), leads to severe structural and topological complexities. This paper introduces a new generalized three-dimensional framework to effectively visualize higher d-valued quantum states of a qudit, in the aspects of ease of illustration, structural simplicity, and natural representation for researchers and engineers. We called this new framework the "multi-axial projective sphere (MAPS)", which consists of n projectional intersecting spatial axes, where d-1 <= n <= 0. We also propose a group of novel d-valued phase axial-based gates, to swivel and shift d-valued quantum states of a qudit along these n axes. Our generalized framework could be used for visualizing high-dimensional data for practical applications, e.g., machine learning, quantum machine learning, and quantum chemistry, where every axis of the MAPS represents a single feature of such data with its corresponding distinct values.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper analyzes Quantum Illumination by replacing idealized entangled probes with generic Haar-random states constrained by symmetry. It rigorously proves that the achievable detection rate is determined solely by the dimension of the accessible symmetry sector, establishing a deep connection between quantum channel discrimination and conservation laws in many-body physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful theoretical generalization for quantum sensing protocols, demonstrating that structural symmetries inherent in physical systems can dictate fundamental resource limits, shifting focus from state preparation to subspace engineering.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates Quantum Illumination (QI), a quantum-assisted protocol for detecting weakly reflecting objects in noisy environments, by analyzing its performance using random probe states.

**Main result.** The asymptotic detection advantage is governed not by the total Hilbert space dimension but by the dimension of the accessible symmetry-protected correlation subspace. This shows that generic many-body states constrained by conservation laws can yield near-optimal quantum hypothesis testing resources.

**Method.** The analysis employs tools from quantum channel discrimination and asymptotic hypothesis testing, specifically calculating the quantum Chernoff exponent ($ar{\xi}$) for ensembles generated by Haar-random unitaries restricted to symmetry-resolved subspaces.

**Model / system.** The model is Quantum Illumination (QI), which treats target detection as distinguishing between two competing quantum channels ($\Phi_0$ vs $\Phi_1$) acting on a signal-idler probe system. The probes are generated using random unitaries sampled from the Haar measure, constrained by symmetry.

**Key observables.** The primary observable is the asymptotic Chernoff exponent ($ar{\xi}$), which quantifies the exponential decay rate of the minimum error probability in distinguishing the two channels.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Key parameters include the dimension of the accessible symmetry sector ($d_\lambda$), the noise strength, and the probe state structure (Haar-random vs. maximally entangled).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the random unitaries are sampled from the Haar measure ($\mu_H$) and relies on concentration inequalities to relate the ensemble average exponent to the mean value.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 schematically illustrates QI using Haar-random probes with a fiducial state, demonstrating the theoretical framework for the analysis.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing QI as a channel discrimination problem (Chunk 2), then generalizing the probe states to random unitaries (Haar measure) (Chunk 3). It then develops the core theory by analyzing how symmetry constraints restrict the accessible correlations, showing that the rate is governed by the symmetry sector dimension rather than the full space dimension (Chunks 4 & 5).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum illumination provides a quantum advantage in detecting weakly reflecting objects embedded in a noisy environment, even when environmental noise destroys most of the initial entanglement. We investigate this advantage using Haar-random probe states constrained to symmetry-resolved subspaces. Employing tools from quantum channel discrimination and asymptotic hypothesis testing, we derive the discrimination exponents associated with Haar-random probe ensembles and identify the role of symmetry in determining their performance. We show that typical states drawn from fixed-charge sectors achieve the same asymptotic quantum-illumination advantage as maximally entangled probes. In particular, we show that the effective thermal-noise suppression and the corresponding Chernoff exponent are governed by the dimension of the accessible symmetry sector. Our results reveal that the operational resource underlying quantum illumination can be generalized from fine-tuned structure of a specific probe state to the existence of a large symmetry-protected correlation subspace. These findings establish a direct connection between quantum illumination, symmetry-resolved typicality, and quantum channel discrimination, and demonstrate that near-optimal quantum hypothesis testing resources can emerge naturally from generic many-body quantum states constrained by conservation laws.

</details>
