**Summary.** This theoretical work analyzes quantum oscillations near high-angular-momentum band inversion using minimal two-band and four-band models. The key finding is that the interference between time-reversal partners causes deviations from standard theory, producing unique temperature-dependent suppression signatures whose number directly tracks the angular momentum $l$. This offers an experimentally accessible fingerprint for characterizing such topological electronic states.

**Why it may be interesting.** The focus on temperature-dependent interference effects and the explicit link between oscillation features (suppression temperatures) and a geometric parameter ($l$) provides a powerful, measurable diagnostic tool for exotic topological phases in condensed matter systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates quantum oscillations (QOs) in electronic systems exhibiting High-Angular-Momentum (HAM) band inversion, particularly focusing on regimes beyond standard metallic Fermi surface quantization.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate that HAM band inversion leads to characteristic deviations from the Lifshitz-Kosevich form, manifesting as non-monotonic temperature dependence and suppression temperatures whose number scales with the angular momentum $l$.

**Method.** Theoretical analysis involves calculating the oscillatory density of states (LEDOS) using semiclassical quantization rules derived from generalized two-band and four-band Hamiltonians.

**Model / system.** The models include a minimal chiral two-band Hamiltonian and an extended time-reversal invariant four-band model, designed to capture topological transitions associated with band inversion ($\delta\mu$).

**Key observables.** Quantum oscillation amplitude, frequency ($F_0$), temperature dependence of the LEDOS, and characteristic suppression temperatures ($T_c$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Angular momentum $l$, detuning parameter $\delta\mu$ (controlling inversion), magnetic field $B$, and temperature $T$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on semiclassical quantization rules for both metallic (Fermi surface crossing) and insulating (band-edge averaging) regimes, and assumes the applicability of thermal averaging kernels.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate band structures showing inversion transitions, Landau level spectra ($E_{1,2}^n$ vs $1/B$), and crucially, detrended LEDOS oscillations confirming spectral weight suppression at characteristic temperatures whose count follows $l$.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first analyzing the two-band model in the insulating regime, then extending to a four-band time-reversal symmetric system. The core development involves deriving the total oscillatory LEDOS via interference between time-reversal partners, leading to the identification of $l$-dependent signatures.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum oscillations provide a fundamental probe of electronic structure in magnetic fields, revealing the Fermi surface topology in metals, and/or the quasiparticle properties even in the insulating regimes. Here we study quantum oscillations in minimal models of high-angular-momentum (HAM) band inversion for both a chiral two-band model and a time-reversal-invariant four-band model. In the former case, finite oscillations can appear at the hybridized Chern-insulating regime due to thermal-activated excitations. In the latter case, interference between the two time-reversal-related blocks drives a strong deviation from the Lifshitz-Kosevich form, producing a non-monotonic temperature dependence of the oscillation amplitude and characteristic suppression temperatures whose number follows the angular momentum $l$. These results identify experimentally accessible signatures of HAM band inversion and provide a framework for other discrete-symmetry-related hybridizations and excitonic pairings.

</details>

**Summary.** This work proposes a novel quantum-classical hybrid framework for time series forecasting by integrating quantum model predictions with classical error correction. The method calculates the initial prediction using a quantum circuit and then refines it by having a classical network predict the remaining systematic error. Results show that this synergistic combination significantly outperforms purely classical or single-model approaches on multiple benchmark datasets.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly related to AMO physics, the methodology of using quantum circuits as feature extractors or pattern recognizers within a complex physical system (like time series data) mirrors concepts in open quantum systems modeling where environmental noise or residual dynamics are modeled classically.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research aims to improve time series forecasting accuracy by developing a novel hybrid model that combines quantum machine learning capabilities with classical error-correction techniques.

**Main result.** The proposed quantum-classical hybrid system consistently provided superior predictive performance across most tested problems compared to single classical or purely classical-classical hybrid models.

**Method.** The core methodology involves using a quantum model to generate an initial prediction, calculating the residual error, and then employing a classical model (like MLP or LSTM) trained on these errors to correct the quantum output. The final prediction is the sum of the quantum estimate and the classically predicted error correction.

**Model / system.** The system utilizes parameterized quantum circuits for the quantum component ($	ext{Q}$) and established deep learning architectures (MLP, LSTM, NBEATS) for the classical component ($	ext{C}$). The hybridization is structured as $\hat{y}_{Q+C} = \hat{y}_Q + \hat{e}_C$, where $\hat{e}_C$ corrects the quantum prediction based on past errors.

**Key observables.** Mean Squared Error (MSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) are used to quantify predictive accuracy across seven benchmark time series datasets (Temperature, Star, Sunspot, Milk, Gasoline, Car, Lake).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of quantum features ($n_Q$) and the structure/hyperparameters of both the quantum circuit and the classical network are key parameters optimized during training.

**Assumptions / limitations.** It is assumed that time series patterns contain components best captured by quantum phenomena, and that these quantum insights can be systematically combined with classical error modeling to yield synergistic improvements.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate performance comparisons via heat maps (showing MSE across various model combinations) and plots demonstrating the cumulative error accumulation over time for different hybrid models on specific datasets like Sunspot.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the need for advanced forecasting, details the quantum-classical error correction framework ($	ext{Q} ightarrow 	ext{Error} ightarrow 	ext{C}$), compares performance metrics (MSE/MAE/MAPE) against classical baselines ($	ext{C}$, $	ext{C}+	ext{C}$), and concludes that the hybrid approach offers significant, though context-dependent, gains.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Time series forecasting largely benefits from combining the strengths of different models, especially using a scheme where a model corrects another model by capturing supplementary patterns from forecasting errors. Concurrently, quantum models are providing a means to augment the classical capacity, including in time series forecasting, by acting alongside classical models in hybrid architectures. In this work, we propose the first forecasting system based on error correction that jointly uses quantum and classical models. Here, quantum models first extract patterns by exploring quantum phenomena, and classical models capture the remaining patterns from the quantum errors. Compared to classical single models and classical-classical hybrid models based on error correction, the complementary capacity that emerges from this quantum-classical system provided the best results in most of the addressed problems. Therefore, this work paves the way to introduce quantum models in established hybridization schemes for time series forecasting.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper presents the CAHR algorithm to reconstruct complex error hypergraphs governing detector noise in Quantum Error Correction codes. It demonstrates that by separating topology discovery from parameter fitting, it can accurately model multi-body errors even with finite experimental data. This methodology is vital for advancing practical fault-tolerant quantum computing hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous mathematical tools to extract physical structure from noisy quantum measurements, which is crucial for designing reliable fault-tolerant hardware protocols. The explicit handling of high-order correlations addresses a major bottleneck in current QEC characterization techniques.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is accurately characterizing complex, multi-body error correlations (high-order hyperedges) from raw experimental syndrome statistics for fault-tolerant quantum computation.

**Main result.** The proposed CAHR algorithm successfully reconstructs the exact physical hypergraph topology for both surface and color codes with zero false positives when sufficient statistics are available. Furthermore, structural topology is shown to be more critical for decoder performance than precise continuous parameter estimation under noise.

**Method.** A Correlation-Analysis-based Hypergraph Reconstruction (CAHR) algorithm is introduced, which uses exact algebraic correlation equations derived from the Detector Error Model (DEM) and a top-down concurrent-pruning strategy to invert syndrome statistics into discrete hypergraphs.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is Quantum Error Correction (QEC), specifically analyzing detector error models represented as hypergraphs. The analysis uses concepts like moment equations derived from the Tensor Network Detector Error Model (TNDEM) applied to codes like the rotated surface code and 2D color code.

**Key observables.** Syndrome variables ($\sigma_i$), correlation moments ($M_{\alpha}$), physical error probabilities ($p_{\alpha}$), and the final Logical Error Rate ($p_L$) from decoding simulations.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Sample size (number of shots, e.g., $5 	imes 10^6$ to $1.5 	imes 10^7$), code distance ($d=5$), and hyperedge order (up to 8-body).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the Pauli error model for noise, relies on a two-stage inference paradigm (topology first, then parameters), and uses Gaussian approximations when analyzing variance cascades.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare end-to-end decoding performance ($p_L$) between an 'Inference DEM' (derived from noisy data) and a 'Given DEM Topology' (ideal structure), showing the latter is far more robust. One figure illustrates the additive accumulation of inference errors (variance cascade) across code depth.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces CAHR as a globally consistent framework, details its two-stage process (topology discovery followed by parameter optimization), validates it on specific codes (surface/color), and concludes by comparing the operational robustness of topology reconstruction versus simple parameter fitting.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Fault-tolerant quantum computing fundamentally relies on the accurate characterization of circuit-level noise to optimize decoding algorithms. However, extracting complex multi-body error correlations remains challenging. Contemporary greedy inference algorithms can suffer from statistical distortion, discarding true physical mechanisms while introducing many unphysical false positives. Here, we introduce the Correlation-Analysis-based Hypergraph Reconstruction (CAHR) algorithm, a globally consistent framework to invert experimental syndrome statistics directly into discrete physical hypergraphs. By coupling exact algebraic correlation equations with a top-down concurrent-pruning strategy, CAHR recovers the fault topology without false positives for both $d=5$ rotated surface codes and dense 8-body 2D color codes in our benchmark settings. Furthermore, we show that exact continuous parameter extraction in dense codes is limited by a \textit{variance cascade}, where absolute statistical variance accumulates linearly from high- to low-degree mechanisms. This motivates a two-stage inference paradigm: utilizing CAHR to extract the fault topology, followed by continuous probability optimization. This provides a practical approach for characterizing and decoding highly correlated noise in realistic quantum hardware.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper demonstrates that dynamically modulating the frequency of a quantum oscillator can significantly enhance precision in frequency estimation beyond static limits. By tailoring the temporal modulation profile $f(t)$, researchers show that the Quantum Fisher Information scales robustly as O(F(t)^2). This establishes a universal paradigm for designing next-generation, high-precision quantum sensors.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a general theoretical framework for optimizing quantum sensors by treating time modulation itself as a controllable resource, which is highly relevant to advanced quantum optics and sensing applications.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to enhance frequency estimation precision beyond conventional limits set by static encoding mechanisms in quantum metrology.

**Main result.** Temporal modulation allows for the deterministic engineering of arbitrary precision scaling, with the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) scaling as O(F(t)^2).

**Method.** The authors analytically derive the QFI using a dynamic encoding protocol driven by time-dependent frequency modulation $\Omega(t) = \omega_0 f(t)$ in the adiabatic limit.

**Model / system.** The model used is the Quantum Harmonic Oscillator (QHO), which serves as a universal platform for continuous variable quantum metrology. The Hamiltonian incorporates the time-dependent frequency modulation $\Omega(t)$.

**Key observables.** Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), $F_g$, and the resulting precision limit governed by the Quantum Cramér-Rao Bound ($\Delta g$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The modulation profile function $f(t)$, its time integral $F(t) = \int f(s)ds$, and the energy constraint $E_0 = E(t)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is performed in the adiabatic regime ($\left|rac{\dot{\Omega}(t)}{\Omega(t)^2}ight| \ll 1$), assuming Gaussian initial states.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the time evolution of the QFI components (shearing, squeezing, rotation) and compare the enhancement ratio $R(t)$ for different modulation profiles (linear, quadratic, exponential).

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem in quantum metrology, introduces the dynamic encoding protocol via $\Omega(t)$, calculates the QFI by decomposing it into components, derives the scaling laws based on the adiabatic approximation, and concludes by demonstrating the universal applicability of this time-dependent control.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Frequency estimation, a cornerstone of quantum metrology, has been significantly enhanced by advanced quantum sensing strategies. However, most protocols rely either on static or time-independent encoding mechanisms, inherently limiting their achievable precision scaling, or on control strategies requiring changing the Hamiltonian and/or implementing feedback mechanisms. To overcome this, we investigate a simpler dynamical encoding protocol where the quantum oscillator is driven by a general continuous temporal frequency modulation $Ω(t) = ω_0 f(t)$. We analytically demonstrate that for a given modulation profile $f(t)$ and its corresponding time-integral $F(t)$, the quantum Fisher information (QFI) scales as $\mathcal{O}(F(t)^2)$. This enhancement stems from the fact that temporal encoding fundamentally alters the mechanism of dynamical phase accumulation. Crucially, when evaluated under the energy and evolution-time constraints, this framework reveals a genuine precision enhancement over the conventional time-independent baseline. By analyzing explicit polynomial and exponential modulations, we establish that arbitrary precision scaling can be deterministically engineered, with ultimate bounds that are asymptotically saturable via optimal homodyne detection. Our framework provides a universal paradigm for exploiting time-dependent quantum control in next-generation sensors.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper addresses the ambiguity in defining quantum superposition by reformulating it geometrically within complex projective space. It proposes that the superposition of two states is uniquely defined as the straight line connecting them in this geometric space. This provides a rigorous mathematical foundation independent of traditional summation rules.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a fundamental, purely geometrical reinterpretation of one of quantum mechanics' most basic concepts, potentially offering insights applicable beyond standard Hilbert space formalism.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The standard description of quantum superposition is mathematically ambiguous because the summation operation used in Hilbert space does not translate cleanly to the quotient projective space ($	ext{CP}(H)$).

**Main result.** A rigorous, geometrical definition of superposition is proposed: it is defined as the unique complex line passing through two distinct pure states viewed as points in $	ext{CP}(H)$.

**Method.** The paper develops a geometric framework by treating quantum states as points in complex projective space and defining superposition based on collinearity axioms.

**Model / system.** The model uses pure quantum states, represented geometrically as points in the complex projective space $	ext{CP}(H)$, where $H$ is a complex Hilbert space. The analysis compares this geometric definition to standard basis expansions.

**Key observables.** Superposition itself (defined as a line/subspace), and the comparison between superposition and classical statistical mixtures derived from orthonormal basis expansions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The structure of the underlying Hilbert space $H$ and its associated projective geometry $	ext{CP}(H)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that viewing quantum states as points in $	ext{CP}(H)$ provides a natural geometric setting, and the definition relies on properties analogous to those found in complex projective geometry.

**Paper structure.** The paper first identifies the ambiguity of superposition in $	ext{CP}(H)$, then proposes the line-based geometric definition for two states. It subsequently contrasts this with basis expansion and discusses generalizations to other mathematical spaces.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The usual description of the superposition of two (pure quantum) states is ambiguous, since the binary operation of summation in a Hilbert space does not pass down to the quotient projective space. Even though Dirac noted this as early as 1930, it is often asserted that the superposition is a binary operation acting on two states with a value that is a unique state. The goal for this note is to motivate a rigorous, geometrical definition of the superposition of states in the setting of complex projective space, which has been argued elsewhere to be the natural geometric phase space for quantum theory. The upshot is that the new definition of the superposition of two pure states, viewed as two distinct points in the projective space, is the unique (complex) line on which those two points lie. Finally, a comparison is given between superposition and expansion in an orthonormal basis.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper resolves a modified version of the Kretschmann-Schlingemann-Werner conjecture concerning quantum channels. It proves an inequality bounding the operator norm difference between two Stinespring isometries by the diamond norm distance between their corresponding quantum channels. This result provides a powerful quantitative tool for comparing quantum processes.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous quantitative link between the operational distance (diamond norm) of quantum processes and the structural distance (operator norm) of their underlying representations, which is fundamental for characterizing process fidelity in open quantum systems theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses a modified version of the Kretschmann-Schlingemann-Werner (KSW) conjecture, which relates the distance between two quantum channels to the distance between their Stinespring representations.

**Main result.** It proves that for any two quantum channels $\Phi_1$ and $\Phi_2$, there exists a unitary $U$ such that the operator norm distance between their respective isometries satisfies $\|V_1-({f1}\otimes U)V_2\|_\infty\leq\sqrt{2}\|\Phi_1-\Phi_2\|_{\diamond}$.

**Method.** The proof utilizes advanced tools from quantum information theory, including the diamond norm ($\|\cdot\|_{\diamond}$), operator norms ($\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$), and properties derived from the Stinespring dilation theorem.

**Model / system.** The system under study involves general quantum channels $\Phi: \mathbb{M}_d(\mathbb{C})	o \mathbb{M}_n(\mathbb{C})$, which are completely positive and trace-preserving maps. These channels are analyzed via their Stinespring isometries $V$.

**Key observables.** Diamond norm distance ($\|\cdot\|_{\diamond}$) between channels, and the minimum operator norm distance $\min_{U\in U(m)} \|V_1 - (1 \otimes U)V_2\|_{\infty}$ between the Stinespring isometries.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The constant factor $\sqrt{2}$ in the derived inequality is shown to be optimal.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The proof holds for any common dilation space $\mathbb{C}^m$ associated with the channels.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes relationships between various norms and uses mathematical tools like Lemma 3 to derive the final inequality, resolving the modified KSW conjecture in the affirmative.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Let $Φ_1, Φ_2 : \mathbb{M}_d(\mathbb{C})\to \mathbb{M}_n(\mathbb{C})$ be two quantum channels with respective Stinespring isometries $V_1, V_2 : \mathbb{C}^{d}\to \mathbb{C}^{n} \otimes \mathbb{C}^{m}$ on any common dilation space $\mathbb{C}^{m}$. We prove that there exists a unitary $U$ on $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ such that $\|V_1-({\bf1}\otimes U)V_2\|_\infty\leq\sqrt{2\|Φ_1-Φ_2\|_\diamond},$ thus resolving vom Ende's modification of the Kretschmann-Schlingemann-Werner conjecture in the affirmative.

</details>

**Summary.** This research investigates how different starting points (initializations) affect the accuracy of electronic structure calculations using a complex quantum ansatz (LUCJ) simulated on a quantum computer. The key finding is that while initial parameters can vary wildly, the final calculated energy remains robustly accurate, suggesting that the core quantum diagonalization process dictates performance rather than the initialization method itself.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the practical implementation challenges of quantum chemistry algorithms on near-term quantum hardware by identifying computationally cheaper, yet accurate, initialization pathways that bypass resource-intensive methods like full CCSD.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study analyzes how different initialization strategies affect the accuracy of electronic energy calculations performed using the Local Unitary Cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz within a quantum-centric supercomputing framework.

**Main result.** The final electronic energies recovered by the SQD algorithm are largely insensitive to the initial parameters, suggesting that configuration recovery during the diagonalization process is more critical than the proximity of the initialization method to CCSD.

**Method.** The authors compare six initialization strategies (including CCSD, MP2, random, and zero) for the LUCJ ansatz by running calculations on molecular systems using the sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) algorithm.

**Model / system.** The model is electronic structure calculation of molecules solved via the Schrödinger equation using a nonrelativistic Born-Oppenheimer Hamiltonian. The wave function employs the LUCJ ansatz, which incorporates unitary orbital rotations and Jastrow factors.

**Key observables.** Mean Absolute Percentage Errors (MAPEs) in $t_2$-amplitudes; resulting SQD electronic energies compared to CCSD reference energy; chemical accuracy ($\pm 1.6$ mEh).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Basis sets tested include STO-3G, cc-pVDZ, and aug-cc-pVDZ; ansatz depths ($L=1$ to $5$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption challenged is that the initial parameters' proximity to CCSD dictates the final energy accuracy in the quantum simulation.

**Figures summary.** Figures summarize MAPE comparisons between initializations and show energy deviation trends ($\Delta E$) across ansatz depths and basis sets, demonstrating the lack of correlation between initialization error and final energy quality.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares multiple initialization methods (CCSD, MP2, ML-derived) for the LUCJ ansatz parameters. It analyzes performance metrics like MAPE in amplitude space versus the resulting converged electronic energies obtained via the SQD algorithm across various molecular systems and basis sets.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this study, we analyze the choice of local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz initialization and sensitivity of the sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) algorithm within the quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) framework. We examine six initialization strategies, including those based on coupled-cluster singles and doubles (CCSD), Møller-Plesset second-order perturbation theory (MP2), data-driven coupled-cluster (DDCC), and trivial (zeroes and random) initializations, across twelve molecular systems and three basis sets (STO-3G, cc-pVDZ, and aug-cc-pVDZ). We find that while the mean absolute percentage errors (MAPEs) between the alternative and CCSD-initialized t2-amplitudes span many orders of magnitude, the resulting SQD energies are largely insensitive to this variation. In particular, most initializations recover energies within chemical accuracy (+/-1.6 mEh) of the CCSD reference, with convergence improving as the basis set size increases. Notably, random initialization achieves performance competitive with CCSD across all basis sets, while zeroes initialization, despite having smaller deviations from CCSD, yields the worst energy agreement. Our results highlight that the proximity to the CCSD initialization is not a reliable predictor of the quality of electronic energies. These findings establish that configuration recovery within SQD, rather than circuit initialization, is the dominant factor governing energy accuracy, and suggest that computationally cheaper initialization strategies are viable alternatives to CCSD for QCSC workflows

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates the feasibility of running NIST PQC algorithms like Dilithium and SPHINCS+ on embedded systems. Testing revealed that standard microcontrollers fail due to memory or time constraints. The authors successfully overcame this by integrating an NTT accelerator into an FPGA fabric, proving that hardware-software co-design is essential for practical quantum-resistant embedded security.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly related to fundamental AMO physics, the rigorous engineering challenge of implementing complex mathematical structures (like polynomial arithmetic in PQC) onto constrained digital hardware shares conceptual parallels with simulating quantum dynamics on limited computational resources.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study addresses the practical implementation challenges of NIST-standardized Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) signature schemes on resource-constrained embedded hardware.

**Main result.** Pure software PQC implementations are non-viable for standard microcontrollers due to severe memory and timing limitations; however, a hardware-software co-design approach using FPGA acceleration achieves millisecond performance rates.

**Method.** The authors conducted a comparative performance analysis by implementing SPHINCS+ and CRYSTALS-Dilithium on two platforms: an STM32 microcontroller (software-only) and a Zynq-7000 SoC (hardware/software co-design).

**Model / system.** The experimental platforms include the ARM Cortex-M4 based STM32F407G microcontroller and the Xilinx Zynq-7000 ZedBoard SoC, which integrates a processor system with an Artix-7 FPGA fabric for acceleration.

**Key observables.** Execution times for key generation and signature generation (measured in minutes vs. milliseconds); feasibility of execution under limited SRAM capacity.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The comparison highlights the limitations imposed by 192 KB SRAM on the MCU versus the capability of offloading computationally heavy primitives like NTT to the FPGA fabric.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The necessity of hardware acceleration is established because general-purpose MCUs lack the necessary resources for high-degree polynomial multiplications required by modern PQC schemes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the setup of both the STM32F407G and Zynq-7000 boards, alongside schematic representations of the signing procedures for Dilithium and SPHINCS+.

**Paper structure.** The paper follows a structure moving from identifying the quantum threat to testing baseline software performance on an MCU (showing failure), and finally proposing and demonstrating a hardware-software co-design solution using FPGA acceleration to achieve practical performance metrics.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The rapid advancement of quantum computing poses a significant threat to classical public-key cryptographic systems, necessitating the transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). This study investigates the implementation challenges of NISTstandardized signature schemes on resource-constrained embedded hardware. We present a comparative analysis of SPHINCS+ and CRYSTALS-Dilithium on an ARM Cortex-M4 (STM32F407G) microcontroller. Our findings reveal that SPHINCS+ is practically unusable in this software-only environment, with impractical execution times. Furthermore, the reference Dilithium implementation failed to execute entirely on the MCU due to severe RAM and timing constraints. To overcome these hardware limitations, we integrated a hardware-accelerated Dilithium core onto a Xilinx Zynq-7000 ZedBoard SoC. By implementing a specialized Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) accelerator in the FPGA fabric, we achieved successful execution with performance rates for key generation and signature generation at millisecond levels. These results demonstrate that while pure software PQC is non-viable for standard microcontrollers, a hardware-software codesign approach provides the necessary efficiency for quantumresistant embedded systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This work systematically studies Ta-doping in WTe2, demonstrating that doping enhances carrier mobility and deepens 2D character, leading to record magnetoresistance. The study reveals that while anisotropy is tunable, the system undergoes a transition to a multi-pocket Fermi surface at higher doping levels. Overall, it establishes that key transport parameters—anisotropy, compensation, and mobility—can be independently controlled in this topological semimetal.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter physics, the ability to tune electronic properties (anisotropy, mobility) via chemical doping provides a model for engineering quantum states or transport channels relevant to advanced quantum devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates whether the anisotropic transport characteristics of WTe2 persist when chemically substituted with Ta, and how doping affects the control mechanisms behind large magnetoresistance (XMR).

**Main result.** Ta substitution enhances carrier mobility and deepens quasi-two-dimensional Fermi surface character, leading to record high MR values; however, at higher doping levels, the system transitions to a multi-pocket Fermi surface regime.

**Method.** The research combines angle-dependent magnetotransport measurements with structural analysis (XRD) and fitting data using mass anisotropy scaling frameworks.

**Model / system.** The physical system is single-crystalline Ta-doped WTe2 ($	ext{Ta}_x	ext{W}_{1-x}	ext{Te}_2$), a layered van der Waals semimetal. Analysis employs semiclassical models for magnetoresistance and nonlinear Hall resistivity to probe multiband transport.

**Key observables.** Magnetoresistance (MR) up to 58,211%; mass anisotropy parameter ($\gamma$); effective carrier mobility ($\mu_{	ext{eff}}$); residual resistivity ratio (RRR).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Doping concentration ($x=0, 0.05, 0.1$); Temperature ($T$); Magnetic field strength ($B$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the mass anisotropy scaling framework and semiclassical models for transport phenomena.

**Figures summary.** Figures show XRD patterns confirming $c$-axis contraction with Ta content, and magnetotransport curves demonstrating a sharp rise in MR at $x=0.1$.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the effect of Ta doping on crystal structure (XRD), transport anisotropy ($\gamma$ scaling), carrier dynamics ($\mu_{	ext{eff}}$ enhancement), and Fermi surface topology (breakdown of single-ellipsoid scaling, nonlinear Hall response).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The observation of extremely large magnetoresistance in WTe2 has attracted considerable attention towards understanding its underlying origin. With its layered van der Waals structure, the question that remains largely unexplored is whether the three-dimensional anisotropic transport characteristics of WTe2 persists under chemical substitution. Here, we present a systematic angle-dependent magneto-transport study of single-crystalline TaxW1-xTe2 (x = 0, 0.05, 0.1). The results are analysed within a mass anisotropy scaling framework to extract the mass anisotropy parameter γ as a function of temperature and doping. It is observed that Ta substitution leads to monotonic increase of γ across all temperatures, indicating a progressive deepening of quasi-two-dimensional Fermi surface character. Ta doping also leads to a substantial improvement in crystalline quality, reflected in a pronounced increase in the residual resistivity ratio. Despite weakening electron-hole compensation, the magnetoresistance rises sharply to ~58,211% at x = 0.1, which is assigned to a substantial enhancement in carrier mobility. Rietveld refinement confirms a systematic c-axis contraction with Ta content, identifying the structural origin of the enhanced anisotropy. The mass anisotropy scaling that holds for x = 0 and x = 0.05 breaks down for x = 0.1, where the angular magneto-resistance anisotropy substantially exceeds single-ellipsoid predictions, pointing to a multi-pocket Fermi surface with distinct anisotropies. Nonlinear Hall resistivity provides independent evidence for the underlying multiband character of transport in this system. These findings demonstrate that Fermi surface anisotropy, carrier compensation, and mobility are independent parameters that can lead to tuneable control of large magnetoresistance in topological semimetal WTe2.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops and compares advanced protocols for generating magic states necessary for fault-tolerant quantum computing. It integrates code switching and lattice surgery to transfer logical information between different QEC codes like color and surface codes. The results propose optimized methods that improve fidelity and reduce resource overhead compared to existing techniques.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides concrete, resource-aware benchmarks for implementing universal quantum computation primitives (magic states) using state-of-the-art QEC structures, which is crucial for scaling up any physical quantum hardware platform.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work aims to thoroughly compare the resource requirements and performance between two methods for generating magic states: code-switch-based factories versus direct magic-state cultivation.

**Main result.** Two new fault-tolerant protocols combining phase-kickback checks with a transversal non-Clifford gate were proposed, showing consistent performance across different noise models and code distances.

**Method.** The study uses end-to-end simulations of the entire magic-state preparation process, involving lattice surgery (LS) to transfer state information between various Quantum Error Correction (QEC) codes like color codes and surface codes.

**Model / system.** The research focuses on fault-tolerant quantum computation using multiple QEC codes, including the 2D/3D color code, rotated surface code, and tetrahedral code. The protocols are designed to generate logical magic states ($T|+ angle_L$ or $S|+ angle_L$).

**Key observables.** Logical infidelity, success rate of magic-state preparation, and the expected space-time volume per successful shot (V).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Physical gate error rates ($\epsilon$), code distances ($d=3, d=5$), and noise models (with/without idling noise).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often approximates noisy circuits due to large qubit counts and sometimes uses $S|+ angle_L$ as a proxy for the non-Clifford $T|+ angle_L$ state preparation.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the workflow of end-to-end magic state preparation using code switching, comparing logical infidelity vs. noise strength across different dimensions and protocols.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops new combined protocols by integrating transversal non-Clifford gates with established techniques like code switching (CS) and lattice surgery (LS), culminating in detailed performance comparisons across various error regimes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Magic-state preparation is a central component of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Recent theoretical and experimental successes in code-switch-based magic-state preparation have underscored the promise of these methods for quantum error correction. Similarly, magic-state cultivation has likewise been demonstrated in both numerical and experimental settings. However, a thorough comparison between magic-state cultivation and code-switch-based magic-state factories is still missing. In this work, we carry out end-to-end simulations of magic-state preparation using code switching and compare its resource requirements and performance against magic-state cultivation. As part of this analysis, we develop a lattice-surgery protocol for transfer between the doubled color code and the rotated surface code. We extend the complete code-switching protocol to the $d=5$ doubled color code and perform the corresponding end-to-end simulations. Finally, we propose two fault-tolerant magic-state preparation protocols that combine phase-kickback checks with a transversal non-Clifford gate.

</details>

**Summary.** The research investigates the structural basis for altermagnetism in $	ext{Ca}_3(	ext{Ru},	ext{Ti})_2	ext{O}_7$. Despite theoretical predictions of a symmetry-lowering phase transition ($Pn21a$), detailed X-ray diffraction experiments found no evidence of this lattice distortion. The authors conclude that the observed electronic symmetry breaking is likely decoupled from measurable structural changes, suggesting an electronically driven mechanism for altermagnetism.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant because it addresses the fundamental question of whether magnetic/electronic phase transitions in correlated oxides are accompanied by measurable lattice distortions or if they can be purely electronic, a key concept in modern condensed matter theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates whether the predicted structural phase transition from a polar altermagnet candidate ($	ext{Ca}_3	ext{Ru}_2	ext{O}_7$) is structurally mandated or purely electronic in origin.

**Main result.** Experimental X-ray diffraction measurements failed to detect the symmetry-lowering $Pn2_1a$ phase, placing tight upper bounds on structural distortions. Instead, evidence suggests that the observed symmetry breaking is primarily electronic, leading to a chemically tunable G-type altermagnetic (G-ALM) state within the higher symmetry $Bb2_1m$ structure.

**Method.** The work combines synchrotron X-ray diffraction measurements with advanced DFT+U calculations incorporating spin-orbit coupling and Hubbard U parameters.

**Model / system.** The system is $	ext{Ca}_3(	ext{Ru},	ext{Ti})_2	ext{O}_7$, a correlated electron oxide exhibiting complex magnetic ordering (AFM, G-ALM) and potential structural transitions between $Bb2_1m$ and $Pn2_1a$.

**Key observables.** Diffraction peak intensities ($I_{HKL}$), structural distortion amplitude ($\lambda$), electronic band gap opening, and magnetic transition temperatures ($T_N, T_S$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The critical comparison is between the DFT-predicted large structural displacement ($\sim 1 	ext{ pm}$) versus the experimentally constrained upper bound on distortion ($\lambda \lesssim 0.08$ to $0.22$), and the role of Ti doping ($x$) as a tuning parameter.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that experimental background noise provides reliable, quantitative upper bounds on structural distortions, and that DFT+U calculations accurately capture the electronic ground state evolution with varying correlation strength (Hubbard U).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the comparison between predicted $Bb21m$ and $Pn21a$ structures, show the absence of expected $Pn21a$ diffraction peaks at low temperatures, and map out phase diagrams showing electronic/magnetic transitions as a function of Ti doping or Hubbard U.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical prediction of a structural transition ($Bb21m 	o Pn21a$), then using high-sensitivity X-ray diffraction to experimentally constrain this distortion, and finally reconciling the negative structural findings with positive electronic measurements (nonlinear transport) by proposing an electronically driven symmetry breaking mechanism.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The interplay between polar and altermagnetic orders remains largely unexplored in the broader landscape of correlated electron systems. Ca$_{3}$Ru$_{2}$O$_{7}$ has been proposed by density functional theory (DFT) as a polar altermagnet, reliant on the transformation of experimentally reported $Bb2_{1}m$ phase to a lower symmetry $Pn2_{1}a$ structure. Here, we perform a targeted search for the $Pn2_{1}a$ phase using synchrotron X-ray diffraction on single crystals of Ca$_{3}$Ru$_{2}$O$_{7}$ and Ca$_{3}$(Ru$_{0.99}$Ti$_{0.01}$)$_{2}$O$_{7}$. No diffraction signature of the $Pn2_{1}a$ structure is detected down to 20 K within experimental limits of $\sim$60-200 fm atomic displacements, significantly smaller than the DFT prediction of $\sim$1 pm. Combined with recent nonlinear transport measurements, our structural study suggests Ca$_{3}$Ru$_{2}$O$_{7}$ as a unique system where strong electron correlations drive an electronic phase transition without any measurable lattice symmetry change. With Ti substitution exceeding $\sim$3%, a chemically tunable altermagnetic phase with $Bb2_{1}m$ structure emerges. The study highlights the importance of sub-picometer metrology towards de-convolving structural versus electronic origins of altermagnets.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces a novel geometric decomposition for calculating the hard-sphere partition function in $d$ dimensions. It factors the total partition function into an upper bound derived from close-packing geometry and an exponential penalty term related to void space fragmentation. This provides a powerful, geometrically controlled framework for understanding fluid thermodynamics across all densities.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the rigorous geometric bounding techniques used to control fluctuations in the void space are highly relevant for developing controlled approximations in quantum many-body systems where local correlations dominate.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To derive a rigorous geometric decomposition for the $d$-dimensional hard-sphere partition function, $Q(N, V, T)$.

**Main result.** The partition function is shown to factorize into a reference upper bound ($Q^*$) and an exponential penalty term: $Q \propto Q^* \exp(-NJ)$, where $J$ depends on the boundary-to-volume ratio of voids.

**Method.** The authors use geometric bounds, inspired by close-packing arguments and formalized via local density certificates (Blichfeldt-type), to establish an upper bound on the configurational integral.

**Model / system.** The system is a classical hard-sphere fluid in $d$ dimensions. The analysis focuses on calculating the partition function based on the available insertion volume ($V_I$) for adding particles without overlap.

**Key observables.** Hard-sphere partition function ($Q$), Insertion Probability ($\Pi_I$), Packing Fraction ($\phi$), and Compressibility Factor ($Z$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Dimensionality ($d$), Close-packing density ($\phi_{cp}$), and the ratio of surface area to volume of excluded regions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The rigorous derivation relies on the existence of a local density certificate that allows bounding the exclusion set volume, particularly at high densities.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare various bounds on the insertion probability ($\Pi_I$) against known exact solutions for low dimensions ($d=1$), and illustrate the decomposition of $Q$ into a reference bound ($Q^*$) and a geometric penalty factor.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically develops the factorization, first establishing upper bounds using geometry (Chunk 1), then deriving the finite-$N$ exact relationship involving insertion volume ratios (Chunk 2), and finally confirming thermodynamic consistency across low-density (van der Waals) and high-density (close-packed limit) regimes (Chunks 3 & 4).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We introduce a geometric decomposition of the hard-sphere partition function. Using a close-packing-inspired geometric bound on the available insertion volume, made rigorous when a corresponding local density certificate is available, we establish a reference upper bound $Q^\ast$ on the configurational integral. Factoring this upper bound out of the statistical geometric partition function of Speedy yields a new form for the $d$-dimensional partition function, $Q(N,V,T)=Q^\ast \exp(-N \mathcal{J})$, where $\mathcal{J}$ depends strictly on the boundary-to-volume ratio of the voids and the close-packing density. Overall, this work deepens our statistical geometric understanding of the hard-sphere system.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates the behavior of electron energy levels in super-heavy atoms ($Z>100$) where standard quantum electrodynamics predicts unphysical singularities. By incorporating the electron's Anomalous Magnetic Dipole Moment (AMDM) into the theoretical framework, the authors demonstrate that this contribution regularizes the wave functions and yields physically acceptable results for high Z numbers.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly tackles fundamental theoretical limitations in QED applied to extreme matter (super-heavy elements), providing an alternative regularization mechanism that has implications for understanding vacuum stability and atomic structure beyond current standard models.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study addresses the singularity issue encountered in standard Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) point-nucleus models when calculating electron energy levels for super-heavy atoms ($Z > 137$).

**Main result.** Incorporating the electron's Anomalous Magnetic Dipole Moment (AMDM) provides a sufficient condition to obtain regular wave functions and physically acceptable energy values even in the idealized point-nucleus limit for very high atomic numbers.

**Method.** The analysis involves modifying Dirac's equation with an effective Pauli Hamiltonian term representing the AMDM, leading to coupled differential equations solved using techniques like Whittaker functions and perturbation theory.

**Model / system.** The system is a single electron orbiting a super-heavy nucleus ($Z > 100$). The model uses a point-nucleus approximation but incorporates the AMDM contribution via an effective Hamiltonian modification to regularize the wave function at the origin.

**Key observables.** Energy eigenvalues $E(Z)$, critical atomic number $Z_{	ext{crit}}$ where $E=-m$, and the behavior of radial wave functions near the nucleus.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Fine structure constant ($\alpha$), AMDM parameter ($a = (g-2)/2$), and the atomic number $Z$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that including the AMDM contribution via an effective theory is sufficient to regularize the wave functions, even though finite nuclear size effects are usually required for full accuracy.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares numerically obtained eigenvalues from the AMDM model against results from finite-nucleus models. Figure 2 illustrates the behavior of a specific function related to the wave function in the point nucleus + AMDM model.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the problem of singularities in QED for super-heavy atoms. It then modifies the Hamiltonian using the AMDM, derives coupled differential equations, and solves them by analyzing near-origin behavior and transforming the problem into a Schrödinger-type equation to determine energy dependence on Z.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Super-heavy atoms ($Z > 100$) are usually studied in the context of the so-called ``Quantum Electrodynamics of Strong Fields''. In this theory the problem of the singularity in the electron energy whenever $Z > 137$ is overcome. This is done by considering the finite size of the nucleus and leads to interesting phenomena, such as the spontaneous production of positrons. Here, we show that taking into account the contribution from the Anomalous Magnetic Dipole Moment of the electron (by means of an effective theory), within a point-nucleus model, is a sufficient condition to obtain regular wave functions and physically acceptable energy values for $Z > 137$.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces QALM, a novel hybrid optimizer designed to improve quantum circuit synthesis. It combines the speed of rule-based optimization with the thoroughness of search algorithms by interleaving these two approaches. This allows QALM to achieve superior gate reduction rates compared to existing methods without incurring prohibitive computational overhead.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses algorithmic bottlenecks in quantum computation resource estimation, which is crucial for designing efficient circuits for near-term hardware devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Quantum circuit optimization aims to find an equivalent quantum circuit with minimum cost (e.g., gate count) by overcoming the limitations of local minima encountered by existing optimizers.

**Main result.** The proposed QALM optimizer outperforms existing rule-based and search-based methods in circuit reduction rates while maintaining high computational efficiency across a comprehensive benchmark suite.

**Method.** QALM employs a hybrid framework that interleaves exhaustive, targeted search capabilities with efficient, greedy rule-based optimization passes.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is quantum circuits represented as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), where qubits are wires and gates are nodes. Optimization requires maintaining circuit equivalence while minimizing cost metrics like gate count or depth.

**Key observables.** Circuit fidelity ($F$), total gate count reduction, two-qubit gate ($	ext{CX}$) reduction percentage, and optimization runtime.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The exploration depth parameter $k$ controls the balance between search (exploration) and rule application (exploitation).

**Assumptions / limitations.** It is assumed that interleaving search and rules provides a superior trade-off compared to using either method in isolation, despite the problem's inherent computational hardness.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare optimization trajectories showing QALM's ability to escape local minima; other figures illustrate performance comparisons across various benchmarks (e.g., fidelity vs. gate reduction).

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the fundamental limitations of greedy and pure search optimizers, proposes the interleaved QALM framework parameterized by an exploration depth $k$, details its iterative algorithm, and validates it against multiple state-of-the-art benchmarks.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum circuit optimizers face a fundamental limitation in how they tolerate temporary cost increases. At one extreme, greedy rule-based optimizers immediately apply any cost-reducing transformation, achieving high efficiency but quickly becoming trapped in local minima. At the other extreme, search-based optimizers accept cost-increasing moves to explore the circuit space and escape such minima. However, because search-based optimizers cannot determine within a reasonable time budget whether a given point is promising, that is, whether its neighborhood contains a deeper local minimum, they must blindly explore higher-cost regions. As a result, escaping the current basin to reach a promising point takes exponentially many steps.   In this work, we show that this limitation can be overcome with a hybrid framework that interleaves the exhaustive exploration capabilities of search algorithms with the efficiency of rule-based optimization. We implement this framework as QALM, a novel optimizer designed to escape local minima without incurring the runtime penalties of pure search. Crucially, our results demonstrate that QALM does not merely strike a balance; it outperforms existing rule-based and search-based optimizers in circuit reduction rates while operating with the computational efficiency of rule-based systems. In a comprehensive evaluation across 248 circuits, QALM matches or exceeds the fidelity of the strongest baseline on 83.9% of these circuits, given the same time budget.

</details>

**Summary.** This work presents a resource-efficient hybrid QAOA framework to solve the NP-hard power system islanding problem by combining quantum optimization with advanced classical post-processing. The method successfully recovers near-optimal, fully feasible islanding partitions on standard benchmark grids using shallow circuits. It establishes that structured post-processing is key to achieving physical validity and demonstrating a clear quantum resource advantage.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous development of energy descent frameworks (M. 3, M. 4, M. 5) with formal proofs of termination and feasibility is highly relevant to developing reliable quantum algorithms for complex physical systems beyond simple Hamiltonian simulation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Solving the NP-hard power system islanding problem, which requires partitioning a grid while satisfying complex physical constraints like power balance and connectivity.

**Main result.** A hybrid QAOA framework combining graph reduction and structured post-processing achieves Gurobi-optimal solution quality with a clear quantum resource advantage over vanilla QAOA on multiple IEEE benchmarks.

**Method.** The approach uses QAOA to minimize an objective function (cut value) encoded in a QUBO, followed by rigorous classical post-processing steps (like DFS and power flow checks) to enforce physical feasibility.

**Model / system.** The system is a power grid modeled as a graph where buses are partitioned into self-sufficient islands. The optimization involves minimizing the cut of active power flow while satisfying constraints on generator capacity, load balance, and connectivity.

**Key observables.** Feasible islanding decisions; minimized cut value (compared to Gurobi optimum); Power support margins ($P_{g,	ext{max}} - P_d$ and $Q_{	ext{max}} - Q_d$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Circuit depth ($p$), shot budget, penalty weights ($\lambda$), graph size (e.g., 57-bus IEEE system).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The core assumption is that structured post-processing can bridge the gap between raw quantum sampling outputs and physically realizable solutions; theoretical analysis relies on specific regularity hypotheses for convergence proofs.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the overall pipeline (setup $ightarrow$ QAOA encoding $ightarrow$ Execution $ightarrow$ Post-processing $ightarrow$ Solution extraction) and compare power flow capabilities across various IEEE test cases.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops from defining the NP-hard problem, formulating it as a constrained QUBO Hamiltonian, proposing graph reduction techniques, detailing multiple staged repair/descent methods (M.1 to M.5), providing theoretical convergence guarantees for these methods, and finally validating the best hybrid workflow on real quantum hardware.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum computing has rapidly emerged as a powerful paradigm for tackling computationally demanding problems. In particular, quantum optimization shows strong promise for hard combinatorial problems in power systems, where increasing distributed energy penetration heightens the need for intentional islanding to maintain grid reliability and resilience. However, power system islanding is an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem that becomes computationally prohibitive for classical solvers as network size grows, motivating the use of quantum computing as a promising alternative pipeline. This study develops a resource-efficient hybrid QAOA islanding framework that brings physics-constrained power-system partitioning into the quantum optimization workflow. The framework combines coherency-informed graph reduction, physics-aware constraint modeling, and structured post-processing to efficiently convert shallow-circuit QAOA samples into high-quality feasible islanding decisions without deep circuits or large shot budgets. The proposed framework is validated on the standard IEEE benchmark systems (9-, 14-, 24-, 30-, 39-, and 57-bus), demonstrating that the hybrid workflow achieves Gurobi-optimal solution quality with a clear quantum resource advantage over vanilla QAOA, while the resulting islanding solutions satisfy all physical feasibility requirements after network separation. This study establishes QAOA-based islanding as a viable quantum approach for critical infrastructure, with structured post-processing as the key enabler of quantum resource efficiency.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper rigorously analyzes why interpreting weights in linear regression fails when input features are highly correlated, even if predictions are accurate. Using eigenmode decomposition, it shows that multicollinearity generates unstable and oscillatory weight patterns. The key takeaway is that while regularization stabilizes the estimates, this stabilization does not equate to true physical interpretability.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous mathematical framework connecting statistical concepts like multicollinearity and model instability to the physical concept of 'interpretability' in data-driven science. It suggests that prediction performance (low MSE) is insufficient for claiming physical understanding.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the fundamental limits of interpretability when using multiple linear regression models, particularly when input features are strongly correlated (multicollinearity). It seeks to explain why weight estimates become unstable or oscillatory even if prediction accuracy remains high.

**Main result.** Multicollinearity causes weight instability through small-eigenvalue modes in the feature correlation matrix. While regularization like Ridge helps stabilize weights by suppressing these modes, it does not guarantee physical interpretability, as the resulting weights are highly dependent on the chosen regularization parameter alpha.

**Method.** The analysis combines theoretical linear algebra (analyzing eigenmodes of the feature correlation matrix) with statistical diagnostics (VIF calculation and analyzing weight fluctuations across bootstrap samples). It compares OLS and Ridge regression estimates.

**Model / system.** The model is Multiple Linear Regression ($\hat{\mathcal{Y}} = \sum \hat{w}(f) X(f)$), applied to diverse physical datasets such as superconductivity properties and glassy-dynamics structural descriptors. The analysis focuses on the mathematical structure imposed by highly correlated input features.

**Key observables.** Weight fluctuations (standard deviation across samples), weight oscillations across physically similar features, Maximum Variance Inflation Factor ($	ext{max } f\{	ext{VIF}(f)\}$), and the roughness measure ($S$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Regularization strength $\alpha$, eigenvalues ($\lambda(k)$) of the feature correlation matrix $C$, and sample size $N_S$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that interpretability requires both statistical robustness (low weight variance) and physical consistency (stable signs/magnitudes for similar features). It models correlations using Toeplitz matrices in some sections.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the three scaling regimes of $	ext{max } f\{	ext{VIF}(f)\}$ vs. $\alpha$ ($\propto \alpha^{-1}$ to $\propto \alpha^{-2}$), show weight oscillations decreasing with increasing regularization strength, and display eigenvectors corresponding to small eigenvalues.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the problem (weight instability under multicollinearity) to developing theoretical tools (eigenmode analysis, VIF generalization for Ridge). It then applies these tools across various datasets, culminating in a detailed mathematical derivation showing how regularization suppresses oscillatory modes associated with small eigenvalues.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Interpreting machine-learning models has attracted increasing attention, particularly in the physical sciences, where one often seeks to understand the underlying mechanisms rather than merely make predictions. Multiple linear regression is often regarded as an interpretable alternative to more complex models, such as deep neural networks, because its predictions are expressed as explicit weighted sums of input features. However, when input features are strongly correlated, namely in the presence of multicollinearity, the learned weights can exhibit large dataset-to-dataset fluctuations and oscillatory behavior across physically similar features, making their interpretation difficult or even impossible. Although the instability of the weights under multicollinearity is well known in statistics, its consequences for physical interpretation, in particular its connection to oscillatory weights across physically similar features, have not been systematically clarified. Here, we theoretically discuss the mechanism behind this loss of interpretability by analyzing the eigenmodes of the feature correlation matrix. We show that small-eigenvalue modes associated with multicollinearity amplify fluctuations in the weights and generate oscillatory patterns that do not necessarily reflect meaningful contributions. We test this theoretical picture numerically on physics datasets and show that Ridge regularization suppresses these unstable modes, although the resulting weights must still be interpreted with caution. We further confirm the generality of our findings beyond physics by analyzing a diverse collection of publicly available datasets. Our results clarify why, in the presence of multicollinearity, physical interpretation can remain difficult even for linear regression models.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper establishes an explicit and unconditional depth hierarchy theorem for constant-depth quantum circuits ($	ext{QNC}^0$). By mapping computational tasks to nonlocal games defined by operator constraints, the authors prove that increasing circuit depth strictly increases computational power. This provides a rigorous measure of quantum advantage based solely on the required depth of the quantum circuit.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides fundamental complexity results by quantifying the resource cost of quantum computation in terms of circuit depth, which is a key metric for physical implementation constraints.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central problem is establishing an explicit, unconditional depth hierarchy for constant-depth quantum computation ($	ext{QNC}^0$), demonstrating that increasing circuit depth strictly increases computational power.

**Main result.** The authors prove a depth hierarchy theorem showing that certain two-round interactive problems require quantum circuits of depth $\Omega(d)$ to solve perfectly, while shallower circuits fail with significant probability. This establishes an unconditional quantum advantage over classical $	ext{NC}^0$ computation based purely on circuit depth.

**Method.** The methodology involves translating the computational problem into a rigid operator-valued constraint system derived from group theory and nonlocal games. Lower bounds are established by showing that perfect solutions require implementing multi-controlled phase operations, which necessitates deep circuits.

**Model / system.** The model is quantum computation realized via bounded fan-in quantum circuits over the Clifford+T gate set. The complexity is analyzed using two-round interactive problems and constraint systems derived from abelian groups like $\mathbb{Z}_m^2$.

**Key observables.** Circuit Depth ($d$), Success Probability ($\epsilon(d)$), Multi-controlled phase operations (e.g., $C_{m-1}(\mathbb{Z})$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Depth $d$, precision $\epsilon$, and the number of qubits/labels $m$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The lower bound proofs rely on constructing constraint systems whose unique faithful solutions require specific non-Clifford gates, and later sections address robustness under approximate state preparation.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 schematically represents the established quantum depth hierarchies. Figure 2 shows logical dependencies for analyzing the quantum-input relation problem; Figure 3 shows dependencies for the classical verifier construction.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops from establishing the basic hierarchy using nonlocal games (Chunk 1), refining this by connecting it to operator constraints and self-testing in semi-quantum settings (Chunks 2, 4, 6), deriving specific depth lower bounds related to multi-controlled gates (Chunk 7), and finally analyzing upper bounds for generalized Toffoli gates (Chunk 8).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Circuit depth is a central resource in complexity theory. While bounded-depth classical circuits admit well-understood hierarchy theorems, the internal structure of constant-depth quantum computation remains comparatively unexplored.   We prove an explicit depth hierarchy theorem for $\mathsf{QNC}^0$. For each $d\ge 12$, we construct a family of two-round interactive problems on which no depth-$(d-1)$ quantum circuit can achieve near-perfect success, regardless of gate set, circuit size, or ancillary qubits. In contrast, we prove that our construction admits realizations by simple bounded fan-in quantum circuits of depth larger than $d$ by a small constant factor. Moreover, all bounded fan-in classical circuits of sublogarithmic depth (in the input size) fail to achieve perfect success on these tasks for every $d$, yielding a hierarchy of problems that show unconditional quantum advantage of $\mathsf{QNC}^0$ over $\mathsf{NC}^0$.   A key obstacle is the scarcity of lower bound techniques for quantum circuits. To address this, we develop methods to analyze how depth affects a circuit's ability to realize nonlocal correlations amongst its output qubits in a fine-grained manner. Our approach exploits the correspondence between constraint systems and nonlocal games, translating group-theoretic constructions into rigid operator-valued constraint systems and then into non-local games. In particular, we construct constraint systems whose unique faithful operator-valued solutions require every perfect strategy, and every near-perfect strategy to a fixed precision, to implement multi-controlled phase operations. This reduces to a nonlocal unitary-synthesis problem, yielding depth lower bounds for both shallow quantum and classical circuits.   These results show that increasing depth strictly increases computational power within $\mathsf{QNC}^0$, establishing a genuinely quantum hierarchy.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper theoretically predicts that the presence of a hyperbolic photon mode near a material can significantly alter its metal-insulator transition point. By coupling charge carriers to the enhanced zero-point electric field fluctuations from this mode, the system is effectively driven towards an insulating state. This effect is highly localized, decaying rapidly over just a few atomic layers.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work bridges quantum optics (hyperbolic modes, vacuum fluctuations) with condensed matter theory (Mott physics). The mechanism—using electromagnetic vacuum structure to tune electronic correlations—is highly relevant for understanding emergent phenomena in nanoscale heterostructures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how coupling a material near a Mott transition to a hyperbolic photon mode (HM) can modify its electronic state.

**Main result.** The HM acts as a 'negative pressure,' significantly shifting the critical interaction strength ($U_c$) and potentially driving a metallic system towards an insulating state, especially at small separations.

**Method.** Theoretical calculations involving self-energy corrections ($\Sigma'$) to the charge boson Green's function, derived from coupling the electronic degrees of freedom to the enhanced photon density of states provided by the HM.

**Model / system.** The model involves an electronic system near a Mott transition (related to the Hubbard model) placed atop hexagonal Boron Nitride ($	ext{hBN}$), coupled via the hyperbolic photon mode. The charge dynamics are treated using a relativistic boson field approximation.

**Key observables.** Shift in the critical interaction strength ($	ilde{U}_c$), zero-point fluctuations in the electric field ($\langle |E(z)|^2 angle$), and the spectral function $ho(\omega)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Distance ($z$) from the HM source (effect decays rapidly, e.g., $1/z^3$ or $1/z^2$), coupling constants ($C_k$, $Z$), and material-specific parameters like bandwidths.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The effect of the HM is assumed to decay rapidly with distance; approximations are made regarding small mass gaps, continuum limits for integration, and neglecting certain terms (e.g., diamagnetic $A^2$ term).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the enhanced momentum phase space covered by the HM compared to ordinary photons, show generalized phase diagrams indicating a shift towards insulating states, and plot calculated functions related to coupling strengths.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the physical mechanism (HM enhancing DOS/field fluctuations) to deriving the theoretical modification of the electronic self-energy ($\Sigma'$), culminating in quantitative predictions for how this modifies the critical Mott transition point ($U_c$).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The hyperbolic mode (HM) refers to a polariton mode where the dielectric function is negative in some direction of propagation. Within a frequency window the light occupies a greatly expanded region in momentum space. We compute the photon density of states and find that the zero point fluctuation in the RMS electric field can reach $MV/cm$, comparable to the largest field used in pump probe experiments in the THz scale. The HM in hexagonal Boron Nitride (hBN) has been under intense study and we consider placing a material that is near the Mott transition directly on top hBN. We find that a substantial shift in the metal-insulator transition is possible, but the effect decays rapidly with distance, so that only a few monolayers are affected. We provide estimates and suggestions for a number of materials of interest.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper reveals that exciton-polariton condensates can spontaneously develop chirality due to spin relaxation effects within the coupled reservoir system. This hidden non-Hermitian potential allows for the controlled, all-optical creation of half-vortices, where polarization components exhibit distinct topological winding numbers.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a clean theoretical framework for generating topological structures (vortices) in quantum optical systems using internal degrees of freedom (spin/polarization) rather than external geometric controls, which is highly relevant to advanced quantum light sources and nonlinear optics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study demonstrates how a spinor exciton-polariton condensate can spontaneously acquire chirality without external chiral driving fields.

**Main result.** This hidden chirality enables the all-optical formation of spin-selective half-vortices, where one polarization component acquires a definite phase winding while the other remains near zero winding.

**Method.** The analysis uses adiabatic elimination of fast reservoir dynamics to derive an effective non-Hermitian potential and subsequently analyzes coupled angular-mode equations.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled by a driven-dissipative Gross-Pitaevskii equation for the spinor order parameter, incorporating coupling to two distinct excitonic reservoirs (active and inactive).

**Key observables.** Spin-selective vorticity ($\sigma-$ component showing $2\pi$ winding vs. $\sigma+$ zero-winding), time-averaged angular momentum ($\langle m_\pm angle_t$), and the existence of Exceptional Points (EPs).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The relative phase shift between reservoir blueshifts, pump modulation depth ($ho$), and parameters governing non-reciprocal coupling near EPs.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on adiabatic elimination of fast reservoir dynamics and approximations derived from low polariton densities in some theoretical sections.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the mechanism (Fig. 1), show half-vortex states ($\sigma-$ winding vs $\sigma+$ dipole) (Fig. 2), map out angular momentum bistability near EPs (Fig. 3), and confirm robustness against fast oscillations from TE-TM splitting (Fig. 4).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the physical mechanism of hidden chirality via spin relaxation to deriving simplified coupled-mode equations, analyzing spectral features like Exceptional Points, and finally simulating the resulting half-vortex formation.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We show that a radially symmetric, nonresonantly pumped spinor exciton-polariton condensate can acquire chirality without a rotating drive, chiral geometry, or pump orbital angular momentum. Spin relaxation in a two-reservoir system shifts the reservoir-induced blueshift relative to the gain profile, creating an effective non-Hermitian chiral potential. A reduced angular-mode theory reveals tunable exceptional points and non-reciprocal coupling between counter-rotating modes. Full driven-dissipative Gross-Pitaevskii simulations show that this hidden chirality enables all-optical formation of spin-selective half-vortices.

</details>
