**Summary.** The paper analyzes a driven synthetic spin chain to understand how its localization properties depend on the external driving frequency ($\omega$). It finds that the system exhibits maximal state localization at an intermediate frequency ($\omega_{	ext{peak}}$), dictated by boundary coupling strengths. This establishes the model as a promising, tunable platform for controlling quantum information storage and retrieval in superconducting circuits.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, tunable mechanism—the Floquet-Sambe bottleneck—to engineer quantum transport properties by controlling the driving frequency, which is highly relevant for superconducting circuit architectures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how driving a synthetic spin chain with spatially inhomogeneous coupling leads to frequency-dependent localization phenomena, termed the Floquet-Sambe bottleneck.

**Main result.** The system exhibits maximal state localization at an intermediate driving frequency ($\omega_{	ext{peak}}$), which is controlled by the weakest boundary hopping scale. This nonmonotonic behavior is robustly observed in both closed and open-system diagnostics.

**Method.** The analysis employs Floquet theory, transforming the time-dependent problem into a static eigenvalue problem in an enlarged space, and utilizes Inverse Participation Ratios (IPR) to quantify localization.

**Model / system.** The model is a finite Floquet chain combining uniform hopping with a periodically rotating, SU(2)-dictated spin-assisted hopping profile. The resulting coupling strength varies spatially, being weakest at the boundaries.

**Key observables.** Mean Inverse Participation Ratio (MIPR) for closed systems and the energy-integrated IPR ($	ext{IPRG}(\omega)$) for open-system transport diagnostics.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Driving frequency ($\omega$), boundary bottleneck scale ($\mu_{-s} \sim \sqrt{2s}$), and the ratio of hopping to driving strength ($\eta_j = \mu_j / \omega$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis involves truncating the Fourier components for numerical simulation, and comparing limits such as $\omega 	o 0$ (adiabatic) and $\omega 	o \infty$ (high-frequency expansion).

**Figures summary.** Figures show the nonmonotonic MIPR profile peaking at $\omega_{	ext{peak}}$ for varying spin dimensions ($s$), and similarly demonstrate the peak in the open-system IPR ($	ext{IPRG}(\omega)$) shifting with $s$.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the system across different frequency regimes: low-$\omega$ (PST revival), intermediate $\omega$ (localization maximum at $\omega_{	ext{peak}}$ due to boundary bottleneck), and high-$\omega$ (effective tight-binding behavior via Magnus expansion).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study a finite Floquet chain in which a uniform nearest-neighbor hopping coexists with a periodically rotating, \textrm{SU(2)}-dictated spin-assisted hopping profile. The resulting coupling is spatially inhomogeneous -- weakest at the chain boundaries and strongest in the bulk -- and produces a frequency-dependent Floquet-Sambe bottleneck. In the closed system, the mean inverse participation ratio (\textrm{MIPR}) of the Floquet eigenstates exhibits a striking nonmonotonic dependence on the driving frequency $ω$: the states remain extended at both low and high frequencies, but become maximally localized at an intermediate frequency. We demonstrate that this localization maximum occurs at $ω_{\mathrm{peak}}\sim μ_{-s}=\sqrt{% 2s}$, a scale controlled by the first boundary bottleneck. To connect these spectral properties to measurable transport, we construct an open-system Floquet-Sambe Green-function inverse participation ratio from the spatial density of the injected scattering state. This open-system diagnostic recovers the same nonmonotonic localization trend as its closed-system counterpart, with the peak shifted to higher frequencies by the static bandwidth and the lead self-energy. These findings establish the driven synthetic spin chain as a directly realizable, frequency-tunable platform for coherent information storage and retrieval, rooted in the interplay of Floquet-Sambe virtual channels, boundary-controlled localization, and frequency-selective transport in emerging multi-level superconducting circuit architectures.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper analyzes how parametric driving and damping stabilize topological edge solitons in a nonlinear SSH lattice model. By deriving an effective amplitude equation, the authors show that these external forces create two distinct soliton branches with vastly different stabilities. This demonstrates that active control mechanisms can enhance the robustness of quantum-like localization phenomena.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides concrete theoretical tools (stability analysis of dissipative nonlinear systems) applicable to understanding robust localized excitations in active or driven quantum/classical lattices, which is highly relevant to open quantum system dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the dynamics and stabilization of topological edge solitons within a nonlinear Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) lattice that is subjected to both parametric driving and linear damping.

**Main result.** Parametric driving and damping fundamentally modify the system's edge-state family, generating two dissipative branches; one branch can exhibit significantly enhanced stability compared to the conservative case.

**Method.** The research employs analytical derivations from a driven pendulum chain, followed by numerical continuation and spectral stability analysis on an effective reduced SSH amplitude model.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled as a 1D lattice of pendula (analogous to SSH) governed by equations derived from a Klein-Gordon equation. The final effective model is a driven-damped discrete nonlinear Schrödinger type equation.

**Key observables.** Topological edge solitons, total power ($P$), and the real parts of linearization eigenvalues ($	ext{Re}(\lambda)$) used to determine stability.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Damping ($\Gamma$), parametric drive strength ($h$), detuning parameter ($\Delta$), and coupling constants ($c_{n}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes weak damping, small-amplitude oscillations, and utilizes an exponentially decaying spatial profile ansatz for the edge state approximation.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate experimental setups (pendulum chain), bifurcation diagrams showing total power vs. detuning, stationary edge-state profiles under different driving conditions, and time evolution comparisons between the reduced model and the full lattice dynamics.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from deriving an effective driven-damped SSH model from a physical pendulum chain to performing analytical calculations for phase-locked states, followed by detailed numerical stability analysis and comparison with direct time-domain simulations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study topological edge solitons in a nonlinear Su--Schrieffer--Heeger (SSH) lattice subject to parametric driving and linear damping. Starting from a vertically driven pendulum chain, we derive an effective driven--damped nonlinear SSH model and investigate its stationary edge-localized states. Analytical calculations reveal the existence of two phase-locked dissipative edge-soliton families that emerge from the nonlinear continuation of the topological edge mode. Using numerical continuation and spectral stability analysis, we construct the corresponding nonlinear branches and determine their stability properties. We show that parametric driving and damping fundamentally modify the conservative edge-state family by generating two dissipative branches with markedly different stability characteristics: one branch remains predominantly unstable, whereas the other develops substantially larger stability regions and significantly weaker instability growth rates. Direct numerical simulations further demonstrate that the robust branch can remain strongly localized over long time intervals even when weakly unstable. Simulations of the full driven--damped Klein--Gordon pendulum chain confirm the persistence of the edge-localized dynamics predicted by the reduced model. These results identify parametric driving and damping as an effective mechanism for enhancing the robustness and persistence of nonlinear topological localization in active lattice systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work examines the Josephson effect in electron-hole bilayers, modeling tunneling currents under an external voltage. By analyzing high-density versus low-density regimes, it reveals fundamental differences in current behavior, particularly the emergence of dissipative damping in the excitonic (low-density) limit. The methodology combines advanced many-body techniques with condensed matter physics principles.

**Why it may be interesting.** It connects concepts from superconductivity (Josephson effect) with quantum gas physics (exciton BEC), providing a rich platform to study non-equilibrium dynamics, dissipation, and phase coherence in artificial quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the non-stationary longitudinal Josephson effect occurring in electron-hole bilayers where pairing occurs between spatially separated electrons and holes.

**Main result.** The system exhibits distinct behaviors depending on carrier density: high-density limits show only supercurrent below a threshold voltage, while low-density regimes feature finite dissipative currents even at zero temperature due to gapless excitations.

**Method.** The analysis employs the tunneling Hamiltonian approach combined with Green's function techniques and perturbation theory to calculate various current components (quasiparticle, superconducting, interference).

**Model / system.** The model is an electron-hole bilayer system weakly coupled by a tunnel junction. It is analyzed in two limits: high-density (momentum space pairing) and low-density (Bose-Einstein condensate of excitons).

**Key observables.** Tunneling current ($I_t$), quasiparticle current ($qI$), supercurrent components, and the relative phase difference ($\varphi_{eh}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** External applied voltage ($V_t$), carrier density (determining high vs. low-density regime), and energy gap ($\Delta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on perturbation theory for weak tunneling, treating the system in both BCS-like (high-density) and bosonic/coherent state (low-density) approximations.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 schematically illustrates the bilayer structure with weak coupling; Figure 2 likely shows phase evolution or current characteristics related to Josephson dynamics.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by setting up the Hamiltonian, deriving current expressions using Green's functions in various limits (high/low density), and finally analyzing the resulting dynamical equations for the superconducting phase difference under applied voltage.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The non-stationary longitudinal Josephson effect in bilayer systems with pairing of spatially separated electrons and holes is investigated. The tunneling current between two (right and left) weakly coupled electron-hole condensates is analyzed in the presence of an external voltage applied along the layers. Two limiting regimes are considered: the high-density regime, where pairing occurs in momentum space similarly to conventional superconductors, and the low-density regime corresponding to a Bose-Einstein condensate of spatially indirect excitons. Using the tunneling Hamiltonian approach, expressions for the quasiparticle, superconducting and interference contributions to the tunneling current are derived. It is shown that in the high-density limit the quasiparticle and interference currents vanish at zero temperature below a threshold voltage determined by the energy gap, so that only the supercurrent remains. In contrast, in the low-density regime the gapless spectrum of collective excitations leads to finite dissipative contributions even at zero temperature, resulting in damping of Josephson oscillations. For spatially separated tunneling barriers with distance exceeding the coherence length, phase jumps occur at each barrier, resulting in voltage oscillations across the electron and hole barriers and a non-sinusoidal current-phase relation governed by the critical currents of the two barriers.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper investigates nonlinear localized states on a pyrochlore lattice modeled by the DNLS equation. It performs detailed stability analyses on solitons and vortices, finding that their stability is strongly dependent on whether the nonlinearity is focusing or defocusing. These results highlight how topology and dispersion govern complex wave behavior in 3D quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the interplay between topology (flat bands), nonlinearity, and wave localization in 3D lattices, which is highly relevant for understanding exotic quantum phenomena in optical or magnetic systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study explores nonlinear localized states, such as solitons and vortices, on a pyrochlore lattice using a dispersive nonlinear dynamical model.

**Main result.** The stability of these localized states depends critically on the nonlinearity type (focusing vs. defocusing) and the topological charge of the vortex, revealing complex interplay between topology and dispersion.

**Method.** Stability analysis is performed by linearizing the system around stationary solutions and calculating eigenvalues of the resulting operator, often utilizing the Anti-Continuum limit for theoretical guidance.

**Model / system.** The model uses the discrete nonlinear Schrödinger (DNLS) equation on a pyrochlore lattice, which is a 3D structure possessing flat bands in its linear spectrum. This system relates to physical contexts like frustrated magnetism or nonlinear optics.

**Key observables.** Stability eigenvalues ($\lambda$), topological charge ($S$), and the existence/stability of compact localized modes.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Nonlinearity coefficient ($\gamma$), coupling strength ($C$), propagation constant ($\mu$), and the nonlinearity regime (focusing vs. defocusing).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often relies on assuming a standing wave Ansatz and analyzing quasi-two-dimensional configurations, though genuine 3D study is suggested for future work.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the lattice structure, the dispersive/flat bands, and show eigenvalue plots demonstrating stability boundaries as functions of $\mu$ for different state types (solitons, vortices).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from setting up the model on the pyrochlore lattice to analyzing linear spectra, then details the analysis of fundamental solitons and vortex structures, culminating in a detailed comparison of their stability across focusing and defocusing nonlinear regimes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In the present work we explore a prototypical three-dimensional (3d) lattice possessing a flat band in the form of a pyrochlore lattice in the context of a dispersive nonlinear dynamical model, namely the discrete nonlinear Schrödinger (DNLS) equation. We set up the corresponding steady state and dynamical problems and discuss the linear spectrum of the relevant model before delving into a more detailed analysis of the nonlinear equilibria of the system. For the latter, we analyze the more well-established -- at the DNLS level -- fundamental discrete soliton states, as well as vortex structures. For the fundamental solitary waves, we connect their existence and stability with how they approach the linear bands. In the vortex case, we identify their stability features for vortices of topological charge $S=1$ and $S=2$ with those of the honeycomb and triangular lattices. An arguably even more intriguing feature of the pyrochlore lattice concerns the compactly supported nonlinear eigenstates stemming from the flat band of the linear spectrum. These compact localized modes are found to possess oscillatory instabilities for a range of propagation constants in the focusing case, although they can be stable in the latter, while they are found to be subject to symmetry-breaking instabilities in the defocusing nonlinearity case. These results offer a glimpse at the nexus of topology, flat band systems and dispersive nonlinear lattices in three spatial dimensions and as such may be a starting point toward a deeper exploration of such an intriguing interplay.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper theoretically explores how applying a periodic drive to a Rashba nanowire can induce a finite momentum Fulde-Ferrell superconducting state. This state manifests as pronounced nonreciprocal supercurrents, leading directly to the Superconducting Diode Effect (SDE). The findings demonstrate that this effect is controllable by tuning the driving parameters.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work bridges concepts from topological superconductivity (Majorana modes) with non-equilibrium transport phenomena (SDE) using time-periodic driving, which is highly relevant for designing novel superconducting electronic devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the emergence of a finite momentum Fulde-Ferrell (FF) superconducting state in a driven Rashba nanowire, linking this phenomenon to the Superconducting Diode Effect (SDE).

**Main result.** The periodic drive stabilizes a Floquet-induced FF superconducting state, enabling controllable switching between topological Majorana modes and realizing pronounced nonreciprocal supercurrent signatures indicative of SDE.

**Method.** Theoretical analysis employing the Floquet formalism combined with self-consistent mean-field calculations to determine the superconducting order parameter and current response.

**Model / system.** The system is a 1D Rashba nanowire proximitized to an s-wave superconductor, subjected to time-periodic modulation of in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields (Floquet drive).

**Key observables.** Nonreciprocal supercurrent signatures ($I^+_c 
eq I^-_c$), Floquet Majorana 0- and $\pi$-modes, diode efficiency ($\eta$), and the finite Cooper pair momentum ($q_0$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Drive amplitude, chemical potential ($\mu$), and the presence/magnitude of a static magnetic field component ($B_y$) are crucial tuning parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the Floquet formalism to treat the time-periodic driving and uses self-consistent mean-field theory for superconducting pairing.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate schematic setups, quasienergy spectra showing topological phase diagrams (0- vs. $\pi$-FMMs), supercurrent density profiles confirming nonreciprocity, and dependence of diode efficiency on driving parameters.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the model Hamiltonian under periodic drive to analyzing the resulting Floquet topology via spectral analysis, followed by self-consistent calculations that confirm finite momentum pairing and quantify the resultant SDE.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Much has been studied on Floquet engineering in Rashba nanowire model regarding topological superconductivity hosting Majorana $0$- and anomalous $π$-modes, here we theoretically investigate the possible emergence of finite momentum Fulde-Ferrell (FF) superconducting state in quasi-energy of the above model under the periodic modulation of in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields while the static limit does not host a FF ground state. We demonstrate controllable switching between Floquet Majorana $0$- and $π$-modes via reversal of the supercurrent direction, revealing pronounced nonreciprocal supercurrent signatures which is a manifestation of the FF pairing. We validate the onset of FF pairing following a self-consistent mean-field analysis where externally applied supercurrent facilitates nonreciprocal signatures in quasi-energy spectra. The above findings directly indicates to the intriguing phenomenon of superconducting diode effect (SDE). The drive amplitude serves as a parameter to regulate the diode efficiency with chemical potential. Our study thus reveals a rich interplay between Floquet topological superconductivity and finite-momentum FF pairing, providing a tunable way to switch between different Floquet Majorana modes and realize the SDE with high efficiency.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors report on the deterministic creation and characterization of single-photon emitters in hexagonal boron nitride ($	ext{hBN}$) using controlled electron irradiation. They establish a dose window that maximizes emitter purity ($g^{(2)}(0) \ll 1$) while also demonstrating remarkable thermal robustness, with functionality maintained up to $300^\circ	ext{C}$. This work advances the field by providing quantitative control over both the creation process and operational temperature range for quantum light sources.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a crucial experimental demonstration of scalable, high-performance quantum light sources operating at ambient temperatures, directly relevant for developing practical photonic quantum technologies.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to systematically investigate how electron dose controls the properties of single-photon emitters (SPEs) in hexagonal boron nitride ($	ext{hBN}$), and to characterize their emission behavior above room temperature.

**Main result.** High-purity SPEs are deterministically created via controlled electron irradiation, exhibiting robust performance with reversible thermal quenching up to $300^\circ	ext{C}$. The purity is confirmed by low second-order correlation values ($g^{(2)}(0) \le 0.16$).

**Method.** The researchers used localized electron-beam irradiation coupled with photoluminescence microscopy, time-resolved measurements, and Hanbury-Brown and Twiss interferometry to characterize the emitters.

**Model / system.** The physical platform is single-photon emitters embedded in hexagonal boron nitride ($	ext{hBN}$), which are activated deterministically using a focused electron beam. The system's performance is mapped against the accumulated electron dose and temperature.

**Key observables.** Second-order autocorrelation function ($g^{(2)}(0)$), spectral purity (ZPL vs. PSB assignment), emission yield, lifetime ($	au$), Signal-to-Background Ratio ($	ext{SBR}$), and photoluminescence intensity as a function of temperature.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Electron dose (controlled by irradiation time), Temperature ($300^\circ	ext{C}$ maximum), $g^{(2)}(0)$ values ($\sim 0.09$ to $0.16$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that the observed spectral features and quantum statistics are dominated by the localized emitter, rather than background or non-radiative processes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate PL maps showing dose dependence (Fig. 2a), spectral evolution vs. dose (Fig. 2b), lifetime/SBR dependence on dose (Figs. 2c/d), and confirmation of high purity across different flake thicknesses (Fig. 3).

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically details the methodology for dose-controlled emitter creation, presents quantitative data mapping performance metrics (purity, spectrum) against electron dose, confirms spectral assignments (PSB/ZPL), and finally demonstrates thermal stability up to $300^\circ	ext{C}$.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Electron-beam irradiation is an established route to create site-controlled, room-temperature single-photon emitters (SPEs) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), but two aspects remain underexplored: how the electron dose governs the properties of the resulting single emitters, and how the emission behaves when the host is heated above room temperature. Here, we create emitters deterministically with a focused electron beam and confirm single-photon emission across three independent flakes, with $g^{(2)}(0)=0.09$, $0.12$, and $0.16$. We map the single-emitter response (yield, spectrum, lifetime, and photon purity) as a function of electron dose, identifying an optimal window for high-purity single emitters. Consistent with recent cryogenic studies, we assign the bright room-temperature feature near 575 n to the phonon sideband (PSB) of a green--yellow emitter whose zero-phonon line (ZPL) lies near 548 nm. Temperature-dependent photoluminescence measured in situ under real-time from room temperature to 300 degrees C reveals a thermal quenching that is fully reversible upon cooling, in contrast to the irreversible annealing-induced degradation reported elsewhere, indicating that transient heating does not permanently damage the centers. These results add quantitative dose control and above-room-temperature operation to the toolbox for deterministic hBN quantum-light sources.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study analyzes the interplay between magnetic impurities and superconducting hosts exhibiting pseudogaps. Using advanced techniques like NRG and RG, it maps out the phase diagram showing a transition between local moment (doublet) and spin-singlet (PSC) ground states. The findings are crucial for understanding exotic quantum phenomena in unconventional superconductors.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses how strong local correlations (Kondo physics) interact with unconventional pairing symmetries (d-wave/pseudogap superconductivity), which is a central theme in modern condensed matter theory relevant to high-Tc superconductors and quantum materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the ground-state phase diagram and single-particle excitations of a magnetic impurity coupled to superconducting or pseudogap host materials.

**Main result.** The system exhibits a doublet-singlet transition, which can be driven by the chemical potential rather than solely by the Kondo coupling strength. The strong coupling limit favors a spin-singlet state (PSC) over a local moment (LM) state when pairing potentials are present.

**Method.** The analysis employs advanced theoretical techniques including effective field theory derived from strong coupling expansions, Numerical Renormalization Group (NRG), and Renormalization Group (RG) flow equations in Nambu space.

**Model / system.** The model describes a spin-1/2 magnetic impurity coupled to itinerant fermions forming a superconducting host with a pseudogap tunneling density of states $ho(\epsilon) \sim |\epsilon|^r$. The Hamiltonian incorporates Kondo coupling, pairing potentials ($\Delta$), and scattering terms.

**Key observables.** Ground state phase diagram (singlet vs. doublet), T-matrix spectral function $A(\omega)$, and the anomalous Green's function components ($F_0$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Kondo coupling strength ($J$), pairing potential ($\Delta$), pseudogap exponent ($r$), chemical potential ($\mu$), and scattering potential ($V$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on strong coupling expansions, low-energy limits (e.g., $|\omega_n| \ll J$ or $\Delta$), and approximations like the BCS mean-field theory for the host.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate phase diagrams showing the competition between singlet and doublet phases as a function of various parameters ($V$, $\mu$, $r$).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by establishing the model Hamiltonian, deriving effective actions via path integrals (integrating out bath degrees of freedom), applying RG analysis to determine stability regimes, and finally analyzing specific spectral features like resonance-like excitations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Combining effective field theory and numerical renormalization-group (NRG), we study the ground-state phase diagram and single-particle excitations of a spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ impurity in a superconducting system with a tunneling density of states behaving as $ρ(ε) \sim |ε|^{r}$, for $|ε|\gg Δ$ ($Δ$ being the $s$-wave pairing potential). We focus on the properties of the doublet-singlet transition at large Kondo coupling. The effective field theory for the singlet phase is inferred from a strong coupling expansion in the Kondo coupling. For $Δ\neq 0$, it contains a local pairing term which drives the system into a spin-singlet phase with enhanced paring correlations. We study how the singet-doublet phase boundary is affected by particle-hole symmetry breaking perturbations such as a scattering potential and/or the chemical potential. Results for the $T$-matrix spectral function are also reported near the transition both at particle-hole symmetry and away from it. It is shown that the singlet-doublet transition can be induced by the chemical potential rather than the Kondo coupling strength. At particle-hole symmetry, a resonance-like feature is observed for $r= 1$ and related to a two-quasiparticle excitation using a single-site model which is derived from effective field theory.

</details>

**Summary.** This work demonstrates that antiferromagnetic skyrmions can be efficiently created and moved in magnetic racetracks solely by manipulating the local magnetization at the sample edges. By comparing these results to ferromagnetic counterparts, the authors show that AFM systems offer superior performance, particularly regarding operational frequency limits and energy efficiency for this boundary-driven process.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the controlled manipulation of topological excitations (skyrmions) via boundary conditions and non-global driving forces shares conceptual links with controlling quantum states in engineered systems, making it relevant to understanding dissipation and state preparation in open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research aims to develop efficient, current-free methods for generating and transporting topological magnetic skyrmions within antiferromagnetic (AFM) racetrack architectures.

**Main result.** Local manipulation of the magnetization at the sample boundary—either through smooth rotation or switching—can efficiently generate and move AFM skyrmions, showing advantages over ferromagnetic counterparts in terms of frequency limits and robustness.

**Method.** The study uses atomistic simulations based on the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, analyzing the dynamics using analytical approximations like the Thiele equation for skyrmion motion.

**Model / system.** The system is an AFM racetrack modeled on a lattice, governed by an effective Hamiltonian derived from the underlying magnetic interactions. Dynamics are simulated by applying local boundary fields ($\mathbf{B}_{	ext{edge}}$) that drive magnetization rotation or switching.

**Key observables.** Skyrmion position ($d$ vs $t$), propagation velocity ($\mathbf{v}_x$), skyrmion number ($|N_T|$), and the energy cost required for creation ($\Delta H_{	ext{skyr}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Edge field amplitude ($\mathbf{B}_{	ext{edge}}$), rotation frequency ($
u$), racetrack width ($N_y$), and material parameters like exchange coupling ($J$) and DMI constants.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes adiabatic changes during edge field manipulation and compares results between FM and AFM systems, noting that the AFM case exhibits unique directional requirements for optimal switching.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate skyrmion positions after boundary rotation (Fig. 1), compare time-dependent displacement and velocity for FM vs. AFM under rotating fields (Fig. 2), map stable creation regions in parameter space (Fig. 3), and show frequency limitations for both types of skyrmions (Fig. 4).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the physical motivation (AFM racetracks avoiding global currents), then detailing the simulation methods using edge field manipulation, presenting comparative results between FM and AFM dynamics under rotation/switching, and finally quantifying the energy efficiency of the process.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Magnetic racetrack architectures that use topological magnetic particles to store information are one of the most promising concepts for future storage applications. Antiferromagnetic racetracks are particularly appealing as they are not susceptible to external magnetic fields. State-of-the-art racetracks use magnetic fields, spin-transfer and spin-orbit torques caused by electric currents to move the bits across the entire circuit. However, the application of currents in many antiferromagnetic racetracks is limited because many of them are insulating. Recently, however, a concept for ferromagnetic racetrack memories that are free of global driving forces has been proposed. It has been demonstrated that various topological entities can be generated and transported over long distances solely through local magnetization rotation at the sample boundaries, independent of global driving forces. Here, we demonstrate that the local rotation of magnetization at the boundary of an antiferromagnetic sample can be exploited in racetracks to efficiently generate and transmit antiferromagnetic skyrmions. Additionally, we demonstrate that local switching of staggered magnetization at the edge of an antiferromagnetic racetrack can be even more successful than the rotational procedure. A comparison of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic processing of skyrmionic bits, together with energy considerations, shows that this procedure is fairly efficient in antiferromagnets.

</details>

**Summary.** This work uses Helium-3 spin-echo spectroscopy to measure the intrinsic linewidths of low-energy phonon modes in few-layer hBN. The key finding is that reducing dimensionality strongly affects phonon decay rates, showing a dramatic increase in confinement-induced broadening for thinner films. This provides fundamental insights into how material structure governs energy dissipation pathways in 2D materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on solid-state phononics, the study of energy dissipation pathways ($\gamma$) in confined systems provides analogous insights to decoherence rates or coupling strengths in open quantum systems, particularly those involving lattice vibrations or phonons mediating interactions.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to understand the intrinsic linewidths of low-energy, often optically silent, phonon modes in few-layer hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). This is crucial for controlling thermal and mechanical properties in nanoscale devices.

**Main result.** The researchers found a strong confinement effect, demonstrating that the phonon lifetime decreases significantly—by nearly an order of magnitude—when moving from four- to two-layer hBN modes. They also characterized temperature dependence dominated by phonon-phonon scattering at higher temperatures.

**Method.** Helium-3 spin-echo (HeSE) spectroscopy was employed to measure the low-energy vibrational spectrum, which is advantageous because it avoids probe-induced heating common in optical techniques.

**Model / system.** The physical system is few-layer hBN. Theoretical models include simple harmonic membrane–substrate coupling theory for flexural modes and the Linear Chain Model (LCM) used to predict interlayer shear mode energies.

**Key observables.** Phonon dispersion relations (flexural, Rayleigh wave, interlayer shear modes), intrinsic linewidths ($\gamma$), bending rigidity ($\kappa$), and temperature dependence of phonon decay rates.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature range ($160-360 	ext{ K}$); layer number (2L, 3L, 4L); confinement strength; scattering mechanisms (phonon-phonon vs. defect-phonon).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The HeSE technique is assumed to provide a surface-sensitive measurement free from optical selection rules or probe heating effects.

**Figures summary.** Figures show the quadratic dispersion of flexural modes, energy transfer spectra for interlayer shear modes at various temperatures, and plots detailing linewidths versus temperature for different layer numbers.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the need to measure intrinsic phonon lifetimes in 2D materials. It then details the use of HeSE spectroscopy to resolve specific low-energy modes (flexural/Rayleigh waves) and interlayer shear modes (ISMs). The core analysis focuses on comparing measured linewidths across different layer numbers and temperatures against theoretical predictions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Understanding lattice vibrations in two-dimensional (2D) materials is essential for controlling thermal transport, mechanical response, and energy dissipation in nanoscale devices. However, the intrinsic lifetimes of low-energy phonon modes, particularly those that are optically silent, remain largely unexplored. Here we use helium-3 spin-echo spectroscopy to resolve low-energy phonons at the surface of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and measure their intrinsic linewidths. We observe the flexural and Rayleigh wave modes and extract the bending rigidity of a quasi-freestanding hBN monolayer. We further report the simultaneous observation of multiple surface-confined interlayer shear modes whose energies agree closely with linear-chain model predictions. By resolving their intrinsic linewidths, we demonstrate a strong confinement-induced reduction in phonon lifetimes, with a near order of magnitude increase in linewidth between the four- and two-layer modes. The temperature dependence of the linewidths indicates that phonon-phonon scattering dominates between 160-360K, while the systematic broadening with decreasing layer number reveals the impact of confinement on phonon decay. These results reveal how reduced dimensionality affects the decay of interlayer shearing modes in hBN, providing direct insight into the phonon lifetimes, confinement effects, and dissipation pathways that govern the dynamical behaviour of two-dimensional materials.

</details>

**Summary.** This work thoroughly analyzes how acoustic waves propagate through a square lattice of waveguides, revealing pronounced directional dependence due to anisotropic dispersion. By developing and comparing multiple theoretical models (Boussinesq, Westervelt) against experiments, the authors characterize wave behavior from linear pulses to nonlinear solitons and shocks across different propagation angles.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical acoustics, the mathematical framework—developing complex nonlinear PDEs (Boussinesq, KdV) that exhibit strong anisotropy and support localized structures (solitons)—is highly relevant to modeling wave dynamics in quantum systems like photonic lattices or Bose-Einstein condensates with engineered periodic potentials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates nonlinear wave propagation, specifically anisotropic cylindrical waves, within a periodic square lattice structure made of acoustic waveguides.

**Main result.** The system exhibits highly direction-dependent dispersion relations and supports waveforms ranging from linear Airy pulses to nonlinear shock fronts or solitons depending on the propagation angle and amplitude.

**Method.** The analysis employs multiple techniques, including theoretical derivations (Transfer Matrix Method, Boussinesq equation), numerical simulations (2D Westervelt equation), and experimental measurements of acoustic fields.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a square lattice network of acoustic waveguides. The modeling progresses from simple Helmholtz equations to effective 2D nonlinear partial differential equations like the Boussinesq or Westervelt equations, capturing wave dynamics across different regimes.

**Key observables.** Anisotropic dispersion relation $\omega(k_d, 	heta)$, pulse width/amplitude evolution, and decay rates ($R^{-5/6}$ vs $R^{-1/2}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Lattice spacing ($d$), waveguide cross-section ($S_w$), wave amplitude (low vs. high), and propagation angle ($	heta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Initial analyses rely on the long-wavelength limit and monomodal approximation; later models use continuum approximations leading to effective PDEs.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate schematic lattice structures, Brillouin zones, contour plots of wave amplitude evolution at different times for various angles ($	heta=0$ vs $	heta=\pi/4$), and comparisons between theoretical dispersion curves (TMM vs. Continuum).

**Paper structure.** The paper builds systematically: first establishing the linear anisotropic dispersion relation using TMM; then deriving an effective 2D Boussinesq equation for weak nonlinearity; subsequently regularizing this PDE into a cKdV form to analyze both low-amplitude decay and high-amplitude soliton/shock formation.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the propagation of cylindrical waves in a square network of acoustic waveguides. We establish, both theoretically and experimentally, the anisotropic dispersion relation governing wave propagation in the network, and demonstrate excellent agreement between experimental measurements and theoretical predictions. Owing to this anisotropic band structure, each propagation direction exhibits distinct dispersive properties. Consequently, the network supports anisotropic cylindrical waves at both low- and high-amplitudes, with waveforms that vary markedly with direction: from nearly dispersionless pulses to Airy-like wave packets in the linear regime, and from sharp shock-like fronts to smooth solitary-like profiles in the nonlinear regime. The theoretical results are further corroborated by numerical simulations based on the two-dimensional Westervelt equation.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper proposes using phase-biased altermagnetic Josephson junctions as a highly controllable platform for generating and manipulating Majorana Corner Modes. By independently tuning the superconducting phase difference and the magnetic order vector, researchers can deterministically move these topological states across a fixed device geometry. The definitive proof of this control is achieved by observing a unique conductance switching signature that confirms the physical relocation of the zero-energy modes.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly tackles the engineering challenges of topological quantum computation by providing a physical mechanism (altermagnetism) to control Majorana modes spatially, which is crucial for building braiding architectures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research addresses two major hurdles in topological quantum computation: deterministically moving Majorana Corner Modes (MCMs) and providing an unambiguous diagnostic to distinguish true MCMs from trivial bound states.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate that by controlling the superconducting phase difference ($\phi$) and the altermagnetic Néel-vector orientation ($\mathbf{n}$), they can deterministically steer MCMs between corners, evidenced by a unique control-correlated conductance switching signature.

**Method.** Theoretical analysis involving solving boundary conditions on a lattice model, utilizing symmetry protection (e.g., time-reversal and particle-hole symmetry at $\phi=\pi$), and projecting the altermagnetic perturbation onto the edge Hamiltonian.

**Model / system.** The platform is a phase-biased altermagnetic Josephson junction realized in a superconducting system exhibiting helical Topological Superconducting (TSC) phases. The physics is governed by coupling between superconductivity, Rashba spin-orbit coupling, and the magnetic order parameter ($\mathbf{n}$).

**Key observables.** Zero-bias conductance peak ($G(0)$), which must switch location precisely when MCMs are relocated; the boundary mass term $m_\vartheta$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Superconducting phase difference ($\phi$), Néel vector orientation ($\mathbf{n}$), and the superconducting gap parameters ($\Delta_1, \Delta_{-1}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often assumes $\mu=0$ for specific gap closing conditions; it relies on continuum limit approximations and lattice regularization techniques.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate phase diagrams showing MCM localization regimes (I-VI), the spatial mapping of boundary mass terms ($m_\vartheta$), and local tunneling spectroscopy confirming the zero-bias conductance switching during mode relocation.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical model, derives the low-energy edge Hamiltonian using symmetry protection, analyzes how external parameters ($\phi$ and $\mathbf{n}$) modulate the effective boundary mass term ($m_\vartheta$), and finally presents the diagnostic signature via local tunneling conductance measurements.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Dynamical manipulation of Majorana zero modes and their unambiguous distinction from topologically trivial states remain paramount challenges in topological quantum computation. Here, we propose a phase-biased altermagnetic Josephson junction as a versatile platform for generating and controlling Majorana corner configurations. Moving beyond conventional global parameter tuning that merely toggles the topological phase in situ, our platform utilizes the macroscopic superconducting phase difference and the Néel-vector orientation as independent control knobs to dynamically reshape the boundary mass. This synergistically enables the deterministic spatial relocation of Majorana corner modes (MCMs) among selected corners of a fixed device geometry. Crucially, this spatial reconfiguration yields a definitive experimental fingerprint: a control-correlated conductance switching. As the MCMs are relocated, the quantized zero-bias peak perfectly emerges at the target corner while simultaneously vanishing at the initial one. This macroscopically phase-locked spatial correlation effectively eliminates false positives from trivial Andreev bound states, establishing a control-correlated diagnostic and a promising route toward future Majorana braiding architectures.

</details>

**Summary.** This work systematically investigates how ionic conductance and energy harvesting scale in large nanopore arrays compared to single pores. The authors demonstrate that pore interactions, concentration polarization, and field suppression cause these properties to deviate significantly from simple linear scaling as the array size increases. This has major implications for designing nanoscale devices like desalination membranes.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on electrochemistry/materials science, the study of non-equilibrium transport phenomena (like ion flux under concentration gradients) involves complex many-body dynamics that share mathematical parallels with open quantum systems or strongly correlated charge transport models.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how nonlinear ion transport phenomena, including ionic conductance, current rectification, and osmotic power generation, scale when moving from single nanopores to large arrays.

**Main result.** Conductance and current rectification effects significantly weaken or vanish as the number of pores increases, showing that simple scaling laws derived from single-pore models overestimate surface charge density. Osmotic power harvesting also shows a dramatic reduction upon upscaling to large arrays.

**Method.** The research combines systematic experimental measurements on fabricated nanopore arrays with rigorous 3D numerical modeling based on Poisson-Nernst-Planck theory.

**Model / system.** The physical system is solid-state nanopore arrays (NPAs) fabricated in $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ membranes, studied across varying pore numbers ($N$) and diameters. The modeling involves solving the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations to capture ion concentration polarization and electric field variations.

**Key observables.** Ionic conductance scaling laws ($	ext{G}_{	ext{NPA}}$ vs $N$), current rectification factor ($	ext{Rf}$), and osmotic power density.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Pore number ($N$ up to 10000), pore diameter (sub-3 nm to sub-20 nm), salt concentration, and interpore distance ($	ext{L}_{	ext{int}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often compares results against single nanopore models, which are shown to be insufficient for large arrays due to neglected pore interactions and polarization effects.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate fabrication methods (EBL/RIE vs. TEM-drilling), conductance measurements versus $N$ and concentration, $	ext{I-V}$ curves showing current rectification ($	ext{Rf}$ vs $N$), and power density scaling comparisons.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically investigates the dependence of ionic transport properties on pore number ($N$) and salt concentration. It first establishes conductance scaling deviations from linearity, then analyzes current rectification weakening with $N$, and finally quantifies the dramatic reduction in osmotic power upon upscaling, attributing these effects to polarization and field suppression.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Understanding the ionic transport and scaling behaviors in nanopore arrays is essential for bridging fundamental ion physics and blue energy applications. By fabricating sub-3 nm and sub-20 nm diameter nanopore arrays (NPAs) spanning from few pores to N ~ 10000, we systematically investigate ionic conductance, ion current rectification, and osmotic energy conversion. We report the ionic conductance scaling laws and nonlinearity with nanopore number, with stronger deviations from linearity at lower salt concentrations. Experimental evidence reveals that surface-charge-governed conductance and ion current rectification progressively weaken with increasing N and even vanish as the NPA scales up to N ~ 10000, resulting in an underestimation of surface charge density. In a sub-3 nm densely packed array (separation ~ 25 nm), the conductance exhibits an anomalous power-law dependence on concentration, deviating markedly from the single nanopore characteristics, attributed to the strong pore interactions. Furthermore, osmotic power harvesting measurements reveal a substantial reduction in power density upon scaling, with decreases of up to three orders of magnitude over the same range. To elucidate the underlying mechanism, we developed rigorous 3D modeling showing that the nonlinear behavior originates from concentration polarization at pore entrances and suppressed electric field across NPAs, collectively hindering ion transport. Our work provides insight into nonlinear ion-transport scaling and reveals fundamental differences between transport phenomena in single nanopores and nanopore arrays.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a predictive framework to engineer strong and broadband nonreciprocal thermal emitters using intrinsic magnetism in topological materials. By combining first-principles calculations with advanced electrodynamics solvers, the authors demonstrate that magnetic Weyl semimetals outperform traditional semiconductors for field-free energy harvesting applications. The key contribution is establishing quantitative scaling laws governing material design.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous derivation of quantitative design rules based on fundamental material parameters (like AHE response) for controlling thermal radiation is highly relevant to open quantum systems, particularly in designing engineered photonic or phononic structures that interact strongly with external fields or environments.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The goal is to design materials that exhibit strong, broadband nonreciprocal thermal radiation without requiring an external magnetic field.

**Main result.** Magnetic topological materials like Co3Sn2S2 were shown to achieve superior, intrinsic nonreciprocity compared to conventional semiconductors. The work established universal material design recipes based on the anomalous Hall response and optical loss.

**Method.** The study combines first-principles DFT calculations with Maxwell electrodynamics solvers (Berreman/S-matrix formalism) to compute frequency-dependent permittivity tensors.

**Model / system.** The physical system is magnetic topological materials, modeled using a gyrotropic dielectric tensor that incorporates magnetization-induced off-diagonal components. The analysis uses generalized $4 	imes 4$ Berreman matrix solvers for semi-infinite substrates.

**Key observables.** Nonreciprocal directional emissivity–absorptivity contrast ($\Delta(\omega, 	heta)$), maximum nonreciprocity ($\Delta_{\max}$), and operational bandwidth ($\Delta\omega$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The material design is governed by the ratio of anomalous Hall response ($g$) to optical loss ($\epsilon''_{d}$) for strength, and $\epsilon''_{d}/eta$ for bandwidth.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on linearizing the permittivity tensor near an epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) crossing frequency ($\omega_0$).

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the nonreciprocity spectra of Co3Sn2S2 against InAs, demonstrating superior performance. Later figures validate derived scaling laws for $\Delta_{\max}$ and $\Delta\omega$ across various candidate materials.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the physical need (field-free nonreciprocity) to developing a theoretical framework using DFT/Kubo calculations, deriving universal scaling laws ($\Delta_{\max} \propto g/(\epsilon''_{d})^p$), and finally validating these laws with advanced numerical solvers.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Breaking reciprocity in thermal radiation opens opportunities for energy harvesting, sensing, and thermal management. Traditional nonreciprocal radiative semiconductor devices need external magnetic field. In this work, we predict a series of magnetic topological materials for magnetic-field-free nonreciprocal thermal radiation in the infrared regime, by combining first-principles calculations with Maxwell electrodynamics. We find strong and broadband nonreciprocity in magnetic Weyl semimetals (e.g., Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$), outperforming the conventional semiconductor such as InAs. Furthermore, we propose universal material design recipes: strong nonreciprocity requires a large anomalous Hall response relative to the optical loss, whereas the broadband response favors large optical loss and small dielectric dispersion. Our work establishes a predictive materials-discovery framework and quantitative design rules for next-generation magnet-free nonreciprocal thermal devices.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper details an advanced microwave measurement technique using a vibrating carbon nanotube resonator to resolve the ambiguity between direct and parametric driving forces. By detecting sidebands at half the drive frequency ($	ext{f}_{	ext{drive}}/2$), the authors confirm parametric excitation, while signals at $	ext{f}_{	ext{drive}}$ confirm direct motion. This methodology is crucial for characterizing nonlinearities in nanoscale mechanical oscillators.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a sophisticated experimental technique for probing nonlinear dynamics in nanoscale mechanical systems by leveraging frequency mixing, which is highly relevant to understanding energy transfer and non-equilibrium physics in quantum devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is unambiguously distinguishing between direct mechanical excitation and parametric driving mechanisms in nanomechanical resonators, as standard electrical readout methods are insufficient.

**Main result.** By operating the device as an electromechanical mixer and measuring microwave sidebands, the authors successfully separated the signatures of direct motion from those of parametric resonance, even when drive frequencies were close.

**Method.** The technique involves using low-noise superconducting amplifiers to detect microwave sidebands ($	ext{f}_{	ext{sb}}$) at $	ext{f}_{	ext{drive}}/2$ (parametric signature) versus measuring signals directly at the drive frequency or DC (direct signature).

**Model / system.** The system is a vibrating carbon nanotube resonator integrated into a single-electron transistor (SET) structure. The analysis combines experimental measurements with theoretical models describing nonlinear stiffness terms and parametric resonance conditions.

**Key observables.** Sideband frequencies ($	ext{f}_{	ext{sb}}$), output power ($P_{	ext{out}}$) dependence on drive power, and the ratio of measured sidebands to the drive frequency (e.g., $	ext{f}_{	ext{drive}}/2$ vs. $	ext{f}_{	ext{drive}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Drive frequencies ($	ext{f}_{	ext{drive}}$), probe frequency ($	ext{f}_{	ext{probe}}$), and the order of nonlinearity ($\ell$) governing parametric coupling.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method assumes that direct driving yields signals at $	ext{f}_{	ext{drive}}$, while parametric driving generates distinct sidebands, allowing for spectral separation. Theoretical models rely on Taylor expansion of conductance and perturbation theory for resonance conditions.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare DC current measurements with AC detection at different sideband frequencies ($	ext{f}_{	ext{drive}}$ vs $	ext{f}_{	ext{drive}}/2$) to differentiate excitation types, and show power dependence fitting to theoretical models for both mechanisms.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the ambiguity of standard readout, introduces the mixer/sideband detection technique, demonstrates its success in separating direct ($	ext{f} \pm 1$ or $	ext{f}_{	ext{drive}}$) from parametric ($	ext{f} \pm 0$ or $	ext{f}_{	ext{drive}}/2$) responses for different modes, and finally extends the analysis to high-order nonlinearities.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Parametric driving is a powerful route to amplification and nonlinear control in nanomechanical resonators, but its signatures can be ambiguous because standard dc electrical readout does not directly reveal the frequency of motion. Here we resolve this ambiguity by measuring the motional frequency of a vibrating carbon nanotube independently of the drive frequency. We operate the nanotube as an electromechanical mixer and detect microwave sidebands using a low-noise superconducting amplifier. This frequency-resolved readout distinguishes direct motion of the first overtone from parametric motion of the fundamental, even when the corresponding drive frequencies nearly coincide. The two mechanisms are further separated by their drive-power dependence. Beyond conventional parametric resonance at $2f_0$, we observe responses to driving at $3f_0$ and $4f_0$, consistent with high-order parametric excitation associated with nonlinear stiffness terms.

</details>

**Summary.** This work establishes a rigorous criterion, the intrinsic decay length, to quantify when localized solutions in finite elastic structures approach their infinite-domain limits. By analyzing prototypical models from mechanics, it provides a unified framework explaining the convergence rate and the differing validity regimes of weakly nonlinear approximations in both finite and infinite settings.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical elasticity, the mathematical machinery—comparing solutions based on different topological structures (periodic vs. homoclinic) and identifying a characteristic length scale ($\ell_{dec}$) that dictates the breakdown of approximations—is highly relevant to understanding crossover regimes in quantum systems or disordered media.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is determining when localized solutions in finite elastic structures can be accurately approximated by their simpler infinite-domain counterparts.

**Main result.** Convergence occurs exponentially once the structural length exceeds a characteristic intrinsic decay length, which governs the validity of both approximations and weakly nonlinear theories.

**Method.** Theoretical analysis using phase-plane methods, asymptotic matching (inner/outer regions), and quantitative error estimation via Grönwall-type inequalities.

**Model / system.** The study uses prototypical localization models derived from continuum mechanics, applied to physical systems like bulging in membrane tubes or helical buckling in twisted rods. The analysis compares solutions governed by periodic orbits (finite domain) to those governed by homoclinic orbits (infinite domain).

**Key observables.** Intrinsic decay length ($\ell_{dec}$), amplitude measures of localized deformation, and the difference between finite-domain and infinite-domain solution profiles.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Structural length ($L$), loading parameter ($\gamma$), and the intrinsic decay length ($\ell_{dec}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the system can be modeled by a prototypical nonlinear ODE, allowing for comparison between periodic (finite) and homoclinic (infinite) solutions.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare amplitude measures and centerline positions of localized states across varying loading parameters ($\gamma$), showing rapid convergence towards the infinite-domain solution as $\gamma$ decreases or $L$ increases relative to $\ell_{dec}$.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops a unified geometric framework by comparing finite-domain boundary value problems (periodic orbits) with their infinite-domain limits (homoclinic orbits). It applies this framework sequentially to membrane bulging and helical buckling, culminating in the definition of the intrinsic decay length.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Localization in finite elastic structures is often studied using infinite-domain solutions, which avoid the explicit treatment of boundaries and admit simpler analytical descriptions. Yet it remains poorly understood when finite-domain localized states can be accurately approximated by their infinite-domain counterparts. In this work, we show that the accuracy is controlled by an intrinsic decay length. Using a prototypical localization model, we show that finite-domain localized solutions converge exponentially to the corresponding infinite-domain localized solution once the structural length exceeds the intrinsic decay length. The intrinsic decay length also explains the markedly different validity regimes of finite- and infinite-domain weakly nonlinear approximations. It further has important implications for numerical computation, since once the structural length exceeds the intrinsic decay length, localized solutions corresponding to different domain lengths differ only by exponentially small quantities, making them increasingly difficult to distinguish numerically. The theoretical predictions are validated using two representative localization problems: bulging in membrane tubes and localized helical buckling in twisted rods. The present work provides a unified geometric framework for understanding localization transition, asymptotic validity, and numerical computation in elastic localization.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports on an experimental method utilizing Terahertz Time-domain Spectroscopy to optically detect the topological surface charge accumulation predicted by the Topological Magnetoelectric Effect in topological insulator thin films. By measuring Faraday rotation at oblique incidence, the authors demonstrate a technique robust against material conductivity limitations, providing a direct pathway toward verifying fundamental quantum electrodynamic effects.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly related to standard AMO topics like cold atoms or cavity QED, this work involves probing fundamental quantum electrodynamics effects (magnetoelectric coupling) using advanced optical spectroscopy techniques that share conceptual links with light-matter interaction studies in open systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to develop an optical method using THz-TDS to directly detect the quantized surface charge accumulation ($\eta/B_z$) associated with the Topological Magnetoelectric Effect (TME) in 3D topological insulators.

**Main result.** The technique successfully measures Faraday rotation at oblique incidence, demonstrating robustness against finite longitudinal conductivity and showing consistent results across different incident angles ($45^\circ$ vs $60^\circ$).

**Method.** Terahertz Time-domain Spectroscopy (THz-TDS) is employed to measure the Faraday rotation angle ($	heta_F$) in thin films under oblique incidence, allowing for the extraction of surface charge density.

**Model / system.** The study uses chromium-doped $(	ext{Bi},	ext{Sb})_2	ext{Te}_3$ thin films exhibiting topological properties. The physics is governed by the TME, which predicts a quantized surface charge accumulation proportional to an applied magnetic field component ($B_z$).

**Key observables.** Faraday rotation angle ($	heta_F$), extracted surface charge density ($\eta/B_z$), and the frequency-linear imaginary part of the Faraday rotation for axion insulators.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Oblique incidence angles ($45^\circ, 60^\circ$); low temperatures (e.g., $2	ext{ K}$); comparison between optical vs. transport measurements ($\sigma_L/\sigma_T$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation relies on modeling the transmitted electric field using transmission and propagation matrices; for axion insulators, approximations like $\phi \ll 1$ are used.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the THz-TDS setup geometry (oblique incidence), time-domain waveforms showing $E_X$ and $E_Y$, angular dependence of Faraday rotation, and comparisons demonstrating the optical method's robustness against longitudinal conductivity ($\sigma_L$).

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the TME in TIs, details the THz-TDS experimental setup for measuring oblique incidence effects, derives the relationship between $	heta_F$ and $\eta/B_z$, presents measurements confirming consistency across angles, and discusses extensions to axion insulators.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The topological magnetoelectric effect (TME) in three-dimensional topological insulators manifests as a quantized surface charge accumulation proportional to an applied magnetic field. Here we demonstrate an optical method using terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS) to detect surface charge accumulation in a chromium-doped (Bi,Sb)$_2$Te$_3$ thin film under oblique incidence, achieving sub-milliradian Faraday rotation precision. Unlike transport probes that require ultralow longitudinal conductivity, this optical technique is robust against finite $σ_L$, degrading by less than $0.3\%$ even when $σ_L \sim σ_T$. We extract the charge accumulation $η/B_z$ from the measured Faraday rotation and show results at $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ coincide within experimental uncertainty. Extending this to axion insulators, we predict that the TME produces an imaginary Faraday rotation linear in frequency, whose slope directly reflects the single-surface charge density. With improved sample thickness and precision, this optical scheme provides a viable pathway toward direct verification of the TME and four-dimensional quantum Hall effect.

</details>

**Summary.** This work demonstrates that interfacial oxidation provides a powerful handle to engineer efficient conversion from spin angular momentum to orbital angular momentum in heavy-metal heterostructures. By measuring ultrafast THz emission, the authors prove this effect is maximized at oxidized interfaces, opening a general route for designing high-performance orbitronic terahertz emitters.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly related to quantum information protocols, the study involves ultrafast dynamics, spin-orbit coupling effects, and engineered electronic states, which are foundational concepts in condensed matter physics relevant to advanced quantum devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to understand how interfacial oxidation can be engineered to control and enhance spin-to-orbital conversion in heavy-metal/ferromagnetic heterostructures for applications in orbitronic terahertz emitters.

**Main result.** Interfacial oxidation at the W/Co interface drives a highly efficient spin-to-orbital conversion, evidenced by THz emission amplitudes significantly larger than conventional bilayers. This mechanism is shown to be generic across different heavy metals and scales with their spin-orbit coupling strength.

**Method.** The research employs time-resolved Terahertz (THz) emission spectroscopy on engineered thin-film heterostructures, complemented by structural characterization using STEM/EELS and XPS.

**Model / system.** The physical system consists of multilayered metal/oxide heterostructures, primarily W/Co/SiO2. The mechanism relies on the electronic structure modification (orbital texture) induced by oxygen incorporation at the interfaces between heavy metals and ferromagnets.

**Key observables.** THz emission amplitude enhancement ($\sim 3	imes$ over Co/Pt), linear time delay scaling with W thickness, and chemical states confirmed via XPS.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Heavy metal type (e.g., Pt, Ta vs Ti, Cu), layer thicknesses ($t_W$, $t_{Co}$), and the degree of interfacial oxidation.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The observed THz enhancement is directly attributable to orbital-current transport originating from the oxidized interface, which acts as a trigger for spin-to-orbital conversion.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare THz signals across various heterostructures and show the linear dependence of the time delay on W thickness. Structural characterization confirms interfacial intermixing and oxidation states in the critical W/Co/SiO2 structure.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem by noting the unexplored role of oxidation in spin-to-orbital conversion, presents THz measurements showing enhancement in W/Co/SiO2, systematically varies layer parameters to pinpoint the oxidation mechanism, and concludes with a general framework for orbitronic emitter design.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Oxidation engineering provides a route to control orbital degrees of freedom, yet its role in spin-to-orbital conversion remains largely unexplored. Here, we report an efficient spin-to-orbital conversion mechanism driven by interfacial oxidation at heavy-metal interfaces. In W/Co/SiO2 heterostructures, terahertz emission exhibits a time delay that scales linearly with the W thickness, identifying orbital-current transport as the dominant origin. The emission amplitude is approximately three times larger than that of Co/Pt bilayers, indicating highly efficient conversion from spin to orbital angular momentum. Systematic variation of Co thickness, stoichiometry, and interface configuration reveals that the effect originates from oxidation of the W layer at the W/Co interface, which modulates the interfacial orbital texture. We further show that this mechanism is generic across different heavy metals and scales with their spin-orbit coupling strength. These results establish oxidation as an effective handle to engineer spin-to-orbital conversion and provide a general route toward orbitronic terahertz emitters.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces an optical technique using structured light beams to measure the intrinsic loop-current chirality within moiré materials like twisted bilayer graphene. By exploiting the threefold ($C_3$) rotational symmetry, they demonstrate that this chiral signature is uniquely isolated in the $\Delta\ell=3$ channel of a measured photocurrent. This provides a powerful, symmetry-resolved diagnostic tool for characterizing geometric properties in quantum electronic systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work bridges concepts from topological physics (Berry curvature, chirality) with advanced quantum optics techniques (OAM filtering), providing a concrete, measurable protocol to detect subtle geometric properties in solid-state systems that might otherwise be masked by disorder or symmetry breaking.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The authors propose a method to optically probe the intrinsic loop-current chirality present in moiré materials, such as twisted bilayer graphene.

**Main result.** They show that preserving $C_3$ symmetry allows the intrinsic chiral contribution to be isolated specifically in the $\Delta\ell=3$ channel of the helicity-dependent dc photocurrent. This establishes angular-momentum-resolved nonlinear optics as a powerful diagnostic tool for geometric chirality.

**Method.** The method uses interfering optical vortex beams carrying Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) ($\ell$) to act as an angular-momentum filter, projecting the nonlinear response onto specific harmonic channels ($\Delta\ell$).

**Model / system.** The primary system is moiré materials, exemplified by twisted bilayer graphene (TBG), which hosts electronic circulation and geometric phases on triangular plaquettes. The theoretical framework involves analyzing the nonlinear optical response kernel $K_{\omega}(\mathbf{k})$ based on the Bistritzer–MacDonald Hamiltonian.

**Key observables.** Helicity-dependent dc photocurrent, decomposed into OAM-resolved spectral weights $A(\Delta\ell)(\omega)$, and the loop phase accumulation $\Phi_	riangle$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The selection rule depends critically on the preservation of $C_3$ symmetry; strain or perturbations break this symmetry, activating different channels like $\Delta\ell=2$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that local $C_3$ symmetry dictates the selection rules for the OAM channels, even when considering finite beam waists or rotational disorder.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the schematic of TBG moiré superlattices, the elementary triangular plaquettes forming closed loops, and intensity profiles demonstrating how optical vortices interact with $C_3$ symmetry.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops a theoretical framework linking intrinsic geometric chirality (related to loop currents) to specific angular harmonics ($\Delta\ell=3$) in the nonlinear optical response. It contrasts this intrinsic signal against contributions from symmetry-breaking perturbations ($\Delta\ell=2$), proposing diagnostic ratios for experimental verification.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose a symmetry-resolved optical probe of intrinsic loop-current chirality in moiré materials, with twisted bilayer graphene as a representative realization. Interlayer interference generates chiral electronic circulation on triangular plaquettes, giving rise to an intrinsic geometric chirality that enters the second-order response through a $C_3$-selected angular harmonic of the Berry curvature and can be isolated by the orbital-angular-momentum difference $Δ\ell$ of interfering optical vortex beams. When moiré $C_3$ symmetry is preserved, the intrinsic contribution appears in the $Δ\ell=3$ channel of the helicity-dependent dc photocurrent, whereas $C_3$-breaking perturbations activate additional channels. These results establish angular-momentum-resolved nonlinear optics as a route to probing geometric chirality in moiré and other symmetry-engineered quantum materials.

</details>
