**Summary.** This theoretical work elucidates that domain walls in valley-polarized graphene act as electronic valves, blocking current unless intervalley hybridization is present. This mechanism is critical both for mediating normal state electron transport and sustaining supercurrent flow across superconducting junctions connecting opposite-chirality regions.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of a 'valley valve' controlling charge transport via symmetry-protected coupling mechanisms is highly relevant to understanding topological superconductivity and engineered quantum devices in 2D materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how electron transport across domain walls separating regions with opposite valley polarization is governed by intervalley interactions in symmetry-broken rhombohedral graphene.

**Main result.** Intervalley coupling is crucial, acting as a 'valve' that enables both electron transmission in the normal state and supports an appreciable supercurrent in the superconducting state.

**Method.** The work employs Green's function formalism, Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) theory for superconductivity, and numerical simulations to solve boundary value problems across domain walls.

**Model / system.** The system is rhombohedral multilayer graphene polarized by a displacement field, exhibiting time-reversal symmetry breaking. The analysis uses effective Hamiltonians incorporating valley polarization ($\epsilon_K(x), \epsilon_{K'}(x)$) and superconducting pairing amplitudes ($\Delta_{	ext{SC}}$).

**Key observables.** Electron transmission coefficient ($T$), Supercurrent density ($J_c$), Current-Phase Relation (CPR).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Domain wall width ($w$), intervalley coupling strength ($m$), gap magnitude ($\Delta$), and chemical potential ($\mu$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often assumes an abrupt domain wall approximation or uses continuum models for the superconducting phase; spin polarization is sometimes assumed uniform.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate schematic domain walls, transmission dependence on coupling strength ($m$) and angle ($	heta$), and the Current-Phase Relation (CPR) showing supercurrent modulation with the pairing phase $\phi$.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from analyzing normal state transport across abrupt domain walls to deriving the necessary intervalley couplings. It then extends this analysis to the superconducting regime using BdG theory, calculating the resulting Josephson supercurrent.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Rhombohedral multilayer graphene polarized by a moderate perpendicular displacement field hosts a time-reversal-symmetry-breaking valley-and-spin-polarized metallic phase that may condense into a chiral superconductor. Recent magnetic imaging and transport measurements in this unconventional system suggest the presence of domain walls both in the metallic and superconducting phases. In this work, we show that valley domain walls are impenetrable barriers to transport in the metallic regime. Transmission through such a domain wall must therefore be mediated by intervalley interactions. We derive the symmetry-allowed terms and show via microscopic numerical simulations that they enable the transmission of electrons across the domain wall. In the superconducting phase, we find that intervalley mixing is crucial for supporting an appreciable supercurrent through a SNS' Josephson junction that connects opposite-chirality superconducting regions. Taken together, our work elucidates the nature of domain walls in these experimentally relevant multilayer systems and emphasizes the critical role of intervalley hybridization plays in governing their transport properties.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study proposes an oxide-driven approach to realize robust valleytronic devices by creating a $	ext{V}_2	ext{O}_3/	ext{WSe}_2$ heterostructure. The intrinsic ferromagnetism of the oxide induces a significant, field-free valley splitting in $	ext{WSe}_2$. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that applying external electric fields can enhance this valley polarization and maintain high operational temperatures.

**Why it may be interesting.** The ability to engineer robust quantum phenomena like valley polarization using proximity coupling with a correlated oxide ($	ext{V}_2	ext{O}_3$) provides a powerful, tunable platform for simulating spin-valley coupling mechanisms relevant in AMO physics and open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Achieving a robust valley splitting in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) at zero magnetic field is challenging for next-generation valleytronic and spintronic devices.

**Main result.** The $	ext{V}_2	ext{O}_3/	ext{WSe}_2$ heterostructure exhibits a spontaneous valley splitting of $\sim 10.41 	ext{ meV}$ due to the magnetic proximity effect, which is tunable by external electric fields.

**Method.** The study relies heavily on first-principles calculations (DFT+U) combined with advanced simulations like Metropolis Monte Carlo for thermal properties.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is a van der Waals heterostructure composed of $	ext{WSe}_2$ coupled with a ferromagnetic monolayer ($	ext{ML}$) of $	ext{V}_2	ext{O}_3$. The calculations investigate structural stability, electronic band structure, and magnetic coupling.

**Key observables.** Valley splitting magnitude ($\sim 10.41 	ext{ meV}$), Curie temperature ($500 	ext{ K}$), Magnetocrystalline Anisotropy Energy (MAE), and charge transfer across the interface.

**Important parameters / regimes.** External electric field strength ($\pm 0.1 	ext{ eV}/	ext{\AA}$), $	ext{U}_{	ext{eff}}$ parameter for V $3d$ electrons, and lattice mismatch strain values.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The calculations assume the use of DFT-D3 vdW corrections and that the magnetic proximity effect is the dominant mechanism inducing valley splitting.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate SOC-resolved MAE dependence on electric field, electrostatic potential profiles showing dipole moment changes, and temperature-dependent magnetization curves confirming high Curie temperatures.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes structural optimization, electronic band structure (including Dirac points), magnetic properties ($T_c$, MAE), and finally demonstrates the control mechanism by applying external perpendicular electric fields to enhance valley splitting.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

To achieve a robust valley splitting in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) at zero magnetic field is a challenging and elusive goal for valleytronic and spintronic devices. Therefore, in the current study, using the first principles calculations, we introduce an oxide-driven valleytronic platform by employing a two-dimensional ferromagnetic oxide (V2O3) as a magnetic proximity partner for WSe2. We found that the intrinsic ferromagnetism of V2O3 induces a prominent and spontaneous valley splitting of ~ 10.41 meV in WSe2. This pronounced valley polarization mainly originates from the strong interfacial exchange coupling interaction and charge redistribution mediated by V 3d electrons, coupled with the intrinsic spin-orbit coupling of WSe2. Interestingly, this value is significantly greater than the previously reported value for CrI3/WSe2, which corresponds to an effective magnetic field of ~ 10 T. Besides, we also have a high Curie temperature of 500 K, and an out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) of 0.31 meV, indicating that this oxide-based heterostructure can also be used for near-room temperature operation. Importantly, under the external electric field with a step of 0.1 eV/Å, the ferromagnetism is preserved and an enhancement in Curie temperature and MAE makes this oxide-based heterostructure more valuable for the next generation valleytronic devices. Therefore, these findings establish a new paradigm for realizing tunable, robust, and magnetic field-free valleytronic and spintronic devices for this oxide-based heterostructure. Moreover, this concept can be generalized to other correlated oxide-based TMD systems, providing a versatile strategy for next-generation quantum and functional materials.

</details>

**Summary.** The study investigates magnetotransport in $	ext{NiI}_2$/Graphene heterostructures to read out the magnetic state of the insulating $	ext{NiI}_2$. By measuring linear and nonlinear electrical responses, the authors show that characteristic anomalies track $	ext{NiI}_2$'s magnetic transitions. This establishes graphene as a sensitive, non-invasive probe for spintronic applications using insulating van der Waals magnets.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is interesting because it demonstrates an electrical readout mechanism for magnetism in insulating materials using 2D conductors, providing a platform analogous to how quantum systems are probed via coupling to external fields or substrates.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to probe magnetic phase behavior within electrically insulating van der Waals magnets ($	ext{NiI}_2$) using electrical transport measurements.

**Main result.** Magnetotransport features, particularly large anisotropic low-field peaks in the first harmonic and distinct nonlinear signals in the second harmonic, are observed in graphene/$	ext{NiI}_2$ heterostructures, confirming an interfacial coupling to $	ext{NiI}_2$'s magnetic state.

**Method.** The research employs magnetotransport measurements (longitudinal magnetoresistance) and temperature-dependent analysis of nonlinear electrical responses ($	ext{2}\omega$ and $	ext{3}\omega$) on the heterostructure, comparing results against a graphene/h-BN control device.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a van der Waals heterostructure composed of monolayer graphene (the conducting readout layer) interfaced with the insulating helical antiferromagnet $	ext{NiI}_2$. The measurements probe magnetic proximity effects at this interface.

**Key observables.** First-harmonic longitudinal magnetoresistance ($	ext{MR}$), second-harmonic resistance ($2\omega$), third-harmonic resistance ($3\omega$), and magnetic susceptibility ($\chi$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Multiferroic transition temperature of $	ext{NiI}_2$ ($	ext{T}_{	ext{N}2} \approx 59 	ext{ K}$), in-plane vs. out-of-plane magnetic fields, and measurement harmonics.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that the observed transport anomalies are due to interfacial coupling with $	ext{NiI}_2$'s magnetic state, rather than generic graphene properties or purely thermal effects (though Joule heating remains a concern for higher harmonics).

**Figures summary.** Figures show basic device diagrams and SQUID M-H curves; subsequent figures detail temperature dependence of linear resistance, first derivative, second harmonic ($2\omega$), and third harmonic ($3\omega$) responses, alongside $	ext{MR}$ sweeps comparing the heterostructure to control graphene.

**Paper structure.** The paper follows a structure of presenting the physical system ($	ext{NiI}_2$/Graphene), detailing multiple measurement techniques (linear MR, nonlinear harmonics, temperature dependence), and systematically contrasting the results against a non-magnetic control device to isolate the magnetic contribution.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate magnetotransport in a van der Waals heterostructure composed of monolayer graphene and the insulating helical antiferromagnet NiI$_2$. While NiI$_2$ is highly resistive and thus poorly suited for direct transport measurements, we demonstrate that magnetotransport in an adjacent graphene layer provides an electrical readout of magnetic-state-dependent interfacial behavior. Most notably, first-harmonic longitudinal magnetoresistance under in-plane magnetic fields exhibits large, anisotropic low-field peaks that are absent from a monolayer graphene/h-BN control device and are suppressed above the multiferroic transition temperature of NiI$_2$. Temperature-dependent harmonic measurements provide complementary evidence: the second-harmonic resistance shows the clearest nonlinear contrast relative to the control device, while the third harmonic contains a larger generic nonlinear and thermal background that is nevertheless modified in the heterostructure. These results demonstrate that graphene-based transport measurements offer a sensitive, non-invasive probe of magnetic phase behavior in electrically insulating van der Waals magnets, opening routes toward spintronic devices based on insulating vdW multiferroics.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a comprehensive variational theory to find solitary wave solutions for the extended Korteweg-de Vries (eKdV) equation, which models dispersive water waves. By employing an augmented Lagrangian method, the authors derive explicit formulas for soliton parameters and successfully apply these results to estimate characteristics of Dispersive Shock Waves. The findings are validated by strong agreement with direct numerical simulations.

**Why it may be interesting.** Although focused on fluid dynamics, the rigorous application of generalized variational principles (like those involving Luke's Lagrangian) to derive exact solutions for complex nonlinear PDEs is a powerful mathematical technique relevant to finding conserved quantities or effective Hamiltonians in quantum field theories or open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To derive and analyze single solitary wave solutions for the Extended Korteweg-de Vries (eKdV) equation, which models dispersive hydrodynamic phenomena.

**Main result.** The authors derived explicit second-order formulas for the solitary wave height, velocity, and inverse width, showing strong agreement with direct numerical simulations for both isolated solitons and Dispersive Shock Waves (DSWs).

**Method.** The primary method involves extending the averaged Lagrangian approach using an augmented Lagrangian model incorporating Lagrange multipliers to handle non-conservative constraints.

**Model / system.** The system is governed by the eKdV equation, a fifth-order nonlinear dispersive PDE arising from approximations of shallow water wave equations. This models phenomena in fluid mechanics and plasma physics.

**Key observables.** Solitary wave height ($A_s$), solitary wave velocity ($V_s$), inverse width ($\omega_s$), and the leading edge parameters for DSWs.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Small amplitude/long wavelength parameters ($\alpha, eta$) are crucial; the results show asymptotic reduction to classical KdV when higher-order terms vanish.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a single solitary wave solution with a sech^2 profile and utilizes approximations like the DSW equal amplitude approximation for shock dynamics.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare theoretical variational predictions against direct numerical simulations, showing agreement for both isolated solitons and the lead edge of dispersive shock waves across various parameter regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically develops the theory by first deriving the eKdV equation from shallow water wave approximations (Boussinesq equations), then applying advanced variational techniques using an augmented Lagrangian to find the solitary wave solution, and finally applying this framework to estimate parameters for DSWs.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this work, we extend the method of averaged Lagrangian to the study of the general second-order (non-conservative) extended Korteweg--de Vries equation, known as the eKdV equation. Building on the framework introduced in [18], we construct a master (augmented) Lagrangian, modeled on Luke's Lagrangian, that incorporates the governing constraints at the appropriate asymptotic orders via the method of Lagrange multipliers. Averaging the resulting Euler-Lagrange equations in the traveling wave setting yields the existence of a (single) solitary wave solution with a $\operatorname{sech}^2$ profile. Explicit second-order formulas are obtained for the height of the solitary wave, together with the solitary wave velocity and inverse width, in terms of a fixed amplitude parameter. A key feature of the derived expressions is their asymptotic reduction to the classical KdV results when the first-order terms are retained. To assess the robustness and utility of the variational solitonic solutions, the derived formulas are subsequently applied, via the dispersive shock equal amplitude approximation method, to estimate the height and velocity of the leading solitary wave edge of dispersive shock waves governed by the eKdV Riemann problem. Theoretical predictions for the relevant wave parameters in both the eKdV solitary wave and dispersive shock wave problems are compared with direct numerical simulations and found to be in strong agreement.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper theoretically investigates how an applied in-plane electric field controls spin polarization during electron transport across a hybrid junction linking a non-magnetic wire to an antiferromagnetic ring. **Why it may be interesting.** This work models spin-filtering effects in low-dimensional magnetic nanostructures using advanced quantum transport theory (NEGF), which is highly relevant for understanding engineered spintronic devices that interact with external fields.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates spin-dependent electron transfer through a hybrid magnetic system composed of an NM wire coupled to an AFM mesoscopic ring.

**Main result.** The in-plane electric field acts as a powerful, externally controllable tuning parameter capable of inducing or enhancing significant spin polarization (SP) in the junction.

**Method.** Transport properties are calculated using the Non-Equilibrium Green's Function (NEGF) formalism within a tight-binding framework.

**Model / system.** The system consists of an NM wire coupled to a side-attached AFM mesoscopic ring, placed between two non-magnetic electrodes. The Hamiltonian incorporates coupling terms and is analyzed for single-coupled versus double-coupled junction geometries.

**Key observables.** Spin Polarization (SP), spin-resolved currents ($I_\sigma$), and transmission probabilities ($T_\sigma(E)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** In-plane electric field strength ($\epsilon$), coupling strengths ($\gamma$), bias voltage ($V$), and temperature ($\Theta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a clean NM wire and impurity-free AFM ring, though robustness checks are performed across various parameters.

It first establishes baseline transport, then demonstrates how the electric field breaks symmetry to induce large SP, concluding with robustness checks across temperature and size.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study spin-dependent transport in a hybrid magnetic system, where a non-magnetic (NM) wire is coupled to a side-attached antiferromagnetic (AFM) mesoscopic ring, placed between two non-magnetic electrodes subject to an in-plane electric field oriented perpendicular to the NM wire. The system is described within a tight-binding (TB) framework, and transport properties are computed using the non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism. We consider two junction configurations distinguished by the wire-ring coupling: a single-coupled junction and a double-coupled junction. In the single-coupled configuration, the coupling geometry alone breaks the spin symmetry, yielding a finite spin polarization (SP) even without any external field. The in-plane electric field further enhances the symmetry breaking in both configurations, serving as an efficient tuning parameter that drives the SP nearly $100\%$ in the low-bias region. In the double-coupled configuration, spin symmetry is preserved in the absence of the external field, and the electric field acts as a sole source of symmetry breaking, producing a large SP. Finite temperature effects and different system sizes are examined, confirming the robustness of the observed features. To validate the findings over a wide parameter space, we considered different sets of parameters and found that the key signatures remain unchanged. Our results demonstrate that such hybrid structures are promising candidates for realizing an externally controllable spintronic device in low-dimensional systems.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to obtain spectral information from extremely weak light emission sources, such as Scanning Tunneling Microscopy Luminescence (STML), while minimizing noise and complexity compared to conventional grating spectrometers.

**Main result.** The Time-of-Flight Photon Spectrometer (TOFS) was demonstrated to be a straightforward, cost-effective addition to existing STML setups, successfully reproducing spectral profiles in the near-infrared range.

**Method.** Spectral analysis is achieved by exploiting the wavelength-dependent group refractive index of a long dispersive optical fiber, which converts photon arrival times into wavelength information via time-of-flight measurement.

**Model / system.** The experiment couples STML (exciting plasmons on Ag(111) using voltage pulses) with a TOFS setup. The core physical principle relies on the dispersion relation within an optical fiber, where arrival times are measured by single-photon detectors.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We build and commission a time-of-flight photon spectrometer (TOFS) for scanning tunneling microscopy luminescence (STML). We obtain the spectrum by exploiting the wavelength dependent refractive index of a long dispersive optical fiber that converts photon arrival times into wavelength information; blue photons are delayed more than red photons. The setup uses a pulsed excitation source, either laser flashes or voltage pulses, to launch the photons from the junction into a single photon detector. The TOFS calibration can be performed and transferred to the STML setup from a separate benchtop experiment using pulsed light sources with known wavelength. We verify the TOFS during STML operation by simultaneously recording luminescence from the Ag-Ag(111) plasmon using a conventional grating spectrometer. Our experiments show that the TOFS is a straightforward and cost-effective addition to existing STML setups with good performance in the near-infrared range. The TOFS is compatible with a drop-in replacement of the single photon detector such as a superconducting nanowire single photon detector or even bolometers that may expand the useful spectral range beyond the abilities of current STML setups.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a generalized long-wave limit method incorporating spectral perturbations to systematically construct higher-order, degenerate lump solutions for integrable equations like the KP-I equation. By controlling phase parameters through asymptotic expansions, the authors demonstrate an enhanced ability to generate complex multi-lump structures and analyze anomalous scattering dynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly about quantum systems, the mathematical techniques developed—analyzing complex multi-soliton interactions, spectral degeneracies, and asymptotic behavior of nonlinear PDEs—are highly relevant to understanding wave phenomena in quantum optics or Bose-Einstein condensates.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is constructing higher-order, degenerate lump solutions for integrable nonlinear wave equations, specifically focusing on the Kadomtsev–Petviashvili I (KP-I) equation.

**Main result.** The proposed generalized long-wave limit method successfully generates a broader family of higher-order lump solutions than previous techniques, allowing control over up to M(M+1)/2 degenerate lumps from an M-lump chain.

**Method.** It employs a generalized long-wave limit framework that incorporates spectral perturbations and systematically tunes phase parameters through asymptotic expansions of auxiliary functions.

**Model / system.** The study is centered on integrable systems, particularly the KP-I equation. The solutions analyzed are non-singular rational structures known as lump solutions, which exhibit complex scattering behavior.

**Key observables.** Lump solution amplitudes and velocities; anomalous scattering patterns; the number of supported degenerate lump waves (up to M(M+1)/2).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The small parameter $\epsilon$ controlling the long-wave limit, and spectral parameters ($\lambda_j$) which are perturbed as $\lambda + i d_j \epsilon$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method relies on expanding solutions in powers of a small parameter $\epsilon$, and specific algebraic conditions must be solved by setting lower-order coefficients to zero.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the comparison between normal (elastic) and anomalous scattering for two and three lumps, showing curved paths characteristic of energy redistribution. They also show pattern transformations of multi-lump solutions at $t=0$ based on free parameters.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the generalized method by first establishing the framework using spectral perturbations, then applying it to derive second- and third-order lump solutions for KP-I, demonstrating how different parameter choices control structural modes (e.g., merging vs. polygonal arrangements).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

A generalized long-wave limit method that introduces spectral perturbations into the long-wave limit framework is proposed for constructing higher-order lump solutions. Within a unified small-parameter framework, the method simultaneously accounts for the degeneracy of spectral parameters, different vanishing rates of wave numbers, and higher-order modulations of the phase parameters. By tuning the phase parameters to push the leading term of the auxiliary function expansion to a prescribed order, the resulting solutions support a controllable number of lump waves and exhibit rich anomalous scattering behavior. Applied to the Kadomtsev--Petviashvili-I equation, second- and third-order lump solutions are systematically derived, and the degeneration of lump chains into higher-order lumps is transparently revealed in the long-wave limit. The method can generate degenerate solutions with up to \(M(M+1)/2\) lumps from an \(M\)-lump chain. Moreover, compared with the previously proposed improved long-wave limit method, the present approach is capable of producing higher-order lump solutions whose long-time asymptotic behavior is independent of the Yablonskii--Vorob'ev polynomials. Its extension to hybrid higher-order lump solutions with distinct spectral parameters is also discussed.

</details>

**Summary.** This work establishes a comprehensive, physically-informed framework to predict the morphology of hybrid lipid-diblock copolymer membranes. By incorporating concepts like chemical immiscibility and hydrophobic mismatch into theoretical models validated by molecular dynamics, the authors map out phase diagrams that explain transitions between mixed, laterally separated, unzipped, and polymer-rich states.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on soft matter self-assembly rather than quantum phenomena, the rigorous application of statistical mechanics principles (free energy functionals, phase diagrams) to predict complex emergent structures is highly relevant for understanding many-body interactions in confined or fluctuating systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is developing a rational design framework for hybrid lipid-diblock copolymer membranes due to the multitude of parameters governing their nanoscale morphology and properties.

**Main result.** The authors identified four key morphologies (mixed, laterally phase-separated, unzipped, polymer-rich) and provided mechanistic rules based on chemical immiscibility, hydrophobic mismatch, and areal density to predict transitions between them.

**Method.** The study combines theoretical extensions of amphiphilic monolayer theory with validation using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations across a wide parameter space.

**Model / system.** The system consists of hybrid membranes combining lipids (e.g., DPPC) and diblock copolymers ($	ext{PBD-}b	ext{-PEO}$). The theoretical framework models the free energy functional, while simulations track structural evolution under varying block lengths and compositions.

**Key observables.** Membrane thickness, phase order parameter ($\langle\psi_{xy}angle$), conditional entropy of mixing, and characteristic morphologies (mixed, LPS, unzipped, polymer-rich).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Hydrophobic mismatch ($\Delta L$), areal density ($	ext{a}_{	ext{polymer}} \cdot \phi$ vs $	ext{a}_{	ext{lipid}}(1-\phi)$), PBD/PEO block lengths ($n_{PBD}, n_{PEO}$), and temperature.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model assumes the bilayer can be treated as two uncoupled monolayers, and certain geometric arguments are used to predict transitions between different morphological states.

**Figures summary.** Figures include phase maps classifying morphologies based on system parameters (e.g., polymer content vs. block length) and plots showing thickness dependence on chain lengths.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from developing a theoretical free energy functional to identifying key driving forces for morphology transitions, which are then rigorously tested and unified using extensive molecular dynamics simulations across multiple lipid/polymer combinations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Hybrid lipid block copolymer membranes are promising for many applications in drug delivery, single molecule detection, in-membrane protein folding, and synthetic cells. However, rational design is difficult due to the many design parameters which determine the nano- and micron-scale morphology and properties. In this work, we propose a physically-informed framework which incorporates chemical immiscibility, hydrophobic thickness mismatch and geometric constraints to predict the morphology of hybrid membranes. For this purpose, we extend existing theory for amphiphilic monolayers to model the thickness of diblock copolymer bilayers, demonstrating that both the hydrophobic and hydrophilic block lengths determine the thickness. We identify and rationalize the four primary membrane morphologies observed: mixed, laterally phase-separated, unzipped (thick-thin coexistence), and polymer-rich. Specifically, chemical immiscibility differentiates mixed membranes from laterally phase separated membranes, and hydrophobic mismatch drives transitions to unzipped or polymer-rich morphologies. Areal density, finally, determines the crossover between unzipped and polymer-rich states. We validate our theoretical predictions using coarse-grained molecular dynamics across a broad parameter space, including multiple lipid species (DOPC, DPPC), polymer species (1,4 PBD-b-PEO, 1,2 PBD-b-PEO, PE-b-PEO), block lengths, temperatures, and compositions. The resulting phase maps unify previously reported experimental and simulation observations and enable a generic and mechanistic understanding for the effect of system parameters on the nanoscale morphology.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a unified analytical model describing metal contacts to low-dimensional semiconductors by focusing on Metal-Induced Gap States (MIGS). It successfully links the fundamental physics of MIGS density, governed by semiconductor dimensionality, to measurable transport parameters like contact resistance and Schottky barrier height. The theory provides crucial diagnostic tools for engineering high-performance nanoelectronic devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly related to quantum information protocols, the rigorous theoretical treatment of electronic structure at interfaces—a key area in open quantum systems—provides deep insights into how external coupling modifies intrinsic material properties.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is developing a general physical theory for metal contacts to low-dimensional semiconductors, which dictates device performance in nanoelectronics.

**Main result.** The authors present an analytical model revealing universal scaling laws for Metal-Induced Gap States (MIGS) and providing unified formulations for Schottky barrier height and contact resistance across different dimensions.

**Method.** The theory uses Green's function formalism, Fermi's Golden Rule, and charge neutrality principles to derive expressions for MIGS density and transport properties.

**Model / system.** The focus is on metal-semiconductor interfaces involving low-dimensional semiconductors (1D CNTs, 2D TMDs). The model explicitly incorporates the physics of Metal-Induced Gap States (MIGS) which govern Fermi Level Pinning (FLP).

**Key observables.** Schottky barrier height ($\Phi_B$), contact resistance ($R_C$), transfer length ($L_t$), and MIGS density ($ho_X$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Semiconductor dimensionality ($n$), coupling strength ($\Gamma(E)$), defect concentration (e.g., sulfur vacancies in $	ext{MoS}_2$), and metal work function ($E_{FM}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model relies on the effective-mass approximation for the semiconductor density of states and assumes that charge conservation principles can be mapped onto the Green's function formalism, though it extends beyond simple zero-crossing criteria.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the dimensional dependence of conduction-band MIGS ($ho_c^X$) in 1D, 2D, and 3D, and show how $\Phi_B$ varies with CNT chirality or how $E_F$ de-pins when using semimetals.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing the general physical problem (lack of theory) to deriving core equations for MIGS ($ho_X$), linking these states to macroscopic observables like $\Phi_B$ and $R_C$, and finally applying this framework to specific systems (CNTs, TMDs, semimetals).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Metal contacts to low-dimensional semiconductors are critical for nanoelectronics, yet a general physical description has remained elusive. We present an analytical model for metal-induced gap states (MIGS), revealing a universal scaling law governed by semiconductor dimensionality. Linking MIGS to transport observables, we provide a unified formulation of Schottky barrier height, transfer length, and contact resistance. Our model explains recent experiments on carbon nanotubes and 2D materials, clarifying the fundamental criteria for achieving scalable, low-resistance contacts.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes solitary waves in a plasma-relevant Nonlinear Schrödinger equation with ponderomotive nonlinearity. It establishes that while certain complex structures are unstable, simple 2D solitons are stable enough to undergo collisions. The most notable finding is the prediction of transverse splitting during longitudinal soliton collisions.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rich theoretical framework for understanding nonlinear wave interactions (solitons) in physical media like plasmas, which is highly relevant to quantum optics and nonlinear wave physics often studied alongside AMO topics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the stability and collision dynamics of solitary waves and vortices governed by a Nonlinear Schrödinger equation incorporating ponderomotive nonlinearity.

**Main result.** Stable solitary waves are found in both 1D and 2D, while line solitons and vortices ($S=1, S=2$) are spectrally unstable. Collisions can result in merger, dispersion, or an intriguing transverse splitting of the solitons.

**Method.** The analysis combines spectral stability theory (using perturbation methods) with numerical simulations of head-on collisions using high-order Runge-Kutta integrators.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled by a Nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring ponderomotive nonlinearity, relevant for self-trapped laser beams in plasma. The analysis extends from 1D stationary solutions to full 2D structures like radial and vortex solitons.

**Key observables.** Soliton speed ($c$), oscillation frequency ($\omega$), topological charge ($S$), spectral growth rates ($\lambda$), and density split ratio ($R$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The parameters governing the nonlinearity strength, wave number components ($k_	heta, k_y$), and collision velocities/frequencies are crucial for determining the outcome.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes specific forms for perturbations to test stability and focuses on head-on collisions of non-topological, spectrally stable solitons.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate profiles of 1D, radial, and vortex solitons; diagrams map out collision regimes in the $(\omega, c)$ plane (e.g., trapping, dispersion); and power density plots show the evolution during specific collisions or instability growth.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically moves from establishing the governing equation and finding stationary solutions to performing detailed spectral stability analyses for different soliton types, culminating in extensive numerical simulations of collision dynamics across various parameter regimes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In the present work we revisit a ponderomotive nonlinearity model used to examine self-trapped laser beams in plasma. Upon briefly considering the exact stationary 1D solutions of the model, we extend considerations to two spatial dimensions where we find both solitonic and vortical structures. The solitary waves localized in both directions are found to be spectrally stable. However, all other structures that we consider in this model, including line solitons -- which are homogeneous 2D extensions of 1D solitons -- and vortices of topological charge S=1 and S=2 are found to be spectrally unstable. The focal point of our studies then turns to the examination of the collisions of the stable two-dimensional solitary waves for which we map a two-parameter space of soliton speeds and frequencies, in terms of the potential outcomes. While the standard scenarios of merger, inelastic collision leading to separation, separation that leaves behind a localized pulse are all possible, the intriguing outcome that we highlight here is that of a longitudinal collision yielding a transverse spliting of the solitons, either with or without a localized pulse remnant.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces SkeleGen, a novel computational framework that overcomes the limitations of cataloged crystal motifs by treating flat-band connectivity as a continuous geometric property. By using symmetry-aware generative models guided by latent space analysis, the authors successfully designed and screened thousands of chemically plausible materials predicted to host exotic flat electronic bands.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on solid-state physics, the methodology—using generative AI (diffusion/GNN) constrained by fundamental physical symmetries to explore vast chemical spaces—is highly relevant for designing quantum materials with specific electronic properties.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The design of flat electronic bands for strongly correlated and topological phenomena is limited by a small, known catalogue of geometric crystal motifs.

**Main result.** The authors developed SkeleGen to generate 9,352 novel, stable crystal candidates that retain the desired flat-band character traceable to unconventional sublattices.

**Method.** A symmetry-aware generative model (SkeleGen) combines continuous geometric representation with structural constraints derived from Graph Neural Networks trained on sublattice embeddings.

**Model / system.** The focus is on electronic band structure arising from specific lattice connectivity patterns, modeled by identifying and embedding 'flat-band skeletons' within larger crystal structures. Validation involves high-throughput DFT calculations.

**Key observables.** Band flatness (dispersionless bands), Novelty score ($	ext{S}_{	ext{novelty}}$), Flatness score ($S_{	ext{total}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** DFT calculation parameters (PBEsol functional, PAW potentials); Latent space thresholds (e.g., 50th percentile for novelty).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The electronic properties are primarily determined by the connectivity of the underlying sublattice skeleton, allowing a geometric design principle to guide material discovery.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the workflow: mapping known vs. unexplored latent space regions (UMAP), detailing the four-step constrained generation pipeline (SkeleGen), and showing representative candidates with their derived band structures.

**Paper structure.** The paper follows a progression from identifying the limitation of existing motifs to developing a continuous geometric representation via GNNs, generating novel skeletons using SkeleGen under symmetry constraints, and finally validating these generated structures through high-throughput DFT calculations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Flat electronic bands underlie a range of strongly correlated and topological phenomena, whose design in real materials has so far relied on a small catalogue of named geometric motifs such as kagome, Lieb, and pyrochlore nets. This discrete catalogue is by no means to exhaust the geometries that support flat bands in real compounds, as band flatness is a property of network connectivity. Here we combine a continuous geometric representation of crystal sublattices, with a symmetry-constrained generative model, to access a broader design space for materials hosting flat bands. The key step is to choose sublattice motifs that are outside the known geometric clusters, ensuring the novelty of the generated structures. We then introduce SkeleGen, which pins these unconventional skeletons to symmetry-compatible Wyckoff positions while denoising the surrounding chemistry, resulting in 9,352 crystal candidates that survive stability and flatnessscreening. Band flatness is confirmed using high throughput full DFT calculations, which agree well also with the tight-binding spectra of the isolated skeletons, supporting a geometric origin of the band flatness. We demonstrate "out-of-distribution" motifs as a new design principle to dramatically expand geometric repertoire for materials discovery, potentially beyond flat bands.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work develops a model for helical carbon coil microwave absorbers, treating an intermediate anchoring layer as a tunable parameter. By optimizing the thickness of this layer using impedance matching principles, the authors demonstrate a significant enhancement in microwave absorption efficiency. This provides practical design guidelines for high-performance metamaterial absorbers.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on microwave engineering, the use of effective medium theory, boundary condition matching (impedance tuning), and modeling complex material interfaces is relevant to open quantum systems where coupling to external environments or structured media dictates energy dissipation/coupling rates.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to enhance microwave absorption efficiency in helical carbon coil (HCC) absorbers by optimizing impedance matching.

**Main result.** Introducing a carbon-based anchoring layer with an optimized thickness significantly enhances the impedance-matched absorption of microwaves at specific frequencies.

**Method.** The study employs a coarse-grained electrodynamic model and transmission-line framework to calculate reflection and absorption fractions across different layered structures.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a microwave absorber composed of helical carbon coils on a quartz substrate, modeled as a multilayer structure: Air $ightarrow$ HCC active layer $ightarrow$ Tunable Anchoring layer $ightarrow$ Substrate. The model uses effective medium theory and impedance matching principles.

**Key observables.** Absorption fraction (A), Reflection coefficient (R), Input Impedance ($Z_{in}$)

**Important parameters / regimes.** Anchoring layer thickness ($d_a$), Frequency range (2 to 18 GHz), Effective refractive index ($n_{eff}$)

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model uses a coarse-grained effective medium approximation, and initial analyses neglect the contribution of the chiral parameter ($\kappa$) for simplification.

**Figures summary.** Figure 2 shows absorption/reflection vs. HCC thickness for bare structures; Figure 3 demonstrates that varying the anchoring layer thickness ($d_a$) leads to maximal absorption at an optimal value (e.g., $\approx 4.7$ mm).

**Paper structure.** The paper develops a layered electromagnetic model, calculates input impedance using transmission-line theory, and then systematically varies the anchoring layer thickness as a tunable parameter to maximize absorption.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Helical carbon coils exhibit unique three dimensional chiral architectures that can effectively interact with microwaves in the 2 to 18 GHz range. Inspired by recent experimental studies, we develop a coarse grained electrodynamic model for helical carbon coil arrays supported on quartz substrates, and examine their potential as microwave absorbers. Guided by the heuristic relation $f_{\mathrm{res}} = c / (n_{\mathrm{eff}} p)$, we compute absorption and reflection fractions for both bare helical carbon coil on substrate and helical carbon coil with anchoring layer on substrate configurations. The anchoring layer thickness is treated as a tunable parameter to improve absorption at selected frequencies. We find that the introduction of a carbon based anchoring layer of optimized thickness enhances impedance matching absorption. The parameters are chosen as representative values for demonstration purposes, and may vary within a certain range depending on preparation conditions. Our results serve to illustrate the potential of helical carbon coils as microwave absorbing devices, and to identify possible active tuning strategies. In the discussion section, we consider extensions of the present model to account for circular dichroism absorption, and examine the influence of actual interfacial reflection on microwave absorption and reflection.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a comprehensive modulation theory to describe how stable, localized 'lumps' of solutions interact within the two-dimensional Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation. By deriving and analyzing an integrable hyperbolic system governing these modulations, the authors provide quantitative predictions for whether a lump will pass through or become trapped by a background mean field wave.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical nonlinear PDEs, the mathematical techniques—such as deriving integrable modulation equations for localized structures—share conceptual parallels with effective theories used in quantum field theory or semiclassical approximations in AMO physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research aims to develop a modulation theory for localized structures called 'lumps' within the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili (KP) equation when these lumps interact with a slowly varying mean field.

**Main result.** The authors derived precise theoretical predictions describing how lump parameters change during interactions, successfully predicting both transmission and trapping scenarios based on initial conditions.

**Method.** The approach involves deriving a hyperbolic modulation system from integral identities, testing its integrability using the Haantjes tensor test, and solving resulting ODEs via method of characteristics.

**Model / system.** The primary model is the (2+1)-dimensional Kadomtsev-Petviashvili I (KPI) equation. The analysis focuses on the modulation of stable, localized rational solutions (lumps) interacting with a mean field governed by the dispersionless KP (dKP) equation.

**Key observables.** Lump parameters ($a, q$), final amplitude ($A_{out}$), phase shift ($\delta$), and the time evolution of these quantities during interaction.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The small parameter $\epsilon$ used in the multiple scale ansatz; initial lump amplitudes ($A_0$) and transverse wave numbers ($q_0$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the assumption that the mean field satisfies the dKP equation, and it treats the modulation as a slow evolution process ($\epsilon \ll 1$).

**Figures summary.** Figures compare analytical predictions of lump amplitude $a(t)$ against numerical measurements for transmission/trapping cases, and show time evolution plots for parameters like $q(t)$.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from deriving the governing four-component hyperbolic modulation system (2.19) to proving its integrability, analyzing specific reductions (e.g., $Y$-independent), and finally applying these tools to solve the physical problem of lump interaction with a rarefaction wave.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

A (2+1)-dimensional hyperbolic system of four quasi-linear partial differential equations is derived that describes the modulations of lump solutions of the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili I (KPI) equation in the presence of a mean field. The system is then shown to satisfy the necessary conditions for integrability of hydrodynamic chains. Moreover, a suitable reduction of the resulting modulation system is applied to study the interactions between lumps and a rarefaction wave for the mean field. Precise conditions are derived that describe how the lump parameters change as a result of the interaction, and which in particular determine whether the lump is transmitted through or trapped inside the rarefaction wave. The theoretical predictions are compared to direct numerical simulations of the KPI equation, showing excellent agreement.

</details>

**Summary.** This work presents a novel, highly localized technique for measuring pyroelectric coefficients in van der Waals nanogenerators using Scanning Thermal Microscopy. By employing harmonic detection and finite-element modeling, the researchers successfully separated the intrinsic thermal response from parasitic electrical effects. This method provides unprecedented spatial resolution to map local performance limitations within these advanced energy harvesting devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on solid-state physics, the rigorous application of localized thermal probing combined with harmonic signal processing shares methodological parallels with techniques used to probe local energy dissipation or coupling mechanisms in quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a method for direct nanoscale pyroelectric characterization of van der Waals nanogenerators, overcoming limitations associated with conventional spatially averaged measurements.

**Main result.** The authors successfully established a versatile platform using SThM and harmonic detection to quantitatively measure the local pyroelectric coefficient ($p$) in $	ext{CuInP}_2	ext{S}_6$ devices while resolving nanoscale defects.

**Method.** The technique combines Scanning Thermal Microscopy (SThM) as a localized heat source with lock-in detection, utilizing harmonic analysis to isolate the second-harmonic pyroelectric signal from parasitic first-harmonic electromechanical contributions.

**Model / system.** The physical system is an out-of-plane van der Waals capacitor made of $	ext{CuInP}_2	ext{S}_6$ (CIPS) sandwiched between few-layer graphene electrodes. The analysis involves both electrical measurements and finite-element thermal modeling to determine the local pyroelectric coefficient.

**Key observables.** Pyroelectric voltage signal ($\Delta V$) measured at $2\omega$, localized pyroelectric coefficient ($p$), temperature distribution ($\Delta T$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Local pyroelectric coefficient range of $1.91$ to $11.25 \mu	ext{C m}^{-2} 	ext{K}^{-1}$; device thickness $\sim 220-260 	ext{ nm}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method assumes that harmonic analysis can perfectly separate the pyroelectric signal from electromechanical artifacts, and FEA models rely on accurate material properties like thermal conductivity.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the SThM setup, frequency dependence of signals (showing $2\omega$ vs. $1\omega$), spatial maps revealing defects, and FEA simulations comparing temperature profiles when the tip contacts graphene versus CIPS.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the physical basis for pyroelectric energy harvesting to detailing the advanced SThM measurement technique (harmonic separation), presenting quantitative results for $p$, and finally using thermal modeling to interpret the role of electrode contact in heat transfer.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Pyroelectric energy conversion offers a route for harvesting time-dependent thermalfluctuations that are abundant in natural and technological environments. Twodimensional ferroelectrics are particularly attractive for this purpose because reduced dimensionality enables ultrathin, mechanically compliant device architectures. Here, we demonstrate direct nanoscale pyroelectric characterization of an out-of-plane van der Waals nanogenerator based on CuInP2S6 (CIPS) encapsulated between few-layer graphene electrodes. A scanning thermal microscopy (SThM) probe is employed as a localized nanoscale heat source while the electrically generated response is measured in situ through the device electrodes. Harmonic detection isolates the pyroelectric signal from parasitic first-harmonic electromechanical contributions, while finite-element thermal modeling combined with probe calibration enables direct determination of the local pyroelectric coefficient from the measured electrical response. Beyond quantitative characterization, the spatially resolved measurements directly identify electrically inactive regions associated with device defects, revealing local performance-limiting features that remain hidden in conventional spatially averaged pyroelectric measurements. The presented approach establishes a versatile platform for quantitative nanoscale pyroelectric characterization and the optimization of van der Waals pyroelectric devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a robust machine learning framework to solve the inverse design problem in milling, aiming to find process parameters that yield specific target surface roughness. It trains Deep Neural Networks and Random Forests on simulated data and uses Bayesian Optimization to navigate the complex parameter space. The methodology demonstrates high accuracy by successfully identifying multiple feasible solutions for desired surface quality.

**Why it may be interesting.** While applied to mechanical engineering, the methodology—using complex physical simulations to generate training data for deep learning surrogate models, followed by optimization in an ill-posed inverse problem—is highly relevant to developing physics-informed machine learning tools for quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is performing inverse design for surface milling processes: determining optimal machining and tool parameters required to achieve a target surface roughness.

**Main result.** A machine learning framework combining DNNs/RFs with Bayesian Optimization successfully identifies multiple feasible process configurations, achieving low average relative errors (below 5%) compared to reference simulations.

**Method.** The authors train ML models on high-fidelity synthetic datasets generated from computational fluid dynamics simulations and then use these trained models within a Bayesian Optimization loop to solve the ill-posed inverse problem.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a face milling process involving an indexable cutter. The model relies on generating synthetic data by simulating cutting-edge motion over time/space using complex coordinate transformations, treating components as rigid bodies.

**Key observables.** Average surface roughness (Sa) and maximum surface height (Sz).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Cutting speed ($v_c$), feed rate ($f_z$), number of inserts ($z$), insert radius ($r_i$), radial run-out ($\epsilon_r$), and axial run-out ($\epsilon_a$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The ML performance is highly dependent on the quality of the synthetic training dataset, and the computational model disregards material properties.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate 3D surface topographies, convergence plots for optimization (DNN/RF), parity plots comparing predicted vs. actual roughness values, and visualizations of the solution space across different target regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the need for inverse design in manufacturing. It details generating synthetic data via simulation, trains DNN and RF models on this data, analyzes the inherent many-to-one mapping challenge, and finally integrates these ML surrogates into a Bayesian Optimization framework to propose optimal parameter sets.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Interest in applying data-driven approaches in manufacturing has grown significantly, particularly for mapping complex, high-dimensional relationships. The milling process is one area where predictive models can link influential parameters to surface roughness metrics prior to in situ operations. While this approach offers clear advantages, it faces challenges due to limited datasets and robustness issues in inverse design paradigms. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a machine learning (ML)-based framework for the inverse design of the surface milling process, with a focus on surface roughness as the design objective. The framework employs forward training of two ML models, a deep neural network (DNN) and a random forest (RF) ensemble, both developed using a high-fidelity synthetic dataset generated from a computational simulation framework. These trained models are integrated into a Bayesian optimization (BO) procedure to overcome the multiplicity problem arising from the many-to-one mapping inherent in the dataset. The approach identifies top-performing milling process configurations, considering both process and tool parameters, and presents them from the full solution space. The models achieve average relative errors below 5% when compared to reference results, thereby demonstrating the robustness and reliability of the proposed methodology.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates the source of current-induced torques in alpha-W/ferromagnet interfaces using advanced, artifact-free experimental setups. By analyzing ST-FMR data across varying W thicknesses, the authors conclude that the torque is overwhelmingly dominated by the Spin Hall Effect and that orbital contributions are negligible. This challenges existing theoretical models regarding universal orbital currents in such systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** While primarily condensed matter physics, understanding spin-orbit torque mechanisms is crucial for spintronics devices which can interface with quantum computing components or novel memory elements. The rigorous elimination of artifacts provides a cleaner benchmark for fundamental material properties.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to clarify the physical origin of current-induced torque (Spin-Orbit Torque, SOT) in alpha-W/ferromagnet heterostructures by determining whether it is dominated by the Spin Hall Effect (SHE) or the Orbital Hall Effect.

**Main result.** The spin-orbit torque from W remains negative and is predominantly due to the SHE across all measured thicknesses, suggesting that the orbital Hall torque contribution from alpha-W is negligible.

**Method.** The authors used fabricated, artifact-free angular momentum detectors (Cu/Ni/Cu and Cu/FeCoB/Cu) combined with Spin-Torque Ferromagnetic Resonance (ST-FMR) measurements to quantify torque efficiencies.

**Model / system.** The research focuses on $\alpha$-W/ferromagnet heterostructures, specifically using multilayers like Cu/Ni/Cu/W and Cu/FeCoB/Cu/W. The system involves analyzing the structural phase transition of W from beta-W to alpha-W.

**Key observables.** Damping-like torque efficiency ($\xi_{DL}^j$), field-like torque efficiency ($\xi_{FL}^j$), Spin Hall Conductivity ($\sigma_{SH}$), and Orbital Hall Conductivity ($\sigma_{OH}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** W thickness ($t_W$), particularly the transition regime around 5 nm, and the magnetic properties of the ferromagnet layers.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that using specific detector geometries (Cu/Ni/Cu etc.) successfully eliminates artifact torques such as self-induced torque and spin-vorticity torque.

**Figures summary.** Figures show theoretical calculations of Hall conductivities, ST-FMR spectra vs. field for varying W thickness, and plots detailing the monotonic decay of damping-like torque efficiency correlated with structural phase transitions.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the problem regarding SOT origins in $\alpha$-W/ferromagnet systems. It then presents experimental measurements using specialized detectors to quantify torques as a function of W thickness, leading to the conclusion that SHE dominates and orbital contributions are negligible.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

α-phased W was theoretically predicted to have a negative spin Hall conductivity and a positive orbital Hall conductivity at the same time, leaving the physical origin of the current-induced torque a critical open question. Here, we develop two angular momentum detectors of Cu/Ni/Cu and Cu/FeCoB/Cu that are free of artifacts torques (e.g., self-induced torque and spin-vorticity torque) and clarify that the spin-orbit torque contributed by W remains negative and predominantly from the spin Hall effect in the entire thickness regime. With both detectors, the damping-like torque exhibits a monotonic decay as the W thickness increases above 5 nm, which results from the structural phase transition from \b{eta}-W to α-W. The negative torque in the entire thickness regime suggests negligible orbital Hall torque and orbital current from the α-W. This result is consistent with the theory that the orbital Hall effect from simplified band structure calculations is not a non-local angular momentum source. These findings suggest poor generality or even universal absence of orbital current.

</details>

**Summary.** The study uses first-principles calculations to investigate rare-earth doped nickelates ($	ext{La}_2	ext{R}	ext{Ni}_2	ext{O}_7$) as model superconductors. It demonstrates that doping and pressure induce structural transitions accompanied by key electronic changes, such as the formation of flat $d_{z^2}$ bands at the Fermi level. These findings provide a microscopic understanding of how chemical tuning affects superconductivity in these correlated materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides detailed first-principles insights into how subtle chemical substitutions (R-doping) can tune electronic correlations and structural instabilities, which is a key area of research relevant to understanding unconventional superconductivity mechanisms.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To systematically explore how rare-earth (R) doping affects the crystal structure and electronic properties of Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) nickelates, specifically $	ext{La}_2	ext{R}	ext{Ni}_2	ext{O}_7$, in relation to superconductivity.

**Main result.** The study finds that R-doping causes a progressive decrease in volume and an increase in planar hopping while decreasing out-of-plane hopping, and a pressure-induced structural transition to tetragonal symmetry coincides with the emergence of superconducting electronic features (flat $d_{z^2}$ bands).

**Method.** First-principles calculations using PBE GGA+U functional were employed to optimize structures and analyze electronic band structures and hopping parameters.

**Model / system.** The physical system is the bilayer RP nickelate superconductor $	ext{La}_2	ext{R}	ext{Ni}_2	ext{O}_7$ ($	ext{R} = 	ext{Pr}, 	ext{Nd}, 	ext{Sm}$), studied under varying chemical doping and hydrostatic pressure.

**Key observables.** Crystal structure symmetry ($P2_1/m$ vs $I4/mmm$), lattice parameters, planar/out-of-plane hopping integrals, and the emergence of flat $d_{z^2}$ bands at the Fermi level.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Rare-earth element identity (R), doping concentration, and applied pressure (e.g., 9.5 GPa to 20.5 GPa).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The calculations use GGA+U approximation for Ni-$3d$ states; the connection between structural/electronic changes and $T_c$ is inferred from theoretical trends.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate crystal structures, lattice parameter changes with pressure/doping, and electronic band structures showing the emergence of hole-like $	ext{d}_{z^2}$ pockets at high pressure.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares the structural and electronic properties across different R dopants ($	ext{Pr}, 	ext{Nd}, 	ext{Sm}$) under ambient and high pressures, linking observed changes in hopping parameters and band structure to the superconducting phase transition.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The discovery of superconductivity in bilayer La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ under pressure has sparked tremendous attention on Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) nickelates. Recently, a higher superconducting transition temperature of 96 K was reported in Sm-doped La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ single crystals at $\sim$ 22 GPa. Motivated by this experimental observation, we systematically explore the crystal structure and electronic properties of La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ doped with different rare-earth elements in comparison to the undoped counterpart. As expected due to the effect of chemical pressure, we find that the volume of La$_{2}$$R$Ni$_2$O$_7$ ($R=$ Pr, Nd, Sm) progressively decreases with doping from Pr to Sm. We further find a pressure-induced structural transition to tetragonal symmetry that approximately coincides with the emergence of superconductivity in all cases. This transition is characterized by the emergence of flat $d_{z^2}$ bands at the Fermi level in the electronic structure. Despite subtle distinctions in the electronic structure between undoped and $R$-doped La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$, an increase in the dominant planar hopping is obtained as the $R$ size decreases. In contrast, the out-of-plane hopping decreases (in spite of the $c$ lattice constant compression), due to the decrease in the apical Ni-O$_{\rm rocksalt}$ bond length. Our findings provide further microscopic insights into the effects of $R$-doping in the electronic structure of RP nickelate superconductors in connection to $T_c$.

</details>

**Summary.** This research successfully optimized Fe2VAl-based thermoelectric materials using high-entropy engineering to achieve extremely low thermal conductivity. By fabricating and testing a large, multi-leg module, the authors demonstrated record conversion efficiencies for this material class, proving its potential for scalable energy harvesting applications.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly related to quantum phenomena, the focus on disorder engineering to suppress lattice vibrations ($\kappa_L$) is conceptually related to minimizing energy dissipation mechanisms studied in condensed matter theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing thermoelectric (TE) materials that combine high efficiency with favorable secondary properties like low cost, non-toxicity, and scalability for practical energy harvesting.

**Main result.** A fabricated 36-leg TE module based on Fe2VAl-based full-Heusler compounds achieved a record-high conversion efficiency of 1.2% at a temperature difference of 375 K without requiring nanostructuring.

**Method.** The study utilized high-entropy engineering via heavy-element doping and controlled off-stoichiometry, followed by hot pressing for large-scale synthesis and direct brazing into functional TE modules.

**Model / system.** The physical system is the Fe2VAl-based full-Heusler compound. Performance optimization relies on inducing substitutional disorder through high-entropy alloying to achieve an ultra-low lattice thermal conductivity (kappa_L ~ 2.3 W m^-1 K^-1).

**Key observables.** Figure of Merit (zT), average zT (~0.3 from 300-500 K), output power, and conversion efficiency.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature range (300–673 K), lattice thermal conductivity (kappa_L), and the degree of substitutional disorder achieved via doping/off-stoichiometry.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The study assumes that high entropy engineering can simultaneously optimize electronic transport (high PF) and minimize thermal transport ($\kappa_L$) in a mechanically robust manner, avoiding complex nanostructuring techniques.

**Figures summary.** Figures summarize the optimization of TE properties using heavy-element co-substitution across different material compositions and show comparative performance data for fabricated modules over temperature ranges.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the need for practical TE materials to detailing the high-entropy engineering approach, presenting synthesis methods (hot pressing), characterizing electrical/thermal properties, and culminating in the fabrication and testing of a large-scale module.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Thermoelectric (TE) materials enable the direct conversion of heat into electricity and are attractive for sustainable energy applications. For practical deployment, TE materials must combine high efficiency with low cost, non-toxicity, and scalability. In this work, we optimize the TE performance of low-cost and robust Fe$_2$VAl-based full-Heusler compounds through high-entropy engineering: a synergistic combination of heavy-element doping and controlled off-stoichiometry results in substitutional disorder on all lattice sites, triggering one of the lowest lattice thermal conductivities, $κ_\text{L}\sim2.3$ W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, reported so far for full-Heusler systems. The resulting materials exhibit improved values of the average figure of merit $zT_\text{ave}\approx 0.3$ from $300-500$ K. To demonstrate reproducibility and technological relevance, a full TE module (TEM) based on the optimized alloys was fabricated and characterized. Scaled-up material batches were synthesized by hot pressing, exhibiting TE properties in excellent agreement with laboratory-scale samples, with only slightly increased resistivities in absence of post-annealing treatments. Owing to the excellent mechanical workability of Fe$_2$VAl-based materials, the TEM legs were directly brazed onto copper electrodes, enabling robust module fabrication. A ($6\times 6$)-leg TEM was assembled and systematically characterized. The device exhibits the highest output power and one of the highest conversion efficiencies reported to date for Fe$_2$VAl-based generators over the broad temperature range of $300-673$ K, underscoring the potential of this material system for scalable TE energy harvesting.

</details>
